Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York; / And all the clouds that lour'd upon our house / In the deep bosom of the ocean buried. / Now are our brows bound with victorious wreaths; / Our bruised arms hung up for monuments; / Our stern alarums chang'd to merry meetings, / Our dreadful marches to delightful measures. / Grim-visag'd war hath smooth'd his wrinkled front; / And now,--instead of mounting barbed steeds / To fright the souls of fearful adversaries,-- / He capers nimbly in a lady's chamber / To the lascivious pleasing of a lute. / But I,--that am not shap'd for sportive tricks, / Nor made to court an amorous looking-glass; / I, that am rudely stamp'd, and want love's majesty / To strut before a wanton ambling nymph; / I, that am curtail'd of this fair proportion, / Cheated of feature by dissembling nature, / Deform'd, unfinish'd, sent before my time / Into this breathing world scarce half made up, / And that so lamely and unfashionable / That dogs bark at me as I halt by them;-- / Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace, / Have no delight to pass away the time, / Unless to spy my shadow in the sun, / And descant on mine own deformity: / And therefore,--since I cannot prove a lover, / To entertain these fair well-spoken days,-- / I am determined to prove a villain, / And hate the idle pleasures of these days. / Plots have I laid, inductions dangerous, / By drunken prophecies, libels, and dreams, / To set my brother Clarence and the king / In deadly hate the one against the other: / And if King Edward be as true and just / As I am subtle, false, and treacherous, / This day should Clarence closely be mew'd up,-- / About a prophecy which says that G / Of Edward's heirs the murderer shall be. / Dive, thoughts, down to my soul:--here Clarence comes.

Now the bleak winter of our troubles has turned into glorious summer under this sun of York, King Edward, and every cloud that hung over our family lies buried deep in the ocean. Now we wear victory wreaths, our battered armour hangs up as trophies, our war alarms have turned into parties and our grim marches into dances. War itself has smoothed its frowning face; instead of riding armoured horses to terrify the enemy, he skips about in ladies' bedrooms to the sexy music of a lute. But I am not built for these games, or for admiring myself in a mirror. I was roughly made, without the good looks to strut in front of a flirtatious girl. Nature cheated me of a proper shape: deformed, unfinished, born too early and barely half made, so lame and awkward that dogs bark at me as I limp past. So in this feeble, piping time of peace I have nothing to enjoy except watching my shadow in the sun and making up songs about my own deformity. And since I can't be a lover in these pleasant days, I am determined to be a villain and hate the empty pleasures of the age. I have laid plots and dangerous first moves, using drunken prophecies, libels and dreams, to set my brother Clarence and the King against each other in deadly hatred. If King Edward is as honest and fair as I am cunning, false and treacherous, Clarence will be locked up today, because of a prophecy that someone called G will murder Edward's heirs. Sink down into my soul, thoughts: here comes Clarence.
Brother, good day: what means this armed guard / That waits upon your grace?
Good day, brother. Why is there an armed guard with you?
His majesty, / Tendering my person's safety, hath appointed / This conduct to convey me to the Tower.
The King, out of concern for my safety, has appointed this escort to take me to the Tower.

Alack, my lord, that fault is none of yours; / He should, for that, commit your godfathers:-- / O, belike his majesty hath some intent / That you should be new-christen'd in the Tower. / But what's the matter, Clarence? may I know?
That's not your fault, my lord; he should lock up your godfathers instead. Perhaps the King means to have you re-baptised in the Tower. But what's really going on, Clarence? Can I know?

Yea, Richard, when I know; for I protest / As yet I do not: but, as I can learn, / He hearkens after prophecies and dreams; / And from the cross-row plucks the letter G, / And says a wizard told him that by G / His issue disinherited should be; / And, for my name of George begins with G, / It follows in his thought that I am he. / These, as I learn, and such like toys as these, / Hath mov'd his highness to commit me now.

Yes, Richard, once I know myself; I swear I don't yet. But as far as I can tell, he listens to prophecies and dreams. He has picked the letter G out of the alphabet and says a wizard told him that G will cut his children out of the succession. And because George begins with G, he concludes I'm the man. That and nonsense like it, I hear, has led him to imprison me.

Why, this it is when men are rul'd by women:-- / 'Tis not the king that sends you to the Tower; / My Lady Grey his wife, Clarence, 'tis she / That tempers him to this extremity. / Was it not she and that good man of worship, / Antony Woodville, her brother there, / That made him send Lord Hastings to the Tower, / From whence this present day he is deliver'd? / We are not safe, Clarence; we are not safe.

This is what happens when men are ruled by women. It isn't the King sending you to the Tower; it's his wife, Lady Grey, who pushes him to these extremes. Wasn't it she and her worthy brother Anthony Woodville who had Lord Hastings sent to the Tower, from which he is released today? We aren't safe, Clarence, we aren't safe.

By heaven, I think there is no man is secure / But the queen's kindred, and night-walking heralds / That trudge betwixt the king and Mistress Shore. / Heard you not what an humble suppliant / Lord Hastings was to her for his delivery?
I swear nobody is safe except the Queen's relatives and the night messengers who run between the King and Mistress Shore. Didn't you hear how humbly Lord Hastings begged her for his release?

Humbly complaining to her deity / Got my Lord Chamberlain his liberty. / I'll tell you what,--I think it is our way, / If we will keep in favour with the king, / To be her men and wear her livery: / The jealous o'er-worn widow, and herself, / Since that our brother dubb'd them gentlewomen, / Are mighty gossips in our monarchy.

By humbly pleading with that goddess, the Lord Chamberlain got his freedom. I'll tell you what: if we want to stay in the King's favour, we'd better become her servants and wear her uniform. The jealous, worn-out widow and Mistress Shore, ever since our brother made them ladies, are powerful gossips in our kingdom.
I beseech your graces both to pardon me; / His majesty hath straitly given in charge / That no man shall have private conference, / Of what degree soever, with your brother.
Please forgive me, your graces, but the King has strictly ordered that no one, whatever his rank, is to talk privately with your brother.

Even so; an't please your worship, Brakenbury, / You may partake of any thing we say: / We speak no treason, man;--we say the king / Is wise and virtuous; and his noble queen / Well struck in years, fair, and not jealous;-- / We say that Shore's wife hath a pretty foot, / A cherry lip, a bonny eye, a passing pleasing tongue; / And that the queen's kindred are made gentlefolks: / How say you, sir? can you deny all this?

Fine. If it please your worship, Brakenbury, you can share in anything we say. We speak no treason. We say the King is wise and good, his noble queen is getting on in years, beautiful and not jealous; we say Shore's wife has a pretty foot, cherry lips, lovely eyes and a very pleasing tongue, and that the Queen's relatives have been made gentry. What do you say, sir? Can you deny any of it?
With this, my lord, myself have naught to do.
I have nothing to do with any of this, my lord.
Naught to do with Mistress Shore! I tell thee, fellow, / He that doth naught with her, excepting one, / Were best to do it secretly alone.
Nothing to do with Mistress Shore? I tell you, fellow, anyone who does anything with her, except one man, had better do it secretly and alone.
Her husband, knave:--wouldst thou betray me?
Her husband, you rogue. Are you trying to trap me?
I do beseech your grace to pardon me; and, withal, / Forbear your conference with the noble duke.
Please forgive me, your grace, and at the same time stop talking to the noble duke.
We know thy charge, Brakenbury, and will obey.
We know your orders, Brakenbury, and will obey.

We are the queen's abjects and must obey.-- / Brother, farewell: I will unto the king; / And whatsoe'er you will employ me in,-- / Were it to call King Edward's widow sister,-- / I will perform it to enfranchise you. / Meantime, this deep disgrace in brotherhood / Touches me deeper than you can imagine.

We are the Queen's lowest servants and must obey. Farewell, brother. I'll go to the King, and whatever you want me to do, even calling King Edward's widow-bride "sister", I'll do it to free you. Meanwhile this disgrace between brothers hurts me more than you can imagine.
I know it pleaseth neither of us well.
I know neither of us likes it.
Well, your imprisonment shall not be long; / I will deliver or else lie for you: / Meantime, have patience.
Well, your imprisonment won't be long. I'll free you or take your place. Meanwhile, be patient.

Go tread the path that thou shalt ne'er return. / Simple, plain Clarence!--I do love thee so / That I will shortly send thy soul to heaven, / If heaven will take the present at our hands.-- / But who comes here? The new-delivered Hastings?

Go down the road you'll never come back along. Simple, honest Clarence! I love you so much I'll soon send your soul to heaven, if heaven will accept a gift from me. But who's this? The newly freed Hastings?
Good time of day unto my gracious lord!
Good day to my gracious lord.
As much unto my good Lord Chamberlain! / Well are you welcome to the open air. / How hath your lordship brook'd imprisonment?
And to my good Lord Chamberlain. Welcome back to the open air. How did your lordship put up with prison?
With patience, noble lord, as prisoners must; / But I shall live, my lord, to give them thanks / That were the cause of my imprisonment.
Patiently, my lord, as prisoners must. But I'll live to thank the people who put me there.
No doubt, no doubt; and so shall Clarence too; / For they that were your enemies are his, / And have prevail'd as much on him as you.
No doubt, and so will Clarence; your enemies are his too and have done as well against him as against you.
More pity that the eagles should be mew'd / Whiles kites and buzzards prey at liberty.
It's a pity that eagles are caged while kites and buzzards hunt freely.
No news so bad abroad as this at home,-- / The king is sickly, weak, and melancholy, / And his physicians fear him mightily.
No news out there is as bad as this at home: the King is sick, weak and depressed, and his doctors are very worried about him.
Now, by Saint Paul, that news is bad indeed. / O, he hath kept an evil diet long, / And overmuch consum'd his royal person: / 'Tis very grievous to be thought upon. / What, is he in his bed?
By Saint Paul, that is bad news. He has lived unhealthily for a long time and worn out his royal body with excess. It's sad to think of. Is he in bed?
Go you before, and I will follow you.
Go ahead and I'll follow you.

He cannot live, I hope; and must not die / Till George be pack'd with posthorse up to heaven. / I'll in, to urge his hatred more to Clarence / With lies well steel'd with weighty arguments; / And, if I fail not in my deep intent, / Clarence hath not another day to live; / Which done, God take King Edward to his mercy, / And leave the world for me to bustle in! / For then I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter: / What though I kill'd her husband and her father? / The readiest way to make the wench amends / Is to become her husband and her father: / The which will I; not all so much for love / As for another secret close intent, / By marrying her, which I must reach unto. / But yet I run before my horse to market: / Clarence still breathes; Edward still lives and reigns: / When they are gone, then must I count my gains.

He can't live, I hope, but he mustn't die until George has been rushed off to heaven. I'll go in and stir his hatred of Clarence with well-armed lies, and if my plan works, Clarence hasn't another day to live. Then God can take King Edward and leave the world for me to bustle in. Then I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter. So what if I killed her husband and her father-in-law? The quickest way to make it up to the girl is to become her husband and her father myself. I'll do it, not so much for love as for another secret purpose I can reach by marrying her. But I'm getting ahead of myself. Clarence still breathes, Edward still lives and reigns. When they're gone, then I'll count my profits.

Set down, set down your honourable load,-- / If honour may be shrouded in a hearse,-- / Whilst I awhile obsequiously lament / Th' untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster.-- / Poor key-cold figure of a holy king! / Pale ashes of the house of Lancaster! / Thou bloodless remnant of that royal blood! / Be it lawful that I invocate thy ghost, / To hear the lamentations of poor Anne, / Wife to thy Edward, to thy slaughter'd son, / Stabb'd by the self-same hand that made these wounds! / Lo, in these windows that let forth thy life, / I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes:-- / O, cursed be the hand that made these holes! / Cursed the heart that had the heart to do it! / Cursed the blood that let this blood from hence! / More direful hap betide that hated wretch / That makes us wretched by the death of thee, / Than I can wish to adders, spiders, toads, / Or any creeping venom'd thing that lives! / If ever he have child, abortive be it, / Prodigious, and untimely brought to light, / Whose ugly and unnatural aspect / May fright the hopeful mother at the view; / And that be heir to his unhappiness! / If ever he have wife, let her be made / More miserable by the death of him / Than I am made by my young lord and thee!-- / Come, now towards Chertsey with your holy load, / Taken from Paul's to be interred there; / And still, as you are weary of this weight, / Rest you, whiles I lament King Henry's corse.

Set down your honourable burden, if honour can be wrapped in a coffin, while I mourn for a while the early death of virtuous Lancaster. Poor stone-cold body of a holy king, pale ashes of the house of Lancaster, bloodless remains of royal blood! May I call on your ghost to hear the laments of poor Anne, wife of your son Edward, murdered by the same hand that made these wounds. Into these wounds that let out your life I pour the useless balm of my tears. Cursed be the hand that made these holes, the heart that had the nerve to do it, the blood that let this blood out! May a worse fate fall on that hated wretch who makes us wretched by your death than I could wish on adders, spiders, toads or any creeping poisonous thing. If he ever has a child, may it be born early, monstrous, so ugly and unnatural that its hopeful mother is terrified at the sight, and may it inherit his evil. If he ever has a wife, may his death make her more miserable than I am made by the deaths of my young husband and you. Come, take your holy burden on towards Chertsey, from St Paul's where it was brought to be buried there. And whenever you're tired of the weight, rest while I mourn over King Henry's body.
Stay, you that bear the corse, and set it down.
Stop, you who carry the body, and put it down.
What black magician conjures up this fiend, / To stop devoted charitable deeds?
What black magician has called up this devil to interrupt a holy act of charity?
Villains, set down the corse; or, by Saint Paul, / I'll make a corse of him that disobeys!
Villains, put down the body, or by Saint Paul I'll make a body of anyone who disobeys.
My lord, stand back, and let the coffin pass.
My lord, stand back and let the coffin pass.
Unmanner'd dog! stand thou, when I command: / Advance thy halberd higher than my breast, / Or, by Saint Paul, I'll strike thee to my foot / And spurn upon thee, beggar, for thy boldness.
Rude dog! Stand still when I order you. Raise your spear away from my chest, or by Saint Paul I'll knock you down and trample you, you beggar, for your cheek.

What, do you tremble? are you all afraid? / Alas, I blame you not; for you are mortal, / And mortal eyes cannot endure the devil.-- / Avaunt, thou dreadful minister of hell! / Thou hadst but power over his mortal body, / His soul thou canst not have; therefore, be gone.

What, are you shaking? Are you all afraid? I don't blame you; you are mortal, and mortal eyes can't stand the sight of the devil. Get away, you terrible agent of hell! You only had power over his body; you can't have his soul. So go.
Sweet saint, for charity, be not so curst.
Sweet saint, for charity's sake, don't be so bad-tempered.

Foul devil, for God's sake, hence and trouble us not; / For thou hast made the happy earth thy hell, / Fill'd it with cursing cries and deep exclaims. / If thou delight to view thy heinous deeds, / Behold this pattern of thy butcheries.-- / O, gentlemen, see, see! dead Henry's wounds / Open their congeal'd mouths and bleed afresh! / Blush, blush, thou lump of foul deformity; / For 'tis thy presence that exhales this blood / From cold and empty veins, where no blood dwells; / Thy deeds, inhuman and unnatural, / Provokes this deluge most unnatural.-- / O God, which this blood mad'st, revenge his death! / O earth, which this blood drink'st, revenge his death! / Either, heaven, with lightning strike the murderer dead; / Or, earth, gape open wide and eat him quick, / As thou dost swallow up this good king's blood, / Which his hell-govern'd arm hath butchered!

Foul devil, for God's sake go and leave us alone. You have turned this happy earth into your hell and filled it with cursing and screams. If you like looking at your terrible deeds, look at this example of your butchery. Gentlemen, look! Dead Henry's wounds are opening their clotted mouths and bleeding again! Blush, you lump of foul deformity, because it's your presence that draws this blood out of cold, empty veins where no blood is left. Your inhuman, unnatural deeds cause this unnatural flood. God who made this blood, avenge his death! Earth who drinks this blood, avenge his death! Either strike the murderer dead with lightning, heaven, or earth, open wide and swallow him alive, as you swallow this good king's blood that his hell-driven arm has spilled.
Lady, you know no rules of charity, / Which renders good for bad, blessings for curses.
Lady, you don't know the rules of charity, which repay bad with good and curses with blessings.
Villain, thou knowest nor law of God nor man: / No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity.
Villain, you know no law of God or man. Even the fiercest beast feels some pity.
But I know none, and therefore am no beast.
I feel none, so I'm no beast.
O wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
How amazing, when devils tell the truth!
More wonderful when angels are so angry.-- / Vouchsafe, divine perfection of a woman, / Of these supposed crimes to give me leave, / By circumstance, but to acquit myself.
More amazing when angels are so angry. Allow me, perfect woman, to clear myself in detail of these supposed crimes.
Vouchsafe, diffus'd infection of a man, / Of these known evils but to give me leave, / By circumstance, to accuse thy cursed self.
Allow me, plague of a man, to accuse your cursed self in detail of these known crimes.
Fairer than tongue can name thee, let me have / Some patient leisure to excuse myself.
You who are lovelier than words can say, give me a little time to excuse myself.
Fouler than heart can think thee, thou canst make / No excuse current but to hang thyself.
You who are fouler than the mind can imagine, the only excuse you can make is to hang yourself.
By such despair I should accuse myself.
Despair like that would only prove my guilt.
And by despairing shalt thou stand excus'd; / For doing worthy vengeance on thyself, / That didst unworthy slaughter upon others.
And by despairing you would be excused, taking just revenge on yourself for your unjust slaughter of others.
Say that I slew them not?
What if I didn't kill them?
Then say they were not slain: / But dead they are, and, devilish slave, by thee.
Then they aren't dead. But they are dead, devilish slave, and by your hand.
I did not kill your husband.
Nay, he is dead; and slain by Edward's hand.
No, he's dead, killed by Edward.
In thy foul throat thou liest: Queen Margaret saw / Thy murderous falchion smoking in his blood; / The which thou once didst bend against her breast, / But that thy brothers beat aside the point.
You lie through your filthy throat. Queen Margaret saw your murderous sword steaming with his blood, the same sword you once turned on her, until your brothers knocked it aside.
I was provoked by her slanderous tongue / That laid their guilt upon my guiltless shoulders.
I was provoked by her slander, which put their guilt on my innocent shoulders.
Thou wast provoked by thy bloody mind, / That never dreamt on aught but butcheries: / Didst thou not kill this king?
You were provoked by your bloody mind, which never dreamed of anything but butchery. Didn't you kill this king?
Dost grant me, hedgehog? then, God grant me too / Thou mayst be damned for that wicked deed! / O, he was gentle, mild, and virtuous.
You admit it, hedgehog? Then God grant that you're damned for that wicked deed! He was gentle, mild and good.
The better for the king of Heaven, that hath him.
All the better for the King of Heaven, who has him now.
He is in heaven, where thou shalt never come.
He is in heaven, where you will never go.
Let him thank me that holp to send him thither, / For he was fitter for that place than earth.
Then he should thank me for helping send him there; he was better suited to that place than to earth.
And thou unfit for any place but hell.
And you're suited to nowhere but hell.
Yes, one place else, if you will hear me name it.
Yes, one other place, if you'll let me name it.
Ill rest betide the chamber where thou liest!
May the room where you lie never have rest!
So will it, madam, till I lie with you.
It won't, madam, until I lie with you.

I know so.--But, gentle Lady Anne,-- / To leave this keen encounter of our wits, / And fall something into a slower method,-- / Is not the causer of the timeless deaths / Of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward, / As blameful as the executioner?

I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne, to leave this sharp contest of wits and take things more slowly: isn't the cause of the untimely deaths of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward, as much to blame as the man who killed them?
Thou wast the cause and most accurs'd effect.
You were both the cause and the most cursed result.
Your beauty was the cause of that effect; / Your beauty, that did haunt me in my sleep / To undertake the death of all the world, / So I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
Your beauty was the cause: your beauty, which haunted my sleep and made me ready to kill the whole world if I could live one hour in your sweet arms.
If I thought that, I tell thee, homicide, / These nails should rend that beauty from my cheeks.
If I thought that, killer, I'd tear the beauty from my cheeks with these nails.
These eyes could not endure that beauty's wreck; / You should not blemish it if I stood by: / As all the world is cheered by the sun, / So I by that; it is my day, my life.
These eyes could not bear to see that beauty ruined; you wouldn't spoil it while I stood by. As the sun cheers the whole world, so your beauty cheers me; it is my day, my life.
Black night o'ershade thy day, and death thy life!
May black night cover your day and death your life!
Curse not thyself, fair creature; thou art both.
Don't curse yourself, lovely creature; you are both.
I would I were, to be reveng'd on thee.
I wish I were, so I could take revenge on you.
It is a quarrel most unnatural, / To be reveng'd on him that loveth thee.
It's a most unnatural quarrel, to take revenge on someone who loves you.
It is a quarrel just and reasonable, / To be reveng'd on him that kill'd my husband.
It's a just and reasonable quarrel, to take revenge on the man who killed my husband.
He that bereft thee, lady, of thy husband, / Did it to help thee to a better husband.
The man who robbed you of your husband did it to help you to a better one.
His better doth not breathe upon the earth.
He lives that loves thee better than he could.
There is someone alive who loves you better than he could.
The self-same name, but one of better nature.
The same name, but a better nature.
Why dost thou spit at me?
Why do you spit at me?
Would it were mortal poison, for thy sake!
I wish it were deadly poison, for your sake.
Never came poison from so sweet a place.
Poison never came from such a sweet place.
Never hung poison on a fouler toad. / Out of my sight! thou dost infect mine eyes.
Poison never landed on a fouler toad. Get out of my sight! You infect my eyes.
Thine eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
Your eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
Would they were basilisks to strike thee dead!
I wish they were basilisks that could kill you with a look!

I would they were, that I might die at once; / For now they kill me with a living death. / Those eyes of thine from mine have drawn salt tears, / Sham'd their aspects with store of childish drops: / These eyes, which never shed remorseful tear, / No, when my father York and Edward wept, / To hear the piteous moan that Rutland made / When black-fac'd Clifford shook his sword at him; / Nor when thy warlike father, like a child, / Told the sad story of my father's death, / And twenty times made pause, to sob and weep, / That all the standers-by had wet their cheeks, / Like trees bedash'd with rain; in that sad time / My manly eyes did scorn an humble tear; / And what these sorrows could not thence exhale, / Thy beauty hath, and made them blind with weeping. / I never su'd to friend nor enemy; / My tongue could never learn sweet smoothing word; / But, now thy beauty is propos'd my fee, / My proud heart sues, and prompts my tongue to speak.

I wish they were, so I could die at once, because now they kill me with a living death. Your eyes have drawn salt tears from mine and shamed them with childish crying, these eyes that never shed a tear of pity, not even when my father York and Edward wept at Rutland's pitiful cries as black-faced Clifford raised his sword over him. Nor when your warlike father told like a child the sad story of my father's death, stopping twenty times to sob, until everyone listening had wet cheeks like trees after rain. In that sad time my manly eyes scorned to shed a tear, and what those sorrows could not draw out, your beauty has, and blinded them with weeping. I never pleaded with friend or enemy; my tongue never learned soft flattering words. But now that your beauty is offered as my reward, my proud heart pleads and urges my tongue to speak.

Teach not thy lip such scorn; for it was made / For kissing, lady, not for such contempt. / If thy revengeful heart cannot forgive, / Lo, here I lend thee this sharp-pointed sword; / Which if thou please to hide in this true breast / And let the soul forth that adoreth thee, / I lay it naked to the deadly stroke, / And humbly beg the death upon my knee, / Nay, do not pause; for I did kill King Henry,--

Don't teach your lips such scorn; they were made for kissing, lady, not for contempt. If your vengeful heart can't forgive, here, I lend you this sharp sword. If you want to bury it in this faithful heart and release the soul that adores you, I bare my chest to the blow and beg for death on my knees. Don't hesitate: I did kill King Henry,
But 'twas thy beauty that provoked me. / Nay, now dispatch; 'twas I that stabb'd young Edward,--
but it was your beauty that drove me to it. Go on, finish it: it was I who stabbed young Edward,
But 'twas thy heavenly face that set me on.
but it was your heavenly face that urged me on.
Take up the sword again, or take up me.
Pick up the sword again, or pick up me.
Arise, dissembler: though I wish thy death, / I will not be thy executioner.
Get up, hypocrite. Though I wish you dead, I won't be your executioner.
Then bid me kill myself, and I will do it.
Then tell me to kill myself and I'll do it.

That was in thy rage: / Speak it again, and even with the word, / This hand, which for thy love did kill thy love; / Shall, for thy love, kill a far truer love; / To both their deaths shalt thou be accessary.
That was in anger. Say it again, and at the word this hand, which for love of you killed your love, will for love of you kill a far truer lover. You'll be an accomplice to both deaths.
I would I knew thy heart.
I wish I knew your heart.
I fear me both are false.
Then no man was ever true.
Well, well, put up your sword.
Well, well, put your sword away.
Say, then, my peace is made.
But shall I live in hope?
But may I live in hope?
All men, I hope, live so.
To take is not to give.

Look, how this ring encompasseth thy finger, / Even so thy breast encloseth my poor heart; / Wear both of them, for both of them are thine. / And if thy poor devoted servant may / But beg one favour at thy gracious hand, / Thou dost confirm his happiness for ever.

Look how this ring encircles your finger: in the same way your heart encloses my poor heart. Wear both, because both are yours. And if your devoted servant may beg one favour from you, you'll make him happy for ever.

That it may please you leave these sad designs / To him that hath most cause to be a mourner, / And presently repair to Crosby Place; / Where,--after I have solemnly interr'd / At Chertsey monastery, this noble king, / And wet his grave with my repentant tears,-- / I will with all expedient duty see you: / For divers unknown reasons, I beseech you, / Grant me this boon.

That you leave these sad duties to the man who has most cause to mourn, and go straight to Crosby Place. After I have solemnly buried this noble king at Chertsey monastery and wet his grave with my tears of repentance, I'll come to you as quickly as I properly can. For various secret reasons, please grant me this.
With all my heart; and much it joys me too / To see you are become so penitent.-- / Tressel and Berkeley, go along with me.
With all my heart, and it pleases me to see you have become so repentant. Tressel and Berkeley, come with me.
'Tis more than you deserve; / But since you teach me how to flatter you, / Imagine I have said farewell already.
It's more than you deserve. But since you're teaching me to flatter you, imagine I've already said it.
No, to White Friars; there attend my coming.
No, to Whitefriars; wait for me there.

Was ever woman in this humour woo'd? / Was ever woman in this humour won? / I'll have her; but I will not keep her long. / What! I that kill'd her husband and his father, / To take her in her heart's extremest hate; / With curses in her mouth, tears in her eyes, / The bleeding witness of her hatred by; / Having God, her conscience, and these bars against me, / And I no friends to back my suit withal, / But the plain devil and dissembling looks, / And yet to win her,--all the world to nothing! / Ha! / Hath she forgot already that brave prince, / Edward, her lord, whom I, some three months since, / Stabb'd in my angry mood at Tewksbury? / A sweeter and a lovelier gentleman,-- / Fram'd in the prodigality of nature, / Young, valiant, wise, and, no doubt, right royal,-- / The spacious world cannot again afford: / And will she yet abase her eyes on me, / That cropp'd the golden prime of this sweet prince, / And made her widow to a woeful bed? / On me, whose all not equals Edward's moiety? / On me, that halt and am misshapen thus? / My dukedom to a beggarly denier, / I do mistake my person all this while: / Upon my life, she finds, although I cannot, / Myself to be a marvellous proper man. / I'll be at charges for a looking-glass; / And entertain a score or two of tailors, / To study fashions to adorn my body: / Since I am crept in favour with myself, / I will maintain it with some little cost. / But first I'll turn yon fellow in his grave; / And then return lamenting to my love.-- / Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass, / That I may see my shadow as I pass.

Was any woman ever wooed in this mood? Was any woman ever won in this mood? I'll have her, but I won't keep her long. What! I, who killed her husband and his father, win her at the height of her hatred, with curses in her mouth, tears in her eyes, the bleeding evidence of her hatred beside her, with God, her conscience and these obstacles against me, and nothing on my side but the devil and false looks? And still win her, against all the odds in the world! Ha! Has she already forgotten that brave prince Edward, her husband, whom I stabbed in a rage at Tewkesbury three months ago? The wide world can't produce a sweeter, lovelier gentleman, made with nature's generosity, young, brave, wise and truly royal. And she'll lower her eyes to me, who cut down this sweet prince in his prime and left her a widow in a sad bed? Me, who is not worth half of Edward? Me, who limps and is misshapen like this? I bet my dukedom against a penny I've been underrating myself all along. I swear she finds me, though I can't see it, a remarkably handsome man. I'll pay for a mirror and hire a couple of dozen tailors to study fashions to decorate my body. Since I've crept into my own good books, I'll keep myself there at some small cost. But first I'll tip that fellow into his grave and then go back to my love, mourning. Shine on, lovely sun, until I've bought a mirror, so I can see my shadow as I walk by.
Have patience, madam: there's no doubt his majesty / Will soon recover his accustom'd health.
Be patient, madam. No doubt his majesty will soon be back to his usual health.
In that you brook it ill, it makes him worse: / Therefore, for God's sake, entertain good comfort, / And cheer his grace with quick and merry eyes.
Taking it so badly makes him worse. So for God's sake cheer up and lift his spirits with lively, happy looks.
If he were dead, what would betide on me?
If he died, what would happen to me?
No other harm but loss of such a lord.
No harm except losing such a husband.
The loss of such a lord includes all harms.
Losing such a husband includes every harm.
The heavens have bless'd you with a goodly son / To be your comforter when he is gone.
Heaven has blessed you with a fine son to comfort you when he's gone.
Ah, he is young; and his minority / Is put unto the trust of Richard Gloster, / A man that loves not me, nor none of you.
Ah, but he's young, and while he's under age he'll be in the care of Richard Gloucester, a man who loves neither me nor any of you.
Is it concluded he shall be protector?
Has it been settled that he'll be Protector?
It is determin'd, not concluded yet: / But so it must be, if the king miscarry.
It's been decided, though not made official. But so it must be, if the King dies.
Here come the Lords of Buckingham and Stanley.
Here come Lord Buckingham and Lord Stanley.
Good time of day unto your royal grace!
Good day to your royal grace.
God make your majesty joyful as you have been!
God make your majesty as happy as you have been.

The Countess Richmond, good my Lord of Stanley, / To your good prayer will scarcely say amen. / Yet, Stanley, notwithstanding she's your wife, / And loves not me, be you, good lord, assur'd / I hate not you for her proud arrogance.

My good Lord Stanley, the Countess of Richmond will hardly say amen to your kind prayer. Still, Stanley, though she's your wife and doesn't love me, rest assured I don't hate you for her proud arrogance.

I do beseech you, either not believe / The envious slanders of her false accusers; / Or, if she be accus'd on true report, / Bear with her weakness, which I think proceeds / From wayward sickness, and no grounded malice.
Please either don't believe the spiteful slanders of her false accusers, or, if the reports are true, put up with her weakness, which I think comes from a fretful illness, not real malice.
Saw you the king to-day, my Lord of Stanley?
Did you see the King today, Lord Stanley?
But now the Duke of Buckingham and I / Are come from visiting his majesty.
The Duke of Buckingham and I have just come from visiting his majesty.
What likelihood of his amendment, lords?
How likely is he to recover, my lords?
Madam, good hope; his grace speaks cheerfully.
There's good hope, madam; his grace speaks cheerfully.
God grant him health! Did you confer with him?
God grant him health! Did you talk with him?
Ay, madam; he desires to make atonement / Between the Duke of Gloster and your brothers, / And between them and my lord chamberlain; / And sent to warn them to his royal presence.
Yes, madam. He wants to make peace between the Duke of Gloucester and your brothers, and between them and the Lord Chamberlain, and has summoned them to appear before him.
Would all were well!--but that will never be: / I fear our happiness is at the height.
I wish all were well, but it never will be. I fear our happiness has reached its peak.

They do me wrong, and I will not endure it:-- / Who are they that complain unto the king / That I, forsooth, am stern and love them not? / By holy Paul, they love his grace but lightly / That fill his ears with such dissentious rumours. / Because I cannot flatter and look fair, / Smile in men's faces, smooth, deceive, and cog, / Duck with French nods and apish courtesy, / I must be held a rancorous enemy. / Cannot a plain man live, and think no harm, / But thus his simple truth must be abus'd / With silken, sly, insinuating Jacks?

They wrong me, and I won't put up with it. Who has been complaining to the King that I am harsh and don't love them? By Saint Paul, people who fill his ears with such divisive gossip don't love him much. Because I can't flatter and put on a pleasant face, smile at people while I deceive and cheat them, bow with French nods and ape-like politeness, I'm taken for a bitter enemy. Can't a plain man live without thinking harm, without having his simple honesty abused by smooth, sly, creeping upstarts?
To who in all this presence speaks your grace?
Which of us here is your grace talking to?

To thee, that hast nor honesty nor grace. / When have I injur'd thee? when done thee wrong?-- / Or thee?--or thee?--or any of your faction? / A plague upon you all! His royal grace,-- / Whom God preserve better than you would wish!-- / Cannot be quiet scarce a breathing while, / But you must trouble him with lewd complaints.

To you, who have neither honesty nor grace. When have I hurt you or done you wrong? Or you? Or you? Or anyone in your party? A plague on you all! His royal grace, God keep him better than you would wish, can hardly have a moment's peace before you pester him with vile complaints.

Brother of Gloster, you mistake the matter. / The king, on his own royal disposition, / And not provok'd by any suitor else-- / Aiming, belike, at your interior hatred / That in your outward action shows itself / Against my children, brothers, and myself-- / Makes him to send; that thereby he may gather / The ground of your ill-will, and so remove it.

Brother Gloucester, you've got it wrong. The King, of his own accord and not urged by anyone, has sent for you, probably because he sees the inner hatred that shows in your behaviour towards my children, my brothers and me. He wants to find the cause of your ill will and remove it.
I cannot tell: the world is grown so bad / That wrens make prey where eagles dare not perch: / Since every Jack became a gentleman, / There's many a gentle person made a Jack.
I can't say. The world has grown so bad that wrens hunt where eagles dare not land. Since every common Jack became a gentleman, many a gentleman has been made a Jack.
Come, come, we know your meaning, brother Gloster; / You envy my advancement, and my friends'; / God grant we never may have need of you!
Come, come, we know what you mean, brother Gloucester. You envy my rise and my family's. God grant we never need you!

Meantime, God grants that we have need of you: / Our brother is imprison'd by your means, / Myself disgrac'd, and the nobility / Held in contempt; while great promotions / Are daily given to ennoble those / That scarce, some two days since, were worth a noble.

Meanwhile God grants that we need you. Our brother is in prison because of you, I am disgraced, and the nobility are despised, while great promotions are handed out daily to people who two days ago were barely worth a coin.

By Him that rais'd me to this careful height / From that contented hap which I enjoy'd, / I never did incense his majesty / Against the Duke of Clarence, but have been / An earnest advocate to plead for him. / My lord, you do me shameful injury / Falsely to draw me in these vile suspects.

By God, who raised me to this anxious height from the contented life I used to enjoy, I never turned the King against the Duke of Clarence; I've been an earnest advocate pleading for him. My lord, you do me a shameful wrong by falsely dragging me into these vile suspicions.
You may deny that you were not the mean / Of my Lord Hastings' late imprisonment.
You might as well deny that you were the cause of Lord Hastings' recent imprisonment.

She may, Lord Rivers?--why, who knows not so? / She may do more, sir, than denying that: / She may help you to many fair preferments; / And then deny her aiding hand therein, / And lay those honours on your high desert. / What may she not? She may,--ay, marry, may she,--

She may, Lord Rivers? Who doesn't know it? She may do more than deny it, sir. She may help you to many fine promotions, then deny she had a hand in them and put those honours down to your great merit. What can't she do? She may, yes, indeed she may...
What, marry, may she! marry with a king, / A bachelor, and a handsome stripling too: / I wis your grandam had a worser match.
Indeed she may? She may marry a king, a bachelor and a handsome young man too. I'm sure your grandmother made a worse match.

My Lord of Gloster, I have too long borne / Your blunt upbraidings and your bitter scoffs: / By heaven, I will acquaint his majesty / Of those gross taunts that oft I have endur'd. / I had rather be a country servant-maid / Than a great queen with this condition,-- / To be so baited, scorn'd, and stormed at.

My lord of Gloucester, I have put up too long with your blunt accusations and bitter mockery. By heaven, I'll tell his majesty about the crude taunts I've often suffered. I'd rather be a country servant-girl than a great queen on these terms, to be baited, scorned and raged at like this.
Small joy have I in being England's queen.
I get little joy from being England's queen.
And lessen'd be that small, God, I beseech Him! / Thy honour, state, and seat, is due to me.
And may God make that little even less, I pray! Your honour, rank and throne belong to me.

What! Threat you me with telling of the king? / Tell him, and spare not: look what I have said / I will avouch in presence of the king: / I dare adventure to be sent to the Tower. / 'Tis time to speak,--my pains are quite forgot.

What! Are you threatening me with telling the King? Tell him, and don't hold back. Whatever I've said, I'll repeat in front of the King. I'll risk being sent to the Tower. It's time to speak up; my services have been completely forgotten.
Out, devil! I do remember them too well: / Thou kill'dst my husband Henry in the Tower, / And Edward, my poor son, at Tewksbury.
Get out, devil! I remember them all too well. You killed my husband Henry in the Tower and my poor son Edward at Tewkesbury.

Ere you were queen, ay, or your husband king, / I was a pack-horse in his great affairs; / A weeder-out of his proud adversaries, / A liberal rewarder of his friends; / To royalize his blood I spilt mine own.
Before you were queen, or your husband king, I was a workhorse in his great business, weeding out his proud enemies and generously rewarding his friends. I spilled my own blood to make his royal.
Ay, and much better blood than his or thine.
Yes, and much better blood than his or yours.

In all which time you and your husband Grey / Were factious for the house of Lancaster;-- / And, Rivers, so were you: was not your husband / In Margaret's battle at Saint Albans slain? / Let me put in your minds, if you forget, / What you have been ere this, and what you are; / Withal, what I have been, and what I am.

All that time you and your husband Grey were partisans of the house of Lancaster. And so were you, Rivers. Wasn't your husband killed fighting on Margaret's side at St Albans? Let me remind you, if you've forgotten, what you were before and what you are now, and what I was and what I am.
A murderous villain, and so still thou art.
A murdering villain, and you still are.
Poor Clarence did forsake his father, Warwick; / Ay, and forswore himself,--which Jesu pardon!--
Poor Clarence abandoned his father-in-law Warwick, yes, and broke his oath, Jesus forgive him...

To fight on Edward's party for the crown; / And for his meed, poor lord, he is mew'd up. / I would to God my heart were flint, like Edward's, / Or Edward's soft and pitiful, like mine: / I am too childish-foolish for this world.

...to fight on Edward's side for the crown, and as a reward, poor lord, he's locked up. I wish to God my heart were flint like Edward's, or Edward's soft and pitying like mine. I'm too childishly simple for this world.
Hie thee to hell for shame and leave this world, / Thou cacodemon! there thy kingdom is.
Then hurry to hell for shame and leave this world, you evil spirit! Your kingdom is there.
My Lord of Gloster, in those busy days / Which here you urge to prove us enemies, / We follow'd then our lord, our sovereign king: / So should we you, if you should be our king.
My lord of Gloucester, in those turbulent days you bring up to prove we were enemies, we were following our lord, our lawful king. We would follow you the same way, if you were our king.
If I should be!--I had rather be a pedler: / Far be it from my heart, the thought thereof!
If I were! I'd rather be a pedlar. Far be the thought from my heart!
As little joy, my lord, as you suppose / You should enjoy, were you this country's king,-- / As little joy you may suppose in me, / That I enjoy, being the queen thereof.
My lord, as little joy as you imagine you'd have as king of this country, just as little joy you may suppose I have as its queen.
As little joy enjoys the queen thereof; / For I am she, and altogether joyless. / I can no longer hold me patient.--
The queen of this country has little joy indeed, because I am she, and completely joyless. I can't hold back any longer.

Hear me, you wrangling pirates, that fall out / In sharing that which you have pill'd from me! / Which of you trembles not that looks on me? / If not that, I am queen, you bow like subjects, / Yet that, by you depos'd, you quake like rebels? / Ah, gentle villain, do not turn away!

Listen to me, you squabbling pirates, falling out over sharing what you've stolen from me! Which of you doesn't tremble to look at me? If you don't bow like subjects because I am your queen, don't you shake like rebels because you deposed me? Ah, noble villain, don't turn away!
Foul wrinkled witch, what mak'st thou in my sight?
Foul wrinkled witch, what are you doing in my sight?
But repetition of what thou hast marr'd, / That will I make before I let thee go.
Only reciting what you have ruined. I'll do that before I let you go.
Wert thou not banished on pain of death?
Weren't you banished on pain of death?

I was; but I do find more pain in banishment / Than death can yield me here by my abode. / A husband and a son thou ow'st to me,-- / And thou a kingdom,--all of you allegiance: / This sorrow that I have, by right is yours; / And all the pleasures you usurp are mine.

I was, but I find banishment more painful than death by staying here. You owe me a husband and a son; you owe me a kingdom; all of you owe me allegiance. The sorrow I have by rights belongs to you, and all the pleasures you've seized belong to me.

The curse my noble father laid on thee, / When thou didst crown his warlike brows with paper, / And with thy scorns drew'st rivers from his eyes; / And then to dry them gav'st the Duke a clout / Steep'd in the faultless blood of pretty Rutland;-- / His curses, then from bitterness of soul / Denounc'd against thee, are all fallen upon thee; / And God, not we, hath plagu'd thy bloody deed.

The curse my noble father put on you when you crowned his warlike head with paper, mocked him till he wept rivers, and then gave him a cloth soaked in innocent little Rutland's blood to dry his eyes: that curse, spoken from the bitterness of his soul, has fallen on you. God, not we, has punished your bloody deed.
So just is God, to right the innocent.
God is that just, to set right a wrong to the innocent.
O, 'twas the foulest deed to slay that babe, / And the most merciless that e'er was heard of.
It was the foulest deed ever, to kill that child, and the most merciless ever heard of.
Tyrants themselves wept when it was reported.
Even tyrants wept when they heard it.
No man but prophesied revenge for it.
Northumberland, then present, wept to see it.
Northumberland, who was there, wept to see it.

What, were you snarling all before I came, / Ready to catch each other by the throat, / And turn you all your hatred now on me? / Did York's dread curse prevail so much with heaven / That Henry's death, my lovely Edward's death, / Their kingdom's loss, my woeful banishment, / Should all but answer for that peevish brat? / Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven?-- / Why, then, give way, dull clouds, to my quick curses!-- / Though not by war, by surfeit die your king, / As ours by murder, to make him a king! / Edward thy son, that now is Prince of Wales, / For Edward our son, that was Prince of Wales, / Die in his youth by like untimely violence! / Thyself a queen, for me that was a queen, / Outlive thy glory, like my wretched self! / Long mayest thou live to wail thy children's death; / And see another, as I see thee now, / Deck'd in thy rights, as thou art stall'd in mine! / Long die thy happy days before thy death; / And, after many lengthen'd hours of grief, / Die neither mother, wife, nor England's queen!-- / Rivers and Dorset, you were standers by,-- / And so wast thou, Lord Hastings,--when my son / Was stabb'd with bloody daggers: God, I pray Him, / That none of you may live his natural age, / But by some unlook'd accident cut off!

What, were you all snarling before I came, ready to grab each other's throats, and now you turn all your hatred on me? Did York's terrible curse have so much power with heaven that Henry's death, my lovely Edward's death, the loss of their kingdom and my miserable banishment are all just payment for that nasty brat? Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven? Then open up, heavy clouds, for my sharp curses! May your king die, not in war, but of excess, as ours died by murder to make him king. May your son Edward, now Prince of Wales, die young by the same untimely violence, in payment for our son Edward who was Prince of Wales. May you, a queen, in payment for me who was a queen, outlive your glory like wretched me. May you live long to mourn your children's death, and see another woman dressed in your rights, as you are now installed in mine. May your happy days die long before you do, and after many long hours of grief may you die neither mother, wife nor Queen of England. Rivers and Dorset, you stood by, and so did you, Lord Hastings, when my son was stabbed with bloody daggers. I pray God none of you lives out his natural life, but is cut off by some unexpected accident.
Have done thy charm, thou hateful wither'd hag.
Finish your spell, you hateful withered hag.

And leave out thee? stay, dog, for thou shalt hear me. / If heaven have any grievous plague in store / Exceeding those that I can wish upon thee, / O, let them keep it till thy sins be ripe, / And then hurl down their indignation / On thee, the troubler of the poor world's peace! / The worm of conscience still be-gnaw thy soul! / Thy friends suspect for traitors while thou liv'st, / And take deep traitors for thy dearest friends! / No sleep close up that deadly eye of thine, / Unless it be while some tormenting dream / Affrights thee with a hell of ugly devils! / Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog! / Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity / The slave of nature and the son of hell! / Thou slander of thy heavy mother's womb! / Thou loathed issue of thy father's loins! / Thou rag of honour! thou detested--

And leave you out? Stay, dog, you will hear me. If heaven has any worse plague in store than those I can wish on you, may it keep it until your sins are ripe, then hurl its anger down on you, the disturber of the poor world's peace. May the worm of conscience always gnaw your soul! May you suspect your friends of treason all your life and take deep traitors for your dearest friends! May sleep never close that deadly eye of yours, unless some tormenting dream terrifies you with a hell of ugly devils! You elf-marked, misbegotten, rooting hog! You who were stamped at birth as nature's slave and hell's son! You disgrace to your mother's heavy womb! You hated offspring of your father! You rag of honour! You detested...
I cry thee mercy then; for I did think / That thou hadst call'd me all these bitter names.
Then I beg your pardon, because I thought you were calling me all those bitter names.
Why, so I did; but look'd for no reply. / O, let me make the period to my curse!
I was, but I didn't expect an answer. Oh, let me finish my curse!
'Tis done by me, and ends in--Margaret.
I've finished it for you: it ends in "Margaret".
Thus have you breath'd your curse against yourself.
So you've breathed your curse against yourself.

Poor painted queen, vain flourish of my fortune! / Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider, / Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about? / Fool, fool! thou whett'st a knife to kill thyself. / The day will come that thou shalt wish for me / To help thee curse this poisonous bunch-back'd toad.

Poor painted queen, empty imitation of my fortune! Why do you sprinkle sugar on that swollen spider whose deadly web is closing round you? Fool, fool! You're sharpening a knife to kill yourself. The day will come when you'll wish for me to help you curse this poisonous hunchbacked toad.
False-boding woman, end thy frantic curse, / Lest to thy harm thou move our patience.
You prophet of doom, stop your mad cursing, or you'll push our patience too far for your own good.
Foul shame upon you! you have all mov'd mine.
Shame on you! You've all pushed mine.
Were you well serv'd, you would be taught your duty.
If you got what you deserved, you'd be taught your duty.
To serve me well, you all should do me duty, / Teach me to be your queen, and you my subjects: / O, serve me well, and teach yourselves that duty!
To give me what I deserve, you'd all do your duty to me, treat me as your queen and yourselves as my subjects. Give me what I deserve, and learn that duty!
Dispute not with her,--she is lunatic.
Don't argue with her; she's mad.

Peace, master marquis, you are malapert: / Your fire-new stamp of honour is scarce current: / O, that your young nobility could judge / What 'twere to lose it, and be miserable! / They that stand high have many blasts to shake them; / And if they fall they dash themselves to pieces.

Quiet, master marquis, you're impudent. Your brand-new title is hardly in circulation yet. If only your new nobility could understand what it would mean to lose it and be miserable! Those who stand high are shaken by many storms, and if they fall they're dashed to pieces.
Good counsel, marry:--learn it, learn it, marquis.
Good advice, indeed. Learn it, learn it, marquis.
It touches you, my lord, as much as me.
It applies to you as much as to me, my lord.
Ay, and much more: but I was born so high, / Our aery buildeth in the cedar's top, / And dallies with the wind, and scorns the sun.
Yes, and much more. But I was born so high: our eagle's nest is built in the top of the cedar, plays with the wind and scorns the sun.

And turns the sun to shade;--alas! alas!-- / Witness my son, now in the shade of death; / Whose bright out-shining beams thy cloudy wrath, / Hath in eternal darkness folded up. / Your aery buildeth in our aery's nest:-- / O God that seest it, do not suffer it; / As it is won with blood, lost be it so!

And turns the sun to shade, alas! Look at my son, now in the shade of death, whose bright shining beams your cloudy anger has wrapped in eternal darkness. Your nest is built in our nest. God, who sees it, don't allow it! As it was won with blood, let it be lost with blood.
Peace, peace, for shame, if not for charity.
Quiet, quiet, out of shame if not charity.

Urge neither charity nor shame to me: / Uncharitably with me have you dealt, / And shamefully my hopes by you are butcher'd. / My charity is outrage, life my shame,-- / And in that shame still live my sorrow's rage!

Don't talk to me of charity or shame. You've treated me without charity, and you've shamefully butchered my hopes. My charity is outrage, my life is shame, and in that shame my sorrow's fury will go on living.

O princely Buckingham, I'll kiss thy hand, / In sign of league and amity with thee: / Now fair befall thee and thy noble house! / Thy garments are not spotted with our blood, / Nor thou within the compass of my curse.
Noble Buckingham, I'll kiss your hand as a sign of alliance and friendship. Good fortune to you and your noble family! Your clothes aren't stained with our blood, and you're not included in my curse.
Nor no one here; for curses never pass / The lips of those that breathe them in the air.
Nor is anyone here, because curses never get further than the lips of those who breathe them.

I will not think but they ascend the sky, / And there awake God's gentle-sleeping peace. / O Buckingham, take heed of yonder dog! / Look, when he fawns he bites; and when he bites, / His venom tooth will rankle to the death: / Have not to do with him, beware of him; / Sin, death, and hell have set their marks on him, / And all their ministers attend on him.

I believe they rise to the sky and wake God's gently sleeping peace. Buckingham, watch out for that dog over there! When he fawns, he bites, and when he bites, his poisonous tooth festers until you die. Have nothing to do with him; beware of him. Sin, death and hell have marked him, and all their agents serve him.
What doth she say, my Lord of Buckingham?
What is she saying, my lord of Buckingham?
Nothing that I respect, my gracious lord.
Nothing I take seriously, my gracious lord.

What, dost thou scorn me for my gentle counsel? / And soothe the devil that I warn thee from? / O, but remember this another day, / When he shall split thy very heart with sorrow, / And say, poor Margaret was a prophetess!-- / Live each of you the subjects to his hate, / And he to yours, and all of you to God's!

What, do you scorn my kind advice and flatter the devil I'm warning you about? Then remember this some day, when he breaks your heart with sorrow, and say: poor Margaret was a prophet! May each of you live subject to his hatred, and he to yours, and all of you to God's!
My hair doth stand an end to hear her curses.
My hair stands on end to hear her curses.
And so doth mine: I muse why she's at liberty.
Mine too. I wonder why she's free.
I cannot blame her: by God's holy mother, / She hath had too much wrong; and I repent / My part thereof that I have done to her.
I can't blame her. By the holy mother of God, she has been badly wronged, and I regret my part in it.
I never did her any, to my knowledge.
I never did her any wrong that I know of.

Yet you have all the vantage of her wrong. / I was too hot to do somebody good, / That is too cold in thinking of it now. / Marry, as for Clarence, he is well repaid; / He is frank'd up to fatting for his pains; / God pardon them that are the cause thereof!

Yet you have all the profit of her wrong. I was too eager to do good to someone who is too cold to remember it now. As for Clarence, he's well rewarded: he's been penned up to be fattened for his pains. God forgive those who are the cause of it!
A virtuous and a Christian-like conclusion, / To pray for them that have done scathe to us!
A virtuous and Christian conclusion, to pray for those who have harmed us.
So do I ever being well advis'd; / [Aside] For had I curs'd now, I had curs'd myself.
I always do, when I'm well advised. (Aside) Because if I had cursed now, I'd have cursed myself.
Madam, his majesty doth can for you,-- / And for your grace,--and you, my noble lords.
Madam, his majesty is calling for you, and for your grace, and for you, my noble lords.
Catesby, I come.--Lords, will you go with me?
Catesby, I'm coming. Lords, will you come with me?

I do the wrong, and first begin to brawl. / The secret mischiefs that I set abroach / I lay unto the grievous charge of others. / Clarence,--whom I indeed have cast in darkness,-- / I do beweep to many simple gulls; / Namely, to Stanley, Hastings, Buckingham; / And tell them 'tis the queen and her allies / That stir the king against the duke my brother. / Now they believe it; and withal whet me / To be reveng'd on Rivers, Vaughn, Grey: / But then I sigh; and, with a piece of Scripture, / Tell them that God bids us do good for evil: / And thus I clothe my naked villany / With odd old ends stol'n forth of holy writ; / And seem a saint when most I play the devil.-- / But, soft, here come my executioners.

I do the wrong and start the quarrel first. The secret mischief I set going I blame on others. Clarence, whom I have in fact put in the dark, I weep over in front of many simple fools, namely Stanley, Hastings and Buckingham, and tell them it's the Queen and her allies who are turning the King against my brother the Duke. Now they believe it and urge me to take revenge on Rivers, Vaughan and Grey. But then I sigh and, with a bit of Scripture, tell them God tells us to do good for evil. So I dress up my naked villainy in odd old scraps stolen from the Bible and seem a saint when I'm most playing the devil. But quiet, here come my executioners.
How now, my hardy stout resolved mates! / Are you now going to dispatch this thing?
Well, my tough, brave, determined friends! Are you on your way to finish this business?
We are, my lord, and come to have the warrant, / That we may be admitted where he is.
We are, my lord, and we've come for the warrant so we can be let in to where he is.
Well thought upon;--I have it here about me:
Good thinking. I have it here with me.

When you have done, repair to Crosby Place. / But, sirs, be sudden in the execution, / Withal obdurate, do not hear him plead; / For Clarence is well-spoken, and perhaps / May move your hearts to pity, if you mark him.

When you're done, come to Crosby Place. But, sirs, be quick about it, and hard-hearted. Don't listen to him plead, because Clarence is a good speaker and might move you to pity if you pay attention to him.
Tut, tut, my lord, we will not stand to prate; / Talkers are no good doers: be assur'd / We go to use our hands, and not our tongues.
Tut, tut, my lord, we won't stand chattering. Talkers aren't doers. Rest assured, we're going to use our hands, not our tongues.
Your eyes drop millstones when fools' eyes fall tears: / I like you, lads;--about your business straight; / Go, go, despatch.
Your eyes drop millstones when fools' eyes drop tears. I like you, lads. Get on with your business right away. Go, go, finish it.
Why looks your grace so heavily to-day?
Why does your grace look so gloomy today?

O, I have pass'd a miserable night, / So full of fearful dreams, of ugly sights, / That, as I am a Christian faithful man, / I would not spend another such a night / Though 'twere to buy a world of happy days,-- / So full of dismal terror was the time!

Oh, I've had a miserable night, so full of frightening dreams and ugly sights that, as I'm a faithful Christian, I wouldn't spend another night like it even to buy a world of happy days, the time was so full of grim terror.
What was your dream, my lord? I pray you tell me.
What was your dream, my lord? Please tell me.

Methoughts that I had broken from the Tower, / And was embark'd to cross to Burgundy; / And, in my company, my brother Gloster; / Who from my cabin tempted me to walk / Upon the hatches: thence we look'd toward England, / And cited up a thousand heavy times, / During the wars of York and Lancaster, / That had befall'n us. As we pac'd along / Upon the giddy footing of the hatches, / Methought that Gloster stumbled; and, in falling, / Struck me, that thought to stay him, overboard / Into the tumbling billows of the main. / O Lord, methought what pain it was to drown! / What dreadful noise of waters in my ears! / What sights of ugly death within my eyes! / Methoughts I saw a thousand fearful wrecks; / A thousand men that fishes gnaw'd upon; / Wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl, / Inestimable stones, unvalued jewels, / All scatt'red in the bottom of the sea: / Some lay in dead men's skulls; and in the holes / Where eyes did once inhabit there were crept,-- / As 'twere in scorn of eyes,--reflecting gems, / That woo'd the slimy bottom of the deep, / And mock'd the dead bones that lay scatter'd by.

I dreamed I had escaped from the Tower and boarded a ship to cross to Burgundy, and my brother Gloucester was with me. He tempted me out of my cabin to walk on the deck. From there we looked towards England and recalled a thousand bad times that had happened to us in the wars of York and Lancaster. As we paced along the unsteady deck, I dreamed Gloucester stumbled, and as he fell he knocked me, when I tried to steady him, overboard into the tumbling waves of the sea. Lord, what pain it was to drown! What dreadful roaring of water in my ears! What sights of ugly death in my eyes! I thought I saw a thousand frightening wrecks, a thousand men gnawed by fish, ingots of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearls, priceless stones and jewels, all scattered on the bottom of the sea. Some lay in dead men's skulls, and in the holes where eyes once lived glittering gems had crept, as if mocking eyes, courting the slimy seabed and mocking the dead bones scattered around.
Had you such leisure in the time of death / To gaze upon these secrets of the deep?
Did you have time, while you were dying, to stare at these secrets of the deep?

Methought I had; and often did I strive / To yield the ghost: but still the envious flood / Stopp'd in my soul, and would not let it forth / To find the empty, vast, and wandering air; / But smother'd it within my panting bulk, / Who almost burst to belch it in the sea.

I thought I did, and I kept trying to give up my soul, but the spiteful sea held it in and wouldn't let it out to find the empty, vast, wandering air. It smothered it inside my gasping body, which almost burst trying to belch it into the sea.
Awak'd you not in this sore agony?
Didn't you wake up in this terrible agony?

No, no, my dream was lengthen'd after life; / O, then began the tempest to my soul! / I pass'd, methought, the melancholy flood / With that grim ferryman which poets write of, / Unto the kingdom of perpetual night. / The first that there did greet my stranger soul / Was my great father-in-law, renowned Warwick; / Who spake aloud, "What scourge for perjury / Can this dark monarchy afford false Clarence?" / And so he vanish'd: then came wandering by / A shadow like an Angel, with bright hair / Dabbled in blood; and he shriek'd out aloud / "Clarence is come,--false, fleeting, perjur'd Clarence,-- / That stabb'd me in the field by Tewksbury;-- / Seize on him, Furies, take him to your torments!" / With that, methoughts, a legion of foul fiends / Environ'd me, and howled in mine ears / Such hideous cries that, with the very noise, / I trembling wak'd, and for a season after / Could not believe but that I was in hell,-- / Such terrible impression made my dream.

No, no, my dream went on after death. Oh, then the storm in my soul began! I dreamed I crossed the gloomy river with that grim ferryman the poets write about, into the kingdom of everlasting night. The first to greet my stranger's soul there was my great father-in-law, famous Warwick, who called out, "What punishment for oath-breaking can this dark kingdom give false Clarence?" And he vanished. Then a shadow like an angel came wandering by, with bright hair spattered with blood, and shrieked, "Clarence has come, false, fickle, oath-breaking Clarence, who stabbed me in the field at Tewkesbury! Seize him, Furies, take him to your torments!" With that, I dreamed, a crowd of foul devils surrounded me and howled such hideous cries in my ears that the very noise woke me trembling, and for a while afterwards I couldn't believe I wasn't in hell, my dream made such a terrible impression.
No marvel, lord, though it affrighted you; / I am afraid, methinks, to hear you tell it.
No wonder it frightened you, my lord. I'm frightened just to hear you tell it.

Ah, Brakenbury, I have done these things / That now give evidence against my soul, / For Edward's sake; and see how he requites me!-- / O God! If my deep prayers cannot appease Thee, / But Thou wilt be aveng'd on my misdeeds, / Yet execute Thy wrath in me alone,-- / O, spare my guiltless wife and my poor children!-- / Keeper, I prithee sit by me awhile; / My soul is heavy, and I fain would sleep.

Ah, Brakenbury, I did these things that now testify against my soul for Edward's sake, and see how he repays me! God, if my deep prayers can't calm you and you must take revenge for my sins, carry out your anger on me alone. Spare my innocent wife and my poor children! Keeper, please sit with me a while. My soul is heavy and I want to sleep.
I will, my lord; God give your grace good rest!--
I will, my lord. God give your grace good rest!

Sorrow breaks seasons and reposing hours, / Makes the night morning and the noontide night. / Princes have but their titles for their glories, / An outward honour for an inward toil; / And, for unfelt imaginations, / They often feel a world of restless cares: / So that, between their tides and low name, / There's nothing differs but the outward fame.

Sorrow breaks up the seasons and the hours of rest, turning night into morning and noon into night. Princes have only their titles for glory, an outward honour for an inner toil, and in place of the pleasures ordinary people imagine they have, they often feel a world of restless worries. So between their titles and a lowly name there's no difference but outward fame.
What wouldst thou, fellow, and how cam'st thou hither?
What do you want, fellow, and how did you get here?
I would speak with Clarence, and I came hither on my legs.
I want to speak to Clarence, and I came here on my legs.
'Tis better, sir, than to be tedious.--Let / him see our commission and talk no more.
Better than being long-winded, sir. Show him our orders and stop talking.

I am, in this, commanded to deliver / The noble Duke of Clarence to your hands:-- / I will not reason what is meant hereby, / Because I will be guiltless of the meaning. / There lies the Duke asleep,--and there the keys; / I'll to the king and signify to him / That thus I have resign'd to you my charge.

This orders me to hand over the noble Duke of Clarence to you. I won't ask what it means, because I want to stay innocent of its meaning. There's the Duke asleep, and there are the keys. I'll go to the King and tell him I've handed my charge over to you.
You may, sir; 'tis a point of wisdom: fare you well.
You may, sir; that's wise. Goodbye.
What, shall we stab him as he sleeps?
What, shall we stab him while he's asleep?
No; he'll say 'twas done cowardly, when he wakes.
No, he'll say it was cowardly when he wakes up.
When he wakes! why, fool, he shall never wake until the great / judgment-day.
When he wakes up! Why, fool, he'll never wake up until Judgement Day.
Why, then he'll say we stabb'd him sleeping.
Then he'll say we stabbed him in his sleep.
The urging of that word "judgment" hath bred a kind of remorse in / me.
Mentioning that word "judgement" has given me a kind of remorse.
Not to kill him, having a warrant for it; but to be damned / for killing him, from the which no warrant can defend me.
Not of killing him, since we have a warrant for it, but of being damned for killing him, and no warrant can protect me from that.
I thought thou hadst been resolute.
So I am, to let him live.
I am: determined to let him live.
I'll back to the Duke of Gloster and tell him so.
I'll go back to the Duke of Gloucester and tell him so.
Nay, I pr'ythee, stay a little: I hope my holy humour will / change; it was wont to hold me but while one tells twenty.
No, please, wait a bit. I hope my holy mood will pass; it usually only lasts while you count to twenty.
How dost thou feel thyself now?
Faith, some certain dregs of conscience are yet within me.
Honestly, there are still some dregs of conscience in me.
Remember our reward, when the deed's done.
Remember our reward when the deed's done.
Zounds, he dies: I had forgot the reward.
By God's wounds, he dies! I'd forgotten the reward.
O, in the Duke of Gloster's purse.
Oh, in the Duke of Gloucester's purse.
So, when he opens his purse to give us our reward, / thy conscience flies out.
So when he opens his purse to pay us, your conscience flies out.
'Tis no matter; let it go; there's few or none will entertain it.
Never mind, let it go. Hardly anyone wants to take it in.
What if it come to thee again?
What if it comes back to you?

I'll not meddle with it,--it makes a man coward; / a man cannot steal, but it accuseth him; a man / cannot swear, but it checks him; a man cannot lie with his / neighbour's wife, but it detects him: 'tis a blushing shame- / faced spirit that mutinies in a man's bosom; it fills a man / full of obstacles: it made me once restore a purse of gold / that by chance I found; it beggars any man that keeps it: / it is turned out of towns and cities for a dangerous thing; / and every man that means to live well endeavours to trust / to himself and live without it.

I won't have anything to do with it; it makes a man a coward. A man can't steal without it accusing him, can't swear without it rebuking him, can't sleep with his neighbour's wife without it catching him out. It's a blushing, shamefaced spirit that rebels inside a man's chest. It fills a man with obstacles. It once made me give back a purse of gold I happened to find. It beggars anyone who keeps it. It's driven out of towns and cities as a dangerous thing, and every man who wants to live well tries to rely on himself and live without it.
Zounds,'tis even now at my elbow, persuading me / not to kill the duke.
By God, it's at my elbow right now, persuading me not to kill the duke.
Take the devil in thy mind, and believe him not; he would / insinuate with thee but to make thee sigh.
Hold on to the devil in your mind and don't believe it. It only wants to worm its way in to make you sigh.
I am strong-framed; he cannot prevail with me.
I'm tough; it can't win me over.
Spoke like a tall man that respects thy reputation. / Come, shall we fall to work?
Spoken like a brave man who cares about his reputation. Come on, shall we get to work?
Take him on the costard with the hilts of thy sword, / and then throw him in the malmsey-butt in the next room.
Hit him on the head with the hilt of your sword, then throw him in the barrel of malmsey wine in the next room.
O excellent device! and make a sop of him.
Excellent plan! And make a wine-soaked sop of him.
Where art thou, keeper? give me a cup of wine.
Where are you, keeper? Give me a cup of wine.
You shall have wine enough, my lord, anon.
You'll have plenty of wine soon, my lord.
In God's name, what art thou?
In God's name, who are you?
But not as I am, royal.
Nor you as we are, loyal.
Thy voice is thunder, but thy looks are humble.
Your voice is like thunder, but you look humble.
My voice is now the king's, my looks mine own.
My voice now speaks for the King; my looks are my own.
How darkly and how deadly dost thou speak! / Your eyes do menace me; why look you pale? / Who sent you hither? Wherefore do you come?
How darkly and deadly you speak! Your eyes threaten me. Why are you pale? Who sent you here? Why have you come?
You scarcely have the hearts to tell me so, / And therefore cannot have the hearts to do it. / Wherein, my friends, have I offended you?
You hardly have the heart to tell me so, so you can't have the heart to do it. How have I offended you, my friends?
Offended us you have not, but the king.
You haven't offended us, but the King.
I shall be reconcil'd to him again.
I'll be reconciled to him again.
Never, my lord; therefore prepare to die.
Never, my lord, so prepare to die.

Are you drawn forth among a world of men / To slay the innocent? What is my offence? / Where is the evidence that doth accuse me? / What lawful quest have given their verdict up / Unto the frowning judge? or who pronounc'd / The bitter sentence of poor Clarence' death? / Before I be convict by course of law, / To threaten me with death is most unlawful. / I charge you, as you hope to have redemption / By Christ's dear blood shed for our grievous sins, / That you depart, and lay no hands on me: / The deed you undertake is damnable.

Have you been picked out of all the world's men to kill the innocent? What is my crime? Where's the evidence against me? What lawful jury has given its verdict to the stern judge? Who passed the bitter sentence of poor Clarence's death? To threaten me with death before I'm convicted by due process of law is completely unlawful. I order you, as you hope to be saved by Christ's precious blood shed for our terrible sins, to leave and not touch me. What you're doing is damnable.
What we will do, we do upon command.
What we do, we do on orders.
And he that hath commanded is our king.
And the one who ordered it is our king.

Erroneous vassals! the great King of kings / Hath in the table of his law commanded / That thou shalt do no murder: will you then / Spurn at His edict and fulfil a man's? / Take heed; for He holds vengeance in His hand / To hurl upon their heads that break His law.

Misguided slaves! The great King of kings has commanded in the tablets of his law, "Thou shalt not kill." Will you scorn his command and carry out a man's? Beware: he holds vengeance in his hand to hurl on the heads of those who break his law.
And that same vengeance doth He hurl on thee / For false forswearing, and for murder too: / Thou didst receive the sacrament to fight / In quarrel of the house of Lancaster.
And he'll hurl that same vengeance on you for perjury and for murder too. You took the sacrament and swore to fight for the house of Lancaster.
And like a traitor to the name of God / Didst break that vow; and with thy treacherous blade / Unripp'dst the bowels of thy sovereign's son.
And like a traitor to God's name you broke that vow and with your treacherous sword ripped open the belly of your king's son.
Whom thou wast sworn to cherish and defend.
Whom you had sworn to cherish and defend.
How canst thou urge God's dreadful law to us, / When thou hast broke it in such dear degree?
