How can you preach God's terrible law to us when you've broken it so grievously?

Alas! for whose sake did I that ill deed? / For Edward, for my brother, for his sake: / He sends you not to murder me for this; / For in that sin he is as deep as I. / If God will be avenged for the deed, / O, know you yet He doth it publicly. / Take not the quarrel from His powerful arm; / He needs no indirect or lawless course / To cut off those that have offended Him.

Alas, for whose sake did I do that evil? For Edward, my brother, for his sake. He isn't sending you to murder me for that, because he is as deep in that sin as I am. If God wants revenge for the deed, know that he takes it openly. Don't take the quarrel out of his powerful hands. He needs no underhand or lawless means to cut off those who have offended him.
Who made thee, then, a bloody minister / When gallant-springing brave Plantagenet, / That princely novice, was struck dead by thee?
Then who made you a bloody agent when that gallant, budding, brave Plantagenet, that young prince, was struck dead by you?
My brother's love, the devil, and my rage.
My love for my brother, the devil and my rage.
Thy brother's love, our duty, and thy faults, / Provoke us hither now to slaughter thee.
Your brother's love, our duty and your faults bring us here now to kill you.

If you do love my brother, hate not me; / I am his brother, and I love him well. / If you are hir'd for meed, go back again, / And I will send you to my brother Gloster, / Who shall reward you better for my life / Than Edward will for tidings of my death.

If you love my brother, don't hate me. I'm his brother and I love him dearly. If you're hired for money, go back, and I'll send you to my brother Gloucester, who will pay you better for my life than Edward will for news of my death.
You are deceiv'd, your brother Gloster hates you.
You're mistaken. Your brother Gloucester hates you.
O, no, he loves me, and he holds me dear: / Go you to him from me.
Oh no, he loves me and values me dearly. Go to him from me.

Tell him when that our princely father York / Bless'd his three sons with his victorious arm / And charg'd us from his soul to love each other, / He little thought of this divided friendship: / Bid Gloster think of this, and he will weep.

Tell him that when our princely father York blessed his three sons with his victorious arm and charged us from his soul to love each other, he never imagined this divided friendship. Tell Gloucester to think of that, and he'll weep.
Ay, millstones; as he lesson'd us to weep.
Yes, millstones, as he taught us to weep.
O, do not slander him, for he is kind.
Oh, don't slander him; he's kind.
Right, as snow in harvest.--Come, you deceive yourself: / 'Tis he that sends us to destroy you here.
Right, as kind as snow at harvest time. Come, you're fooling yourself. It's he who sends us here to destroy you.
It cannot be; for he bewept my fortune, / And hugg'd me in his arms, and swore, with sobs, / That he would labour my delivery.
It can't be. He wept over my misfortune, hugged me and swore with sobs that he'd work for my release.
Why, so he doth, when he delivers you / From this earth's thraldom to the joys of heaven.
And so he does, releasing you from slavery on this earth to the joys of heaven.
Make peace with God, for you must die, my lord.
Make your peace with God, my lord, because you must die.

Have you that holy feeling in your souls, / To counsel me to make my peace with God, / And are you yet to your own souls so blind / That you will war with God by murdering me?-- / O, sirs, consider, they that set you on / To do this deed will hate you for the deed.

Do you have such holy feeling in your souls that you advise me to make my peace with God, and yet are you so blind to your own souls that you'll make war on God by murdering me? Sirs, consider: those who set you on to do this will hate you for doing it.

Not to relent is beastly, savage, devilish. / Which of you, if you were a prince's son, / Being pent from liberty, as I am now,-- / If two such murderers as yourselves came to you,-- / Would not entreat for life?-- / My friend, I spy some pity in thy looks; / O, if thine eye be not a flatterer, / Come thou on my side, and entreat for me, / As you would beg, were you in my distress: / A begging prince what beggar pities not?

Not to relent is beastly, savage and devilish. Which of you, if you were a prince's son, shut away from freedom as I am now, and two murderers like you came to you, wouldn't beg for his life? My friend, I see some pity in your face. If your eyes aren't lying, come over to my side and plead for me, as you would beg if you were in my distress. What beggar doesn't pity a begging prince?
Take that, and that: if all this will not do, / I'll drown you in the malmsey-butt within.
Take that, and that! If all this isn't enough, I'll drown you in the barrel of malmsey in there.
A bloody deed, and desperately dispatch'd! / How fain, like Pilate, would I wash my hands / Of this most grievous murder!
A bloody deed, and recklessly done! How I'd like to wash my hands of this terrible murder, like Pilate.
How now, what mean'st thou that thou help'st me not? / By heavens, the duke shall know how slack you have / been!
What's this? Why didn't you help me? By heaven, the Duke will hear how slack you've been!
I would he knew that I had sav'd his brother! / Take thou the fee, and tell him what I say; / For I repent me that the duke is slain.
I wish he knew I had saved his brother! You take the fee and tell him what I said, because I'm sorry the Duke has been killed.

So do not I: go, coward as thou art.-- / Well, I'll go hide the body in some hole, / Till that the duke give order for his burial: / And when I have my meed, I will away; / For this will out, and then I must not stay.

I'm not. Go on, coward that you are. Well, I'll hide the body in some hole until the Duke gives orders for his burial. And when I have my reward, I'll be off, because this will come out, and then I mustn't stay.

Why, so. Now have I done a good day's work:-- / You peers, continue this united league: / I every day expect an embassage / From my Redeemer, to redeem me hence; / And more at peace my soul shall part to heaven, / Since I have made my friends at peace on earth. / Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand; / Dissemble not your hatred, swear your love.

There. Now I've done a good day's work. You lords, keep this alliance. I expect a message every day from my Redeemer to take me from here, and my soul will go to heaven more at peace now that I've made my friends make peace on earth. Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand. Don't hide your hatred; swear your love.
By heaven, my soul is purg'd from grudging hate; / And with my hand I seal my true heart's love.
By heaven, my soul is cleansed of grudging hate, and with my hand I seal my heart's true love.
So thrive I, as I truly swear the like!
May I prosper as truly as I swear the same!
Take heed you dally not before your king; / Lest He that is the supreme King of kings / Confound your hidden falsehood, and award / Either of you to be the other's end.
Be careful not to play games in front of your king, in case the supreme King of kings punishes your hidden falsehood and makes each of you the cause of the other's death.
So prosper I, as I swear perfect love!
May I prosper as I swear perfect love!
And I, as I love Hastings with my heart!
And I, as I love Hastings with all my heart!

Madam, yourself is not exempt from this;-- / Nor you, son Dorset;--Buckingham, nor you;-- / You have been factious one against the other. / Wife, love Lord Hastings, let him kiss your hand; / And what you do, do it unfeignedly.

Madam, you aren't exempt from this, nor you, stepson Dorset, nor you, Buckingham. You've been in factions against each other. Wife, love Lord Hastings and let him kiss your hand, and whatever you do, do it sincerely.
There, Hastings; I will never more remember / Our former hatred, so thrive I and mine!
There, Hastings. I'll never again remember our old hatred, as I hope my family and I may prosper.
Dorset, embrace him;--Hastings, love lord marquis.
Dorset, embrace him. Hastings, love the lord marquis.
This interchange of love, I here protest, / Upon my part shall be inviolable.
I promise this exchange of love will never be broken on my part.
Now, princely Buckingham, seal thou this league / With thy embracements to my wife's allies, / And make me happy in your unity.
Now, noble Buckingham, seal this alliance by embracing my wife's family, and make me happy with your unity.

Whenever Buckingham doth turn his hate / Upon your grace [to the queen], but with all duteous love / Doth cherish you and yours, God punish me / With hate in those where I expect most love! / When I have most need to employ a friend, / And most assured that he is a friend, / Deep, hollow, treacherous, and full of guile, / Be he unto me!--this do I beg of heaven / When I am cold in love to you or yours.

Whenever Buckingham turns his hatred against your grace (to the Queen) instead of cherishing you and your family with dutiful love, may God punish me with hatred from those I expect most love from! When I most need a friend, and am most sure he is a friend, may he prove deep, hollow, treacherous and full of deceit to me! I ask this of heaven if I ever grow cold in love to you or yours.
A pleasing cordial, princely Buckingham, / Is this thy vow unto my sickly heart. / There wanteth now our brother Gloster here, / To make the blessed period of this peace.
Your vow is a pleasing medicine to my sick heart, noble Buckingham. Now all we need is our brother Gloucester here to bring this peace to a blessed end.
And, in good time, here comes the noble duke.
And here, just in time, comes the noble Duke.
Good morrow to my sovereign king and queen; / And, princely peers, a happy time of day!
Good morning to my royal king and queen, and a happy day to you, princely lords!
Happy, indeed, as we have spent the day. / Gloster, we have done deeds of charity; / Made peace of enmity, fair love of hate, / Between these swelling wrong-incensed peers.
Happy indeed, the way we've spent the day. Gloucester, we've done works of charity, making peace out of hostility and love out of hatred between these angry, aggrieved lords.

A blessed labour, my most sovereign lord,-- / Among this princely heap, if any here, / By false intelligence or wrong surmise, / Hold me a foe; / If I unwittingly, or in my rage, / Have aught committed that is hardly borne / To any in this presence, I desire / To reconcile me to his friendly peace: / 'Tis death to me to be at enmity; / I hate it, and desire all good men's love.-- / First, madam, I entreat true peace of you, / Which I will purchase with my duteous service;-- / Of you, my noble cousin Buckingham, / If ever any grudge were lodg'd between us;-- / Of you, and you, Lord Rivers, and of Dorset, / That all without desert have frown'd on me; / Of you, Lord Woodville, and, Lord Scales, of you;-- / Dukes, earls, lords, gentlemen;--indeed, of all. / I do not know that Englishman alive / With whom my soul is any jot at odds / More than the infant that is born to-night: / I thank my God for my humility.

A blessed work, my royal lord. If anyone in this princely company, through false information or wrong guesses, thinks I'm an enemy; if I have unknowingly or in anger done anything that someone here resents, I want to be reconciled with him in friendly peace. It's death to me to be on bad terms; I hate it and want all good men's love. First, madam, I beg true peace with you, which I'll earn with dutiful service; with you, my noble cousin Buckingham, if any grudge was ever lodged between us; with you, Lord Rivers, and with Dorset, who have frowned at me without cause; with you, Lord Woodville, and you, Lord Scales; dukes, earls, lords, gentlemen, in fact with everyone. I don't know any Englishman alive with whom my soul is any more at odds than a baby born tonight. I thank God for my humility.
A holy day shall this be kept hereafter:-- / I would to God all strifes were well compounded.-- / My sovereign lord, I do beseech your highness / To take our brother Clarence to your grace.
From now on this day will be kept as a holy day. I wish to God all quarrels were so well settled. My royal lord, I beg your highness to take our brother Clarence back into your favour.
Why, madam, have I off'red love for this, / To be so flouted in this royal presence? / Who knows not that the gentle duke is dead?
What, madam, have I offered love only to be mocked like this in the King's presence? Who doesn't know the gentle Duke is dead?
You do him injury to scorn his corse.
You wrong him by mocking his corpse.
Who knows not he is dead! Who knows he is?
Who doesn't know he's dead! Who knows he is?
All-seeing heaven, what a world is this!
All-seeing heaven, what a world this is!
Look I so pale, Lord Dorset, as the rest?
Am I as pale as the others, Lord Dorset?
Ay, my good lord; and no man in the presence / But his red colour hath forsook his cheeks.
Yes, my good lord, and there's no one here whose cheeks haven't lost their colour.
Is Clarence dead? the order was revers'd.
Is Clarence dead? The order was cancelled.

But he, poor man, by your first order died, / And that a winged Mercury did bear; / Some tardy cripple bore the countermand / That came too lag to see him buried. / God grant that some, less noble and less loyal, / Nearer in bloody thoughts, an not in blood, / Deserve not worse than wretched Clarence did, / And yet go current from suspicion!

But the poor man died by your first order, which a winged Mercury carried. Some slow cripple carried the cancellation, which arrived too late even to see him buried. God grant that some who are less noble and less loyal, closer to him in bloody thoughts though not in blood, who deserve worse than wretched Clarence, don't go about free of suspicion!
A boon, my sovereign, for my service done!
A favour, my lord, for the service I have done!
I pr'ythee, peace: my soul is full of sorrow.
Please be quiet. My soul is full of sorrow.
I Will not rise unless your highness hear me.
I won't get up unless your highness hears me.
Then say at once what is it thou request'st.
Then say at once what you are asking for.
The forfeit, sovereign, of my servant's life; / Who slew to-day a riotous gentleman / Lately attendant on the Duke of Norfolk.
The life of my servant, which is forfeit, my lord. Today he killed a rowdy gentleman who was until recently in the Duke of Norfolk's service.

Have I a tongue to doom my brother's death, / And shall that tongue give pardon to a slave? / My brother kill'd no man,--his fault was thought, / And yet his punishment was bitter death. / Who su'd to me for him? who, in my wrath, / Kneel'd at my feet, and bid me be advis'd? / Who spoke of brotherhood? who spoke of love? / Who told me how the poor soul did forsake / The mighty Warwick, and did fight for me? / Who told me, in the field at Tewksbury, / When Oxford had me down, he rescu'd me, / And said "Dear brother, live, and be a king"? / Who told me, when we both lay in the field / Frozen almost to death, how he did lap me / Even in his garments, and did give himself, / All thin and naked, to the numb-cold night? / All this from my remembrance brutish wrath / Sinfully pluck'd, and not a man of you / Had so much grace to put it in my mind. / But when your carters or your waiting-vassals / Have done a drunken slaughter, and defac'd / The precious image of our dear Redeemer, / You straight are on your knees for pardon, pardon; / And I, unjustly too, must grant it you:-- / But for my brother not a man would speak,-- / Nor I, ungracious, speak unto myself / For him, poor soul. The proudest of you all / Have been beholding to him in his life; / Yet none of you would once beg for his life.-- / O God, I fear Thy justice will take hold / On me, and you, and mine, and yours, for this! / Come, Hastings, help me to my closet. / Ah, poor Clarence!

Did I have a tongue to sentence my brother to death, and shall that tongue pardon a slave? My brother killed no one; his crime was only in thought, and yet his punishment was bitter death. Who pleaded with me for him? Who knelt at my feet in my anger and told me to think again? Who spoke of brotherhood, or love? Who reminded me how the poor soul left mighty Warwick and fought for me? Who reminded me how at Tewkesbury, when Oxford had me down, he rescued me and said, "Dear brother, live and be a king"? Who reminded me how, when we both lay in the field nearly frozen to death, he wrapped me in his own clothes and gave himself, thin and naked, to the numbing cold night? Brutal anger sinfully tore all this from my memory, and not one of you had the grace to remind me. But when your carters or servants kill someone in a drunken fight and deface the precious image of our dear Redeemer, you're on your knees at once begging pardon, pardon, and I, unjustly, have to grant it. But for my brother no one would speak, nor did I, ungracious as I am, speak to myself for him, poor soul. The proudest of you owed him something in his life, yet none of you would once beg for his life. O God, I fear your justice will seize on me, and you, and my family and yours, for this! Come, Hastings, help me to my room. Ah, poor Clarence!

This is the fruit of rashness! Mark'd you not / How that the guilty kindred of the queen / Look'd pale when they did hear of Clarence' death? / O, they did urge it still unto the king! / God will revenge it.--Come, lords, will you go / To comfort Edward with our company?

This is the result of rashness! Didn't you notice how the Queen's guilty relatives went pale when they heard of Clarence's death? Oh, they kept pushing the King to it! God will avenge it. Come, lords, shall we go and comfort Edward with our company?
Good grandam, tell us, is our father dead?
Good grandmother, tell us, is our father dead?
Why do you weep so oft, and beat your breast, / And cry "O Clarence, my unhappy son!"
Then why do you weep so often and beat your breast and cry, "O Clarence, my unhappy son"?
Why do you look on us, and shake your head, / And call us orphans, wretches, castaways, / If that our noble father were alive?
Why do you look at us and shake your head and call us orphans, wretches and outcasts, if our noble father is alive?
My pretty cousins, you mistake me both; / I do lament the sickness of the king, / As loath to lose him, not your father's death; / It were lost sorrow to wail one that's lost.

My pretty grandchildren, you both misunderstand me. I'm mourning the King's sickness because I don't want to lose him, not your father's death. It would be wasted sorrow to weep for someone already lost.
Then you conclude, my grandam, he is dead. / The king mine uncle is to blame for this: / God will revenge it; whom I will importune / With earnest prayers all to that effect.
Then you're saying he's dead, grandmother. My uncle the King is to blame for this. God will avenge it, and I'll pester him with earnest prayers to do it.
Peace, children, peace! the king doth love you well: / Incapable and shallow innocents, / You cannot guess who caus'd your father's death.
Quiet, children, quiet! The King loves you dearly. You innocent, simple children, you can't guess who caused your father's death.

Grandam, we can; for my good uncle Gloster / Told me, the king, provok'd to it by the queen, / Devis'd impeachments to imprison him: / And when my uncle told me so, he wept, / And pitied me, and kindly kiss'd my cheek; / Bade me rely on him as on my father, / And he would love me dearly as his child.

We can, grandmother. My good uncle Gloucester told me that the King, urged on by the Queen, invented charges to imprison him. And when my uncle told me, he wept and pitied me and kissed my cheek kindly, and told me to rely on him as on my father, and he would love me dearly as his own child.
Ah, that deceit should steal such gentle shape, / And with a virtuous visard hide deep vice! / He is my son; ay, and therein my shame; / Yet from my dugs he drew not this deceit.
Ah, that deceit should steal such a gentle shape and hide deep evil behind a virtuous mask! He is my son, yes, and that's my shame, but he didn't suck this deceit from my breast.
Think you my uncle did dissemble, grandam?
Do you think my uncle was pretending, grandmother?
I cannot think it.--Hark! what noise is this?
I can't believe it. Listen! What's that noise?
Ah, who shall hinder me to wail and weep, / To chide my fortune, and torment myself? / I'll join with black despair against my soul, / And to myself become an enemy.
Ah, who will stop me from wailing and weeping, cursing my fortune and tormenting myself? I'll side with black despair against my own soul and become my own enemy.
What means this scene of rude impatience?
What does this scene of wild distress mean?

To make an act of tragic violence:-- / Edward, my lord, thy son, our king, is dead.-- / Why grow the branches when the root is gone? / Why wither not the leaves that want their sap?-- / If you will live, lament; if die, be brief, / That our swift-winged souls may catch the king's; / Or, like obedient subjects, follow him / To his new kingdom of perpetual rest.

It's the act of a violent tragedy. Edward, my lord, your son, our king, is dead. Why do the branches grow when the root is gone? Why don't the leaves wither when they have no sap? If you want to live, mourn; if you want to die, be quick, so our swift-winged souls can catch the King's, or follow him like obedient subjects to his new kingdom of everlasting rest.

Ah, so much interest have I in thy sorrow / As I had title in thy noble husband! / I have bewept a worthy husband's death, / And liv'd by looking on his images: / But now two mirrors of his princely semblance / Are crack'd in pieces by malignant death, / And I for comfort have but one false glass, / That grieves me when I see my shame in him. / Thou art a widow, yet thou art a mother, / And hast the comfort of thy children left; / But death hath snatch'd my husband from mine arms, / And pluck'd two crutches from my feeble hands,-- / Clarence and Edward. O, what cause have I,-- / Thine being but a moiety of my moan,-- / To overgo thy woes and drown thy cries?

Ah, I have as great a share in your sorrow as I had a claim on your noble husband. I have wept for a worthy husband's death and lived by looking at his likenesses. But now two mirrors of his princely face have been smashed by malicious death, and for comfort I have only one false mirror, which grieves me when I see my shame in him. You're a widow, but you're a mother and still have the comfort of your children. But death has snatched my husband from my arms and plucked two crutches from my feeble hands, Clarence and Edward. Oh, since your grief is only half of mine, what better cause I have to outdo your woes and drown your cries!
Ah, aunt, you wept not for our father's death! / How can we aid you with our kindred tears?
Ah, aunt, you didn't weep for our father's death! How can we help you with family tears?
Our fatherless distress was left unmoan'd, / Your widow-dolour likewise be unwept!
Our grief at losing our father went unmourned; let your widow's grief go unwept too!

Give me no help in lamentation; / I am not barren to bring forth complaints: / All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes, / That I, being govern'd by the watery moon, / May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world! / Ah for my husband, for my dear Lord Edward!

Don't help me lament. I'm not barren; I can bring forth complaints. Let all springs channel their streams to my eyes, so that I, ruled by the watery moon, can pour out tears enough to drown the world! Ah, for my husband, my dear Lord Edward!
Ah for our father, for our dear Lord Clarence!
Ah, for our father, our dear Lord Clarence!
Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
Alas for both, both my sons, Edward and Clarence!
What stay had I but Edward? and he's gone.
What support did I have but Edward? And he's gone.
What stay had we but Clarence? and he's gone.
What support did we have but Clarence? And he's gone.
What stays had I but they? and they are gone.
What supports did I have but them? And they're gone.
Was never widow had so dear a loss!
No widow ever had so great a loss!
Were never orphans had so dear a loss!
No orphans ever had so great a loss!

Was never mother had so dear a loss! / Alas, I am the mother of these griefs! / Their woes are parcell'd, mine is general. / She for an Edward weeps, and so do I: / I for a Clarence weep, so doth not she: / These babes for Clarence weep, and so do I; / I for an Edward weep, so do not they:-- / Alas, you three, on me, threefold distress'd, / Pour all your tears! I am your sorrow's nurse, / And I will pamper it with lamentation.

No mother ever had so great a loss! Alas, I am the mother of these griefs! Their sorrows are divided; mine is the whole. She weeps for an Edward, and so do I. I weep for a Clarence; she doesn't. These children weep for Clarence, and so do I. I weep for an Edward; they don't. Alas, you three, pour all your tears on me, three times distressed! I'm your sorrow's nurse, and I'll feed it with lamentation.

Comfort, dear mother: God is much displeas'd / That you take with unthankfulness His doing: / In common worldly things 'tis called ungrateful, / With dull unwillingness to repay a debt / Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent; / Much more to be thus opposite with heaven, / For it requires the royal debt it lent you.

Take comfort, dear mother. God is very displeased that you receive his actions with ingratitude. In ordinary worldly matters it's called ungrateful to be reluctant to repay a debt that was generously lent. It's much worse to resist heaven like this because it asks back the royal debt it lent you.

Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother, / Of the young prince your son: send straight for him; / Let him be crown'd; in him your comfort lives. / Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave, / And plant your joys in living Edward's throne.

Madam, think like a careful mother of the young prince, your son. Send for him at once and have him crowned. Your comfort lives in him. Bury your desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave and plant your joys in living Edward's throne.

Sister, have comfort: all of us have cause / To wail the dimming of our shining star; / But none can help our harms by wailing them.-- / Madam, my mother, I do cry you mercy; / I did not see your grace:--humbly on my knee / I crave your blessing.

Take comfort, sister. We all have cause to weep for the dimming of our shining star, but nobody can mend our losses by weeping. Madam, my mother, I beg your pardon; I didn't see your grace. Humbly on my knee I ask your blessing.
God bless thee; and put meekness in thy breast, / Love, charity, obedience, and true duty!
God bless you, and put meekness in your heart, love, charity, obedience and true duty!
Amen! [Aside] / And make me die a good old man!-- / That is the butt end of a mother's blessing; / I marvel that her grace did leave it out.
Amen. (Aside) And make me die a good old man! That's the usual end of a mother's blessing. I'm surprised her grace left it out.

You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers, / That bear this heavy mutual load of moan, / Now cheer each other in each other's love: / Though we have spent our harvest of this king, / We are to reap the harvest of his son. / The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts, / But lately splinter'd, knit, and join'd together, / Must gently be preserv'd, cherish'd, and kept; / Me seemeth good that, with some little train, / Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fetched / Hither to London, to be crown'd our king.

You gloomy princes and heartsick lords who share this heavy load of grief, now cheer each other with your love for each other. Though we've used up our harvest from this king, we're about to reap the harvest of his son. The broken hatred of your swollen hearts, only recently splinted and knitted together, must be gently preserved, cherished and protected. I think it would be good for the young prince to be fetched at once from Ludlow to London with a small escort, to be crowned our king.
Why with some little train, my Lord of Buckingham?
Why with a small escort, my lord of Buckingham?

Marry, my lord, lest by a multitude, / The new-heal'd wound of malice should break out; / Which would be so much the more dangerous / By how much the estate is green and yet ungovern'd: / Where every horse bears his commanding rein / And may direct his course as please himself, / As well the fear of harm as harm apparent, / In my opinion, ought to be prevented.

Because, my lord, with a crowd, the newly healed wound of malice might break open again, which would be all the more dangerous while the state is new and still without a ruler. When every horse has its own reins and can steer wherever it likes, in my opinion the fear of harm should be prevented as much as obvious harm.
I hope the king made peace with all of us; / And the compact is firm and true in me.
I hope the King made peace among all of us. The agreement is firm and true on my part.

And so in me; and so, I think, in all: / Yet, since it is but green, it should be put / To no apparent likelihood of breach, / Which haply by much company might be urg'd: / Therefore I say with noble Buckingham, / That it is meet so few should fetch the prince.

And on mine, and, I think, on everyone's. Still, since it's so new, it shouldn't be put at any obvious risk of breaking, which a large crowd might cause. So I agree with noble Buckingham that only a few should fetch the prince.
Then be it so; and go we to determine / Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow. / Madam,--and you, my mother,--will you go / To give your censures in this business?
Then so be it. Let's go and decide who will ride to Ludlow at once. Madam, and you, my mother, will you come and give your opinions on this business?

My lord, whoever journeys to the prince, / For God'd sake, let not us two stay at home; / For by the way I'll sort occasion, / As index to the story we late talk'd of, / To part the queen's proud kindred from the Prince.

My lord, whoever goes to the prince, for God's sake let's not stay at home ourselves. On the way I'll find an opportunity, as a first step in the plan we talked about, to separate the Queen's proud relatives from the prince.
My other self, my counsel's consistory, / My oracle, my prophet!--my dear cousin, / I, as a child, will go by thy direction. / Toward Ludlow then, for we'll not stay behind.
My other self, my council chamber, my oracle, my prophet! My dear cousin, I'll follow your lead like a child. Off to Ludlow, then; we won't stay behind.
Good morrow, neighbour: whither away so fast?
Good morning, neighbour. Where are you off to so fast?
I promise you, I scarcely know myself: / Hear you the news abroad?
I promise you, I hardly know myself. Have you heard the news?
Yes, that the King is dead.
Ill news, by'r lady; seldom comes the better: / I fear, I fear 'twill prove a giddy world.
Bad news, by Our Lady. Things seldom get better. I fear, I fear the world will turn dizzy.
Doth the news hold of good King Edward's death?
Is the news true that good King Edward is dead?
Ay, sir, it is too true; God help the while!
Yes, sir, it's too true. God help us!
Then, masters, look to see a troublous world.
Then, gentlemen, expect a troubled world.
No, no; by God's good grace, his son shall reign.
No, no, by God's good grace his son will reign.
Woe to that land that's govern'd by a child!
Pity the country that's ruled by a child!
In him there is a hope of government, / Which, in his nonage, council under him, / And, in his full and ripen'd years, himself, / No doubt, shall then, and till then, govern well.
There's hope of good government in him. While he's under age his council will govern for him, and when he's fully grown he'll govern himself, and no doubt govern well then and until then.
So stood the state when Henry the Sixth / Was crown'd in Paris but at nine months old.
That's how things stood when Henry VI was crowned in Paris at only nine months old.
Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot; / For then this land was famously enrich'd / With politic grave counsel; then the king / Had virtuous uncles to protect his grace.
Did things stand like that? No, no, good friends, God knows. Back then this country was famously rich in wise, serious counsellors, and the King had virtuous uncles to protect him.
Why, so hath this, both by his father and mother.
Well, so has this one, on both his father's and his mother's side.

Better it were they all came by his father, / Or by his father there were none at all; / For emulation who shall now be nearest / Will touch us all too near, if God prevent not. / O, full of danger is the Duke of Gloster! / And the queen's sons and brothers haught and proud: / And were they to be rul'd, and not to rule, / This sickly land might solace as before.

It would be better if they were all on his father's side, or none at all on his father's side, because the rivalry over who will be closest to him will hurt us all, if God doesn't prevent it. The Duke of Gloucester is very dangerous, and the Queen's sons and brothers are haughty and proud. If they were ruled instead of ruling, this sick country might be comforted as before.
Come, come, we fear the worst; all will be well.
Come, come, we fear the worst. All will be well.

When clouds are seen, wise men put on their cloaks; / When great leaves fall, then winter is at hand; / When the sun sets, who doth not look for night? / Untimely storms make men expect a dearth. / All may be well; but, if God sort it so, / 'Tis more than we deserve or I expect.

When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks. When big leaves fall, winter is near. When the sun sets, who doesn't expect night? Storms out of season make men expect famine. All may be well, but if God arranges it so, it's more than we deserve or I expect.
Truly, the hearts of men are fun of fear: / You cannot reason almost with a man / That looks not heavily and fun of dread.
Truly, men's hearts are full of fear. You can hardly talk to a man who doesn't look gloomy and full of dread.

Before the days of change, still is it so: / By a divine instinct men's minds mistrust / Ensuing danger; as, by proof, we see / The water swell before a boisterous storm. / But leave it all to God.--Whither away?

It's always like that before times of change. By a God-given instinct, men's minds sense coming danger, just as we see the water swell before a violent storm. But leave it all to God. Where are you going?
Marry, we were sent for to the justices.
We've been summoned by the magistrates.
And so was I; I'll bear you company.
So have I. I'll come with you.
Last night, I hear, they at Northampton lay; / And at Stony-Stratford they do rest to-night: / To-morrow or next day they will be here.
I hear they stayed at Northampton last night, and they're resting at Stony Stratford tonight. They'll be here tomorrow or the next day.
I long with all my heart to see the prince: / I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.
I long with all my heart to see the prince. I hope he has grown a lot since I last saw him.
But I hear no; they say my son of York / Has almost overta'en him in his growth.
I hear he hasn't. They say my son York has almost caught up with him.
Ay, mother; but I would not have it so.
Yes, mother, but I wish he hadn't.
Why, my good cousin? it is good to grow.
Why, my good grandson? It's good to grow.

Grandam, one night as we did sit at supper, / My uncle Rivers talk'd how I did grow / More than my brother. "Ay," quoth my uncle Gloster, / "Small herbs have grace: great weeds do grow apace." / And since, methinks, I would not grow so fast, / Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.

Grandmother, one night at supper my uncle Rivers was talking about how I was growing more than my brother. "Yes," said my uncle Gloucester, "small herbs are graceful; big weeds grow fast." And since then I've wished I didn't grow so quickly, because sweet flowers are slow and weeds hurry.

Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold / In him that did object the same to thee: / He was the wretched'st thing when he was young, / So long a growing and so leisurely, / That, if his rule were true, he should be gracious.

Honestly, the saying didn't hold for the man who used it against you. He was the most wretched thing when he was young, and grew so slowly and lazily that, if his rule were true, he ought to be full of grace.
And so no doubt he is, my gracious madam.
And no doubt he is, my gracious madam.
I hope he is; but yet let mothers doubt.
I hope so, but let mothers have their doubts.
Now, by my troth, if I had been remember'd, / I could have given my uncle's grace a flout / To touch his growth nearer than he touch'd mine.
Now, honestly, if I'd remembered, I could have made a joke about my uncle's growth that hit harder than his did about mine.
How, my young York? I pr'ythee let me hear it.
How, my young York? Please let me hear it.
Marry, they say my uncle grew so fast / That he could gnaw a crust at two hours old: / 'Twas full two years ere I could get a tooth. / Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.
Well, they say my uncle grew so fast he could gnaw a crust when he was two hours old. It was a full two years before I got a tooth. Grandmother, that would have been a biting joke.
I pr'ythee, pretty York, who told thee this?
Please, pretty York, who told you this?
His nurse! why she was dead ere thou wast born.
His nurse! She died before you were born.
If 'twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.
If it wasn't her, I don't know who told me.
A parlous boy!--go to, you are too shrewd.
A dangerous boy! Stop it, you're too sharp.
Good madam, be not angry with the child.
Good madam, don't be angry with the child.
Such news, my lord, as grieves me to report.
News that grieves me to report, my lord.
Well, madam, and in good health.
Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret, / With them Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.
Lord Rivers and Lord Grey have been sent as prisoners to Pomfret, and Sir Thomas Vaughan with them.
The mighty dukes, Gloster and Buckingham.
The mighty dukes, Gloucester and Buckingham.
The sum of all I can, I have disclos'd; / Why or for what the nobles were committed / Is all unknown to me, my gracious lady.
I've told you all I know. Why, or for what, the noblemen were imprisoned I don't know at all, my gracious lady.

Ah me, I see the ruin of my house! / The tiger now hath seiz'd the gentle hind; / Insulting tyranny begins to jet / Upon the innocent and aweless throne:-- / Welcome, destruction, blood, and massacre! / I see, as in a map, the end of all.

Ah, I see the ruin of my family! The tiger has seized the gentle deer. Arrogant tyranny is starting to strut over the innocent throne that commands no fear. Welcome, destruction, blood and massacre! I see, as if on a map, how it will all end.

Accursed and unquiet wrangling days / How many of you have mine eyes beheld? / My husband lost his life to get the crown; / And often up and down my sons were toss'd / For me to joy and weep their gain and loss: / And being seated, and domestic broils / Clean over-blown, themselves, the conquerors / Make war upon themselves; brother to brother, / Blood to blood, self against self: O, preposterous / And frantic outrage, end thy damned spleen; / Or let me die, to look on death no more!

Cursed, restless days of quarrelling, how many of you have my eyes seen? My husband lost his life trying to win the crown, and my sons were tossed up and down so often that I rejoiced and wept at their gains and losses. And now they're on the throne and the civil wars are completely over, the winners make war on each other: brother against brother, blood against blood, self against self. Oh, unnatural, frantic outrage, end your damned fury, or let me die so I don't have to look at death any more!
Come, come, my boy; we will to sanctuary.-- / Madam, farewell.
Come, come, my boy, we'll go to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.
Stay, I will go with you.

[To the queen] My gracious lady, go. / And thither bear your treasure and your goods. / For my part, I'll resign unto your grace / The seal I keep; and so betide to me / As well I tender you and all of yours! / Go, I'll conduct you to the sanctuary.

(To the Queen) Go, my gracious lady, and take your treasure and possessions there. For my part, I'll hand over to your grace the Great Seal I hold, and may I fare as well as I serve you and yours! Come, I'll escort you to the sanctuary.
Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.
Welcome to London, sweet prince, to your royal city.
Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts' sovereign: / The weary way hath made you melancholy.
Welcome, dear nephew, ruler of my thoughts. The tiring journey has made you gloomy.
No, uncle; but our crosses on the way / Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy: / I want more uncles here to welcome me.
No, uncle, but our troubles on the way have made it tedious, tiring and heavy. I'd like more uncles here to welcome me.

Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years / Hath not yet div'd into the world's deceit: / Nor more can you distinguish of a man / Than of his outward show; which, God He knows, / Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart. / Those uncles which you want were dangerous; / Your grace attended to their sugar'd words / But look'd not on the poison of their hearts: / God keep you from them and from such false friends!

Sweet prince, the innocence of your youth hasn't yet looked deeply into the world's deceit. You can't judge a man except by his outward appearance, which, God knows, seldom or never matches his heart. Those uncles you want were dangerous. Your grace listened to their sugary words but didn't see the poison in their hearts. God keep you from them and from such false friends!
God keep me from false friends! but they were none.
God keep me from false friends! But they weren't false.
My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.
My lord, the Mayor of London is coming to greet you.
God bless your grace with health and happy days!
God bless your grace with health and happy days!
I thank you, good my lord;--and thank you all.
Thank you, my good lord, and thank you all.
I thought my mother and my brother York / Would long ere this have met us on the way: / Fie, what a slug is Hastings, that he comes not / To tell us whether they will come or no!
I thought my mother and my brother York would have met us on the way long ago. Shame, what a slug Hastings is, not coming to tell us whether they're coming or not!
And, in good time, here comes the sweating lord.
And here, just in time, comes the sweating lord.
Welcome, my lord: what, will our mother come?
Welcome, my lord. Well, is our mother coming?

On what occasion, God He knows, not I, / The queen your mother and your brother York / Have taken sanctuary: the tender prince / Would fain have come with me to meet your grace, / But by his mother was perforce withheld.
For what reason God knows, not I, the Queen your mother and your brother York have taken sanctuary. The young prince wanted to come with me to meet your grace, but his mother held him back by force.

Fie, what an indirect and peevish course / Is this of hers?--Lord cardinal, will your grace / Persuade the queen to send the Duke of York / Unto his princely brother presently? / If she deny, Lord Hastings, go with him, / And from her jealous arms pluck him perforce.

Shame, what a devious and stubborn way for her to behave! Lord Cardinal, will your grace persuade the Queen to send the Duke of York to his princely brother at once? If she refuses, Lord Hastings, go with him and pull the boy from her jealous arms by force.

My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory / Can from his mother win the Duke of York, / Anon expect him here; but if she be obdurate / To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid / We should infringe the holy privilege / Of blessed sanctuary! not for all this land / Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.

My lord of Buckingham, if my feeble powers of speech can win the Duke of York from his mother, expect him here soon. But if she won't give way to gentle pleading, God in heaven forbid that we should violate the holy right of blessed sanctuary! I wouldn't be guilty of so great a sin for this whole country.

You are too senseless-obstinate, my lord, / Too ceremonious and traditional: / Weigh it but with the grossness of this age, / You break not sanctuary in seizing him. / The benefit thereof is always granted / To those whose dealings have deserv'd the place / And those who have the wit to claim the place: / This prince hath neither claim'd it nor deserv'd it; / And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it: / Then, taking him from thence that is not there, / You break no privilege nor charter there. / Oft have I heard of sanctuary-men; / But sanctuary-children ne'er till now.

You're too stubbornly unreasonable, my lord, too formal and traditional. Judge it by the coarser standards of these times and you don't break sanctuary by seizing him. Its protection is always granted to those whose actions have earned the place and who have the sense to claim it. This prince hasn't claimed it or earned it, so in my opinion he can't have it. So in taking him from a place where he doesn't belong, you break no privilege or charter. I've often heard of sanctuary men, but never until now of sanctuary children.
My lord, you shall o'errule my mind for once.-- / Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
My lord, you'll overrule my mind this once. Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may.
Good lords, be as quick as you can.
Say, uncle Gloster, if our brother come, / Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?
Tell me, uncle Gloucester, if our brother comes, where shall we stay until our coronation?

Where it seems best unto your royal self. / If I may counsel you, some day or two / Your highness shall repose you at the Tower: / Then where you please and shall be thought most fit / For your best health and recreation.

Wherever seems best to your royal self. If I may advise you, your highness should rest at the Tower for a day or two, then go wherever you like and wherever is thought best for your health and recreation.
I do not like the Tower, of any place.-- / Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
I don't like the Tower, of all places. Did Julius Caesar build it, my lord?
He did, my gracious lord, begin that place; / Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.
He began it, my gracious lord, and later ages have rebuilt it since.
Is it upon record, or else reported / Successively from age to age, he built it?
Is it written down that he built it, or just passed on by word of mouth from age to age?
It's written down, my gracious lord.
But say, my lord, it were not register'd, / Methinks the truth should live from age to age, / As 'twere retail'd to all posterity, / Even to the general all-ending day.
But suppose, my lord, it weren't recorded. I think the truth should live from age to age, as if told to all future generations, right up to the Day of Judgement that ends everything.
[Aside] So wise so young, they say, do never live long.
(Aside) So wise and so young, they say, never live long.
I say, without characters, fame lives long.--
I say fame lives long without written records.
Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, / I moralize two meanings in one word.
So, like the stock Vice, Iniquity, in the old plays, I give one word two meanings.

That Julius Caesar was a famous man; / With what his valour did enrich his wit, / His wit set down to make his valour live; / Death makes no conquest of this conqueror; / For now he lives in fame, though not in life.-- / I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham,--

Julius Caesar was a famous man. What his courage added to his wisdom, his wisdom wrote down to keep his courage alive. Death has not conquered this conqueror, because he lives on in fame though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham...
An if I live until I be a man, / I'll win our ancient right in France again, / Or die a soldier as I liv'd a king.
If I live to be a man, I'll win back our ancient right to France, or die a soldier as I lived a king.
[Aside] Short summers lightly have a forward spring.
(Aside) Short summers usually have an early spring.
Now, in good time, here comes the Duke of York.
Now, just in time, here comes the Duke of York.
Richard of York! how fares our loving brother?
Richard of York! How is our loving brother?
Well, my dread lord; so must I call you now.
Well, my dread lord; that's what I must call you now.
Ay brother,--to our grief, as it is yours: / Too late he died that might have kept that title, / Which by his death hath lost much majesty.
Yes, brother, to our grief, as it is to yours. The man who should have kept that title died too soon, and his death has robbed it of much majesty.
How fares our cousin, noble Lord of York?
How is our nephew, the noble lord of York?
I thank you, gentle uncle. O, my lord, / You said that idle weeds are fast in growth: / The prince my brother hath outgrown me far.
Thank you, gentle uncle. My lord, you said useless weeds grow fast. The prince my brother has grown far taller than me.
O, my fair cousin, I must not say so.
Oh, my fair nephew, I mustn't say so.
Then he is more beholding to you than I.
Then he owes you more than I do.
He may command me as my sovereign; / But you have power in me as in a kinsman.
He can command me as my king, but you have a claim on me as a relative.
I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.
Please, uncle, give me this dagger.
My dagger, little cousin? with all my heart!
My dagger, little nephew? With all my heart!
Of my kind uncle, that I know will give, / And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.
From my kind uncle, who I know will give, and it's only a trinket, which costs nothing to give.
A greater gift than that I'll give my cousin.
I'll give my nephew a greater gift than that.
A greater gift! O, that's the sword to it!
A greater gift! Oh, the sword that goes with it!
Ay, gentle cousin, were it light enough.
Yes, gentle nephew, if it were light enough.
O, then, I see you will part but with light gifts; / In weightier things you'll say a beggar nay.
Oh, then I see you'll only part with light gifts. In weightier matters you'll say no to a beggar.
It is too heavy for your grace to wear.
It's too heavy for your grace to wear.
I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.
I'd think it light even if it were heavier.
What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
What, do you want my weapon, little lord?
I would, that I might thank you as you call me.
I do, so I can thank you the way you address me.
My Lord of York will still be cross in talk:-- / Uncle, your grace knows how to bear with him.
My lord of York is always contrary in his talk. Uncle, your grace knows how to bear with him.
You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me:-- / Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me; / Because that I am little, like an ape, / He thinks that you should bear me on your shoulders.
You mean to bear me, not bear with me. Uncle, my brother is mocking both of us. Because I'm small, like a monkey, he thinks you should carry me on your shoulders.
With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons! / To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle, / He prettily and aptly taunts himself: / So cunning and so young is wonderful.
What sharp wit he argues with! To soften the insult to his uncle, he cleverly and neatly mocks himself. So clever and so young: it's remarkable.
My lord, wil't please you pass along? / Myself and my good cousin Buckingham / Will to your mother, to entreat of her / To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
My lord, will you please go on? My good cousin Buckingham and I will go to your mother and ask her to meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?
What, are you going to the Tower, my lord?
My lord protector needs will have it so.
My lord Protector insists on it.
I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.
I won't sleep peacefully in the Tower.
Why, what should you be afraid of?
Marry, my uncle Clarence' angry ghost: / My grandam told me he was murder'd there.
My uncle Clarence's angry ghost. My grandmother told me he was murdered there.
I'm not afraid of dead uncles.
Nor none that live, I hope.
Nor of living ones, I hope.
An if they live, I hope I need not fear. / But come, my lord; and with a heavy heart, / Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.
If they're alive, I hope I needn't be afraid. But come, my lord. With a heavy heart, thinking of them, I'll go to the Tower.
Think you, my lord, this little prating York / Was not incensed by his subtle mother / To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?
Don't you think, my lord, this chattering little York was egged on by his crafty mother to taunt and insult you so shamefully?
No doubt, no doubt: O, 'tis a parlous boy; / Bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable: / He is all the mother's, from the top to toe.
No doubt, no doubt. Oh, he's a dangerous boy: bold, quick, clever, precocious, able. He's his mother's son from top to toe.

Well, let them rest.--Come hither, Catesby. / Thou art sworn as deeply to effect what we intend / As closely to conceal what we impart: / Thou know'st our reasons urg'd upon the way;-- / What think'st thou? is it not an easy matter / To make William Lord Hastings of our mind, / For the instalment of this noble duke / In the seat royal of this famous isle?

Well, leave them be. Come here, Catesby. You're sworn as deeply to carry out what we plan as to keep secret what we tell you. You heard our arguments on the way. What do you think? Won't it be easy to bring William, Lord Hastings, round to our view about installing this noble duke on the royal throne of this famous island?
He for his father's sake so loves the prince / That he will not be won to aught against him.
He loves the prince so much, for his father's sake, that nothing will win him over against him.
What think'st thou then of Stanley? will not he?
What do you think of Stanley, then? Won't he?
He will do all in all as Hastings doth.

Well then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby, / And, as it were far off, sound thou Lord Hastings / How he doth stand affected to our purpose; / And summon him to-morrow to the Tower, / To sit about the coronation. / If thou dost find him tractable to us, / Encourage him, and tell him all our reasons: / If he be leaden, icy, cold, unwilling, / Be thou so too; and so break off the talk, / And give us notice of his inclination: / For we to-morrow hold divided councils, / Wherein thyself shalt highly be employ'd.

Well then, just this. Go, gentle Catesby, and test Lord Hastings from a distance, as it were, to see how he feels about our plan. Summon him to the Tower tomorrow to sit in council about the coronation. If you find him open to us, encourage him and tell him all our reasons. If he is heavy, icy, cold and unwilling, be the same yourself, break off the conversation and let us know how he leans. Tomorrow we're holding separate councils, and you'll have an important part in them.

Commend me to Lord William: tell him, Catesby, / His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries / To-morrow are let blood at Pomfret Castle; / And bid my lord, for joy of this good news, / Give Mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.

Give my regards to Lord William. Tell him, Catesby, that his old gang of dangerous enemies will be bled at Pomfret Castle tomorrow, and tell my lord to celebrate the good news by giving Mistress Shore one more gentle kiss.
Good Catesby, go, effect this business soundly.
Good Catesby, go and do this business thoroughly.
My good lords both, with all the heed I can.
My good lords, I'll be as careful as I can.
Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?
Will we hear from you before we go to bed, Catesby?
At Crosby Place, there shall you find us both.
You'll find us both at Crosby Place.
Now, my lord, what shall we do if we perceive / Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?
Now, my lord, what shall we do if we see Lord Hastings won't go along with our plots?
Chop off his head. man;--somewhat we will do:-- / And, look when I am king, claim thou of me / The earldom of Hereford, and all the movables / Whereof the king my brother was possess'd.
Chop off his head, man. We'll do something. And remember, when I'm king, claim from me the earldom of Hereford and all the movable property that belonged to my brother the King.
I'll claim that promise at your grace's hand.
I'll hold your grace to that promise.
And look to have it yielded with all kindness. / Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards / We may digest our complots in some form.
And expect it to be granted with all kindness. Come, let's have supper early, so that afterwards we can put our plots into some shape.
Cannot my Lord Stanley sleep these tedious nights?
Can't my Lord Stanley sleep these long nights?
So it appears by that I have to say. / First, he commends him to your noble self.
So it seems from what I have to say. First, he sends his regards to your noble self.

Then certifies your lordship that this night / He dreamt the boar had razed off his helm: / Besides, he says there are two councils held; / And that may be determin'd at the one / Which may make you and him to rue at the other. / Therefore he sends to know your lordship's pleasure,-- / If you will presently take horse with him, / And with all speed post with him toward the north, / To shun the danger that his soul divines.

Then he informs your lordship that tonight he dreamed the boar had ripped his helmet off. Also, he says two councils are being held, and something may be decided in one that will make you and him regret attending the other. So he sends to ask what your lordship wants: whether you'll take horse with him at once and ride with all speed to the north to escape the danger his soul foresees.

Go, fellow, go, return unto thy lord; / Bid him not fear the separated councils: / His honour and myself are at the one, / And at the other is my good friend Catesby; / Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us / Whereof I shall not have intelligence. / Tell him his fears are shallow, without instance: / And for his dreams, I wonder he's so simple / To trust the mockery of unquiet slumbers: / To fly the boar before the boar pursues / Were to incense the boar to follow us, / And make pursuit where he did mean no chase. / Go, bid thy master rise and come to me; / And we will both together to the Tower, / Where, he shall see, the boar will use us kindly.

Go, fellow, go back to your lord. Tell him not to fear the separate councils. His honour and I are at one, and my good friend Catesby is at the other, where nothing that concerns us can happen without my hearing of it. Tell him his fears are shallow and groundless. As for his dreams, I'm amazed he's so simple as to trust the illusions of restless sleep. To run from the boar before the boar chases us would provoke the boar to follow us and start a hunt where he meant none. Go, tell your master to get up and come to me, and we'll go to the Tower together, where he'll see the boar will treat us kindly.
I'll go, my lord, and tell him what you say.
I'll go, my lord, and tell him what you say.
Many good morrows to my noble lord!
Many good mornings to my noble lord!
Good morrow, Catesby; you are early stirring: / What news, what news, in this our tottering state?
Good morning, Catesby. You're up early. What's the news in our tottering country?
It is a reeling world indeed, my lord; / And I believe will never stand upright / Till Richard wear the garland of the realm.
It's a reeling world indeed, my lord, and I believe it will never stand straight until Richard wears the garland of the kingdom.
How! wear the garland! dost thou mean the crown?
What! Wear the garland! Do you mean the crown?
I'll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders / Before I'll see the crown so foul misplac'd. / But canst thou guess that he doth aim at it?
I'll have this head of mine cut off before I see the crown so foully misplaced. But can you guess whether he's aiming at it?

Ay, on my life; and hopes to find you forward / Upon his party for the gain thereof: / And thereupon he sends you this good news,-- / That this same very day your enemies, / The kindred of the queen, must die at Pomfret.
Yes, on my life, and he hopes to find you eager on his side to win it. And so he sends you this good news: this very day your enemies, the Queen's relatives, are to die at Pomfret.

Indeed, I am no mourner for that news, / Because they have been still my adversaries: / But that I'll give my voice on Richard's side / To bar my master's heirs in true descent, / God knows I will not do it to the death.
Well, I don't mourn at that news, because they've always been my enemies. But as for supporting Richard to block my master's rightful heirs, God knows I'll never do it, even to my death.
God keep your lordship in that gracious mind!
God keep your lordship in that gracious mind!

But I shall laugh at this a twelve month hence,-- / That they which brought me in my master's hate, / I live to look upon their tragedy. / Well, Catesby, ere a fortnight make me older, / I'll send some packing that yet think not on't.

But I'll laugh about this a year from now: that I lived to see the tragedy of the people who turned my master against me. Well, Catesby, before I'm two weeks older, I'll send some others packing who don't expect it yet.
'Tis a vile thing to die, my gracious lord, / When men are unprepar'd and look not for it.
It's a terrible thing to die, my gracious lord, when men are unprepared and not expecting it.

O monstrous, monstrous! and so falls it out / With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey: and so 'twill do / With some men else that think themselves as safe / As thou and I; who, as thou knowest, are dear / To princely Richard and to Buckingham.

Oh, monstrous, monstrous! And so it turns out for Rivers, Vaughan and Grey, and so it will for some other men who think themselves as safe as you and I, who, as you know, are dear to princely Richard and to Buckingham.
The princes both make high account of you,--
The two princes think highly of you...
For they account his head upon the bridge.
(Aside) ...because they think his head will be on London Bridge.
I know they do, and I have well deserv'd it.
I know they do, and I've well deserved it.
Come on, come on; where is your boar-spear, man? / Fear you the boar, and go so unprovided?
Come on, come on, where's your boar spear, man? You fear the boar and go about unarmed?
My lord, good morrow; and good morrow, Catesby:-- / You may jest on, but, by the holy rood, / I do not like these several councils, I.
Good morning, my lord, and good morning, Catesby. You can joke, but by the holy cross, I don't like these separate councils.

My lord, I hold my life as dear as you do yours; / And never in my days, I do protest, / Was it so precious to me as 'tis now; / Think you, but that I know our state secure, / I would be so triumphant as I am?
My lord, I value my life as much as you value yours, and I swear it was never so precious to me as it is now. Do you think I'd be as triumphant as I am if I didn't know we were safe?

The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London, / Were jocund and suppos'd their states were sure,-- / And they, indeed, had no cause to mistrust; / But yet, you see, how soon the day o'ercast! / This sudden stab of rancour I misdoubt; / Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward. / What, shall we toward the Tower? the day is spent.

The lords at Pomfret were cheerful when they rode out of London and thought they were safe, and they had no reason to suspect anything. But you see how quickly the day clouded over. I distrust this sudden stroke of malice. I pray God I turn out to be a needless coward. Well, shall we go to the Tower? The day is getting on.
Come, come, have with you.--Wot you what, my lord? / To-day the lords you talk'd of are beheaded.
Come, come, I'm with you. Do you know what, my lord? The lords you spoke of are being beheaded today.
They, for their truth, might better wear their heads / Than some that have accus'd them wear their hats.-- / But come, my lord, let's away.
For their loyalty, they deserve to keep their heads more than some who accused them deserve to keep their hats. But come, my lord, let's go.
Go on before; I'll talk with this good fellow.
Go on ahead. I'll talk with this good fellow.
How now, sirrah! how goes the world with thee?
Well, fellow, how is the world treating you?
The better that your lordship please to ask.
All the better for your lordship asking.

I tell thee, man, 'tis better with me now / Than when thou mett'st me last where now we meet: / Then was I going prisoner to the Tower, / By the suggestion of the queen's allies; / But now, I tell thee,--keep it to thyself,-- / This day those enemies are put to death, / And I in better state than e'er I was.

I tell you, man, things are better for me now than when you last met me, here where we're meeting now. Then I was going to the Tower as a prisoner, at the urging of the Queen's allies. But now, I tell you, keep it to yourself, those enemies are being put to death today, and I'm better off than I've ever been.
God hold it, to your honour's good content!
God keep it so, to your honour's satisfaction!
Gramercy, fellow: there, drink that for me.
Thank you, fellow. There, drink that for me.
Well met, my lord; I am glad to see your honour.
Well met, my lord. I'm glad to see your honour.
I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart. / I am in your debt for your last exercise; / Come the next Sabbath, and I will content you.
Thank you with all my heart, good Sir John. I owe you for your last service. Come next Sunday and I'll pay you.
What, talking with a priest, lord chamberlain! / Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest; / Your honour hath no shriving work in hand.
What, talking with a priest, Lord Chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret need the priest. Your honour has no confessing to do.
Good faith, and when I met this holy man, / The men you talk of came into my mind.-- / What, go you toward the Tower?
Honestly, when I met this holy man, the men you mention came into my mind. Well, are you going to the Tower?
I do, my lord, but long I cannot stay there; / I shall return before your lordship thence.
I am, my lord, but I can't stay there long. I'll leave before your lordship.
Nay, like enough, for I stay dinner there.
Very likely, because I'm staying for dinner there.
[Aside] And supper too, although thou knowest it not.-- / Come, will you go?
(Aside) And supper too, though you don't know it. Come, shall we go?
Sir Richard Ratcliff, let me tell thee this,-- / To-day shalt thou behold a subject die / For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
Sir Richard Ratcliff, let me tell you this: today you'll see a subject die for truth, duty and loyalty.
God bless the prince from all the pack of you! / A knot you are of damned blood-suckers.
God protect the prince from the whole pack of you! You're a gang of damned bloodsuckers.
You live that shall cry woe for this hereafter.
Some of you alive now will cry out in grief for this later.
Despatch; the limit of your lives is out.
Hurry up. Your time is up.

O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison, / Fatal and ominous to noble peers! / Within the guilty closure of thy walls / Richard the Second here was hack'd to death: / And, for more slander to thy dismal seat, / We give to thee our guiltless blood to drink.

Pomfret, Pomfret! You bloody prison, fatal and ill-omened to noble lords! Inside your guilty walls Richard II was hacked to death here, and to bring more shame on your grim place, we give you our innocent blood to drink.
Now Margaret's curse is fallen upon our heads, / When she exclaim'd on Hastings, you, and I, / For standing by when Richard stabb'd her son.
Now Margaret's curse has fallen on our heads, when she cried out against Hastings, you and me for standing by while Richard stabbed her son.

Then curs'd she Richard, then curs'd she Buckingham, / Then curs'd she Hastings:--O, remember, God, / To hear her prayer for them, as now for us! / And for my sister, and her princely sons, / Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood, / Which, as Thou know'st, unjustly must be spilt.

She cursed Richard too, she cursed Buckingham, she cursed Hastings. Remember, God, to hear her prayer against them, as you have now against us! And as for my sister and her princely sons, be satisfied with our faithful blood, dear God, which, as you know, must be unjustly spilled.
Make haste; the hour of death is expiate.
Hurry. The hour of your death has come.
Come, Grey;--come, Vaughan;--let us here embrace. / Farewell, until we meet again in heaven.
Come, Grey; come, Vaughan; let's embrace here. Farewell, until we meet again in heaven.
Now, noble peers, the cause why we are met / Is to determine of the coronation. / In God's name speak,--when is the royal day?
Now, noble lords, we've met to decide about the coronation. In God's name, speak: when is the royal day?
Are all things ready for that royal time?
Is everything ready for that royal occasion?
Thery are, and wants but nomination.
It is, and only the date needs naming.
To-morrow, then, I judge a happy day.
Then I think tomorrow would be a happy day.
Who knows the lord protector's mind herein? / Who is most inward with the noble duke?
Who knows the Lord Protector's mind on this? Who is closest to the noble duke?
Your grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
We think your grace would be the first to know his mind.
We know each other's faces: for our hearts, / He knows no more of mine than I of yours; / Or I of his, my lord, than you of mine.-- / Lord Hastings, you and he are near in love.
We know each other's faces. As for our hearts, he knows no more of mine than I know of yours, my lord, or I of his than you of mine. Lord Hastings, you and he are close friends.

I thank his grace, I know he loves me well; / But for his purpose in the coronation / I have not sounded him, nor he deliver'd / His gracious pleasure any way therein: / But you, my honourable lords, may name the time; / And in the duke's behalf I'll give my voice, / Which, I presume, he'll take in gentle part.

I thank his grace; I know he loves me well. But I haven't sounded him out about his intentions for the coronation, nor has he told me his wishes in any way. But you, my honourable lords, can name the day, and I'll speak for the Duke, which I'm sure he'll take kindly.
In happy time, here comes the duke himself.
Just in time, here comes the Duke himself.
My noble lords and cousins all, good morrow. / I have been long a sleeper; but I trust / My absence doth neglect no great design / Which by my presence might have been concluded.
Good morning, my noble lords and cousins all. I've slept late, but I trust my absence hasn't held up any great business that my presence could have settled.
Had you not come upon your cue, my lord, / William Lord Hastings had pronounc'd your part,-- / I mean, your voice,--for crowning of the king.
If you hadn't come on your cue, my lord, William, Lord Hastings, would have spoken your part, I mean, your vote, on crowning the King.

Than my Lord Hastings no man might be bolder; / His lordship knows me well and loves me well.-- / My lord of Ely, when I was last in Holborn / I saw good strawberries in your garden there: / I do beseech you send for some of them.

No man could be bolder with me than my Lord Hastings. His lordship knows me well and loves me well. My lord of Ely, when I was last in Holborn I saw good strawberries in your garden there. Please send for some.
Marry, and will, my lord, with all my heart.
Indeed I will, my lord, with all my heart.
Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you.
Cousin Buckingham, a word with you.

Catesby hath sounded Hastings in our business, / And finds the testy gentleman so hot / That he will lose his head ere give consent / His master's child, as worshipfully he terms it, / Shall lose the royalty of England's throne.

Catesby has sounded out Hastings on our business and finds the touchy gentleman so heated that he'll lose his head before he agrees that his master's child, as he respectfully calls him, should lose the royal throne of England.
Withdraw yourself awhile; I'll go with you.
Step aside for a while; I'll come with you.
We have not yet set down this day of triumph. / To-morrow, in my judgment, is too sudden; / For I myself am not so well provided / As else I would be, were the day prolong'd.
We still haven't fixed this day of celebration. In my opinion tomorrow is too soon, because I'm not as well prepared as I would be if the day were put off.
Where is my lord the Duke of Gloster? / I have sent for these strawberries.
Where is my lord the Duke of Gloucester? I've sent for those strawberries.

His grace looks cheerfully and smooth this morning; / There's some conceit or other likes him well / When that he bids good morrow with such spirit. / I think there's ne'er a man in Christendom / Can lesser hide his love or hate than he; / For by his face straight shall you know his heart.

His grace looks cheerful and calm this morning. Some thought or other pleases him, when he says good morning so heartily. I don't think there's a man in Christendom who can hide his love or hatred less than he can, because you can read his heart in his face at once.
What of his heart perceive you in his face / By any livelihood he showed to-day?
What have you seen of his heart in his face, from any liveliness he showed today?
Marry, that with no man here he is offended; / For, were he, he had shown it in his looks.
Why, that he isn't offended with anyone here, because if he were, it would have shown in his looks.
I pray you all, tell me what they deserve / That do conspire my death with devilish plots / Of damned witchcraft, and that have prevail'd / Upon my body with their hellish charms?
I ask you all, tell me what people deserve who conspire my death with devilish plots of damned witchcraft and have overpowered my body with their hellish spells?
The tender love I bear your grace, my lord, / Makes me most forward in this princely presence / To doom the offenders: whosoe'er they be. / I say, my lord, they have deserved death.
The tender love I have for your grace, my lord, makes me the first in this princely company to condemn the offenders, whoever they are. I say, my lord, they deserve death.

Then be your eyes the witness of their evil: / Look how I am bewitch'd; behold, mine arm / Is, like a blasted sapling, wither'd up: / And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, / Consorted with that harlot-strumpet Shore, / That by their witchcraft thus have marked me.

Then let your eyes witness their evil. Look how I'm bewitched. See, my arm is shrivelled like a blighted sapling. And it's Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, together with that harlot Shore, who have marked me like this with their witchcraft.
If they have done this deed, my noble lord,--
If they have done this, my noble lord...

If!--thou protector of this damned strumpet, / Talk'st thou to me of "ifs"?--Thou art a traitor:-- / Off with his head!--now, by Saint Paul I swear, / I will not dine until I see the same.-- / Lovel and Ratcliff:--look that it be done:-- / The rest, that love me, rise and follow me.

If? You protector of this damned whore, are you talking to me of "ifs"? You're a traitor. Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul, I swear I won't have dinner until I've seen it done. Lovel and Ratcliff, see that it's done. The rest of you who love me, get up and follow me.

Woe, woe, for England! not a whit for me; / For I, too fond, might have prevented this. / Stanley did dream the boar did raze his helm; / And I did scorn it, and disdain to fly. / Three times to-day my foot-cloth horse did stumble, / And started, when he look'd upon the Tower, / As loth to bear me to the slaughter-house. / O, now I need the priest that spake to me: / I now repent I told the pursuivant, / As too triumphing, how mine enemies / To-day at Pomfret bloodily were butcher'd, / And I myself secure in grace and favour. / O Margaret, Margaret, now thy heavy curse / Is lighted on poor Hastings' wretched head!

Woe for England, not a bit for me, because I was too foolish; I could have prevented this. Stanley dreamed the boar ripped off his helmet, and I scorned it and refused to run. Three times today my horse stumbled and shied when he looked at the Tower, as if he didn't want to carry me to the slaughterhouse. Oh, now I need the priest who spoke to me. Now I regret telling the pursuivant so triumphantly how my enemies were bloodily butchered at Pomfret today, while I was safe in favour. O Margaret, Margaret, now your heavy curse has landed on poor Hastings' wretched head!
Come, come, despatch; the duke would be at dinner: / Make a short shrift; he longs to see your head.
Come, come, hurry up. The Duke wants his dinner. Make your confession short; he's longing to see your head.

O momentary grace of mortal men, / Which we more hunt for than the grace of God! / Who builds his hope in air of your good looks / Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, / Ready, with every nod, to tumble down / Into the fatal bowels of the deep.

The fleeting favour of mortal men, which we chase more than the grace of God! Whoever builds his hopes on the air of your smiles lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, ready at every lurch to tumble down into the deadly depths of the sea.
Come, come, despatch; 'tis bootless to exclaim.
Come, come, hurry. It's no use crying out.

O bloody Richard!--miserable England! / I prophesy the fearfull'st time to thee / That ever wretched age hath look'd upon.-- / Come, lead me to the block; bear him my head: / They smile at me who shortly shall be dead.

O bloody Richard! Miserable England! I prophesy the most fearful time for you that any wretched age has seen. Come, take me to the block. Take him my head. Those who smile at me will soon be dead themselves.
Come, cousin, canst thou quake and change thy colour, / Murder thy breath in middle of a word, / And then again begin, and stop again, / As if thou were distraught and mad with terror?
Come, cousin, can you tremble and turn pale, choke your breath in the middle of a word, start again and stop again, as if you were frantic and mad with terror?

Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian; / Speak and look back, and pry on every side, / Tremble and start at wagging of a straw, / Intending deep suspicion: ghastly looks / Are at my service, like enforced smiles; / And both are ready in their offices, / At any time to grace my stratagems. / But what, is Catesby gone?

Tut, I can act the great tragic actor: speak and look behind me, peer all around, tremble and jump at a straw moving, pretending deep suspicion. Ghastly looks are at my service, like forced smiles, and both are ready to do their jobs at any time to dress up my tricks. But is Catesby gone?
He is; and, see, he brings the mayor along.
He is, and look, he's bringing the Mayor.
Lord Mayor, the reason we have sent,--
Lord Mayor, the reason we sent for you...
Look back, defend thee,--here are enemies.
Look behind you, defend yourself, here are enemies!
God and our innocency defend and guard us!
God and our innocence defend and protect us!
