Be patient; they are friends,--Ratcliff and Lovel.
Calm down; they're friends, Ratcliff and Lovel.
Here is the head of that ignoble traitor, / The dangerous and unsuspected Hastings.
Here is the head of that shameful traitor, the dangerous, unsuspected Hastings.

So dear I lov'd the man that I must weep. / I took him for the plainest harmless creature / That breath'd upon the earth a Christian; / Made him my book, wherein my soul recorded / The history of all her secret thoughts: / So smooth he daub'd his vice with show of virtue / That, his apparent open guilt omitted,-- / I mean, his conversation with Shore's wife,-- / He liv'd from all attainder of suspects.

I loved the man so dearly that I have to weep. I took him for the most straightforward, harmless creature who ever lived as a Christian on earth. I made him my book, in which my soul wrote the history of all its secret thoughts. He covered his vice so smoothly with a show of virtue that, apart from his obvious open guilt, I mean his affair with Shore's wife, he lived free of any taint of suspicion.

Well, well, he was the covert'st shelter'd traitor / That ever liv'd.-- / Would you imagine, or almost believe,-- / Were't not that by great preservation / We live to tell it you,--that the subtle traitor / This day had plotted, in the council-house, / To murder me and my good Lord of Gloster!

Well, well, he was the most secretly sheltered traitor who ever lived. Would you imagine, or hardly believe, if by God's great protection we weren't alive to tell you, that the crafty traitor had plotted today in the council chamber to murder me and my good lord of Gloucester?

What! think you we are Turks or Infidels? / Or that we would, against the form of law, / Proceed thus rashly in the villain's death, / But that the extreme peril of the case, / The peace of England and our persons' safety, / Enforc'd us to this execution?

What! Do you think we're Turks or heathens, or that we'd go against the forms of law and rush the villain to his death like this, if the extreme danger of the situation, the peace of England and our own safety, hadn't forced us to execute him?

Now, fair befall you! he deserv'd his death; / And your good graces both have well proceeded, / To warn false traitors from the like attempts. / I never look'd for better at his hands / After he once fell in with Mistress Shore.
Good fortune to you! He deserved his death, and both your graces have done well to warn false traitors off similar attempts. I never expected better of him once he took up with Mistress Shore.

Yet had we not determin'd he should die / Until your lordship came to see his end; / Which now the loving haste of these our friends, / Something against our meanings, have prevented: / Because, my lord, we would have had you heard / The traitor speak, and timorously confess / The manner and the purpose of his treasons; / That you might well have signified the same / Unto the citizens, who haply may / Misconster us in him, and wail his death.

Yet we hadn't decided he should die until your lordship came to see his end, which the loving haste of our friends here has prevented, rather against our wishes. Because, my lord, we wanted you to hear the traitor speak and fearfully confess how and why he committed his treasons, so that you could report it to the citizens, who might misjudge us over him and mourn his death.

But, my good lord, your grace's word shall serve / As well as I had seen and heard him speak: / And do not doubt, right noble princes both, / But I'll acquaint our duteous citizens / With all your just proceedings in this case.

But, my good lord, your grace's word will serve as well as if I had seen and heard him speak. And don't doubt, most noble princes both, that I'll inform our loyal citizens of your just actions in this case.
And to that end we wish'd your lordship here, / To avoid the the the censures of the carping world.
That's why we wanted your lordship here, to avoid the criticism of the fault-finding world.
But since you come too late of our intent, / Yet witness what you hear we did intend: / And so, my good lord mayor, we bid farewell.
But since you came too late for what we intended, at least witness what you've heard we intended. And so, my good Lord Mayor, farewell.

Go, after, after, cousin Buckingham. / The Mayor towards Guildhall hies him in all post:-- / There, at your meet'st advantage of the time, / Infer the bastardy of Edward's children: / Tell them how Edward put to death a citizen, / Only for saying he would make his son / Heir to the crown;--meaning, indeed, his house, / Which, by the sign thereof, was termed so. / Moreover, urge his hateful luxury, / And bestial appetite in change of lust; / Which stretch'd unto their servants, daughters, wives, / Even where his raging eye or savage heart, / Without control, listed to make a prey. / Nay, for a need, thus far come near my person:-- / Tell them, when that my mother went with child / Of that insatiate Edward, noble York, / My princely father, then had wars in France / And, by true computation of the time, / Found that the issue was not his begot; / Which well appeared in his lineaments, / Being nothing like the noble duke my father. / Yet touch this sparingly, as 'twere far off; / Because, my lord, you know my mother lives.

Go after him, after him, cousin Buckingham. The Mayor is rushing to the Guildhall. There, at the best moment you can find, hint that Edward's children are illegitimate. Tell them how Edward put a citizen to death just for saying he would make his son heir to the Crown, meaning in fact his house, which was called that from its sign. Also stress his hateful lechery and his animal appetite for variety in lust, which reached out to their servants, daughters and wives, wherever his raging eye or savage heart chose to take a victim without restraint. And if need be, come this close to me: tell them that when my mother was pregnant with that insatiable Edward, my princely father, noble York, was away at war in France, and by correctly counting the time found the child wasn't his, which showed in his features, since he was nothing like the noble Duke my father. But touch on this sparingly, as if from a distance, because, my lord, you know my mother is alive.
Doubt not, my lord, I'll play the orator / As if the golden fee for which I plead / Were for myself: and so, my lord, adieu.
Don't worry, my lord, I'll play the orator as if the golden prize I'm pleading for were for myself. And so, my lord, goodbye.
If you thrive well, bring them to Baynard's Castle; / Where you shall find me well accompanied / With reverend fathers and well learned bishops.
If you succeed, bring them to Baynard's Castle, where you'll find me in the company of reverend fathers and learned bishops.
I go; and towards three or four o'clock / Look for the news that the Guildhall affords.
I'm going. Expect news from the Guildhall around three or four o'clock.
Go, Lovel, with all speed to Doctor Shaw.-- / Go thou [to CATESBY] to Friar Penker;--bid them both / Meet me within this hour at Baynard's Castle.
Go with all speed to Doctor Shaw, Lovel. (To Catesby) You go to Friar Penker. Tell them both to meet me within the hour at Baynard's Castle.
Now will I in, to take some privy order / To draw the brats of Clarence out of sight; / And to give order that no manner person / Have any time recourse unto the princes.
Now I'll go in and give secret orders to get Clarence's brats out of sight, and order that no one at all is to have access to the princes at any time.

Here is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings; / Which in a set hand fairly is engross'd, / That it may be to-day read o'er in Paul's. / And mark how well the sequel hangs together:-- / Eleven hours I have spent to write it over, / For yesternight by Catesby was it sent me; / The precedent was full as long a-doing: / And yet within these five hours Hastings liv'd, / Untainted, unexamin'd, free, at liberty. / Here's a good world the while! Who is so gross / That cannot see this palpable device! / Yet who so bold but says he sees it not! / Bad is the world; and all will come to naught, / When such ill dealing must be seen in thought.

Here's the indictment of the good Lord Hastings, neatly written out in a formal hand so that it can be read aloud at St Paul's today. And notice how well the sequence fits together. I've spent eleven hours copying it, because Catesby sent it to me last night. The draft took just as long to write. And yet five hours ago Hastings was alive, unaccused, unquestioned, free. What a fine world this is! Who is so stupid he can't see this obvious trick? Yet who is bold enough to say he sees it? The world is bad, and everything will come to nothing when such crooked dealing can only be seen in silence.
How now, how now! what say the citizens?
Well, well! What do the citizens say?
Now, by the holy mother of our Lord, / The citizens are mum, say not a word.
By the holy mother of our Lord, the citizens are dumb and don't say a word.
Touch'd you the bastardy of Edward's children?
Did you touch on the illegitimacy of Edward's children?

I did; with his contract with Lady Lucy, / And his contract by deputy in France; / The insatiate greediness of his desires, / And his enforcement of the city wives; / His tyranny for trifles; his own bastardy,-- / As being got, your father then in France, / And his resemblance, being not like the duke: / Withal I did infer your lineaments,-- / Being the right idea of your father, / Both in your form and nobleness of mind; / Laid open all your victories in Scotland, / Your discipline in war, wisdom in peace, / Your bounty, virtue, fair humility; / Indeed, left nothing fitting for your purpose / Untouch'd or slightly handled in discourse: / And when mine oratory drew toward end / I bid them that did love their country's good / Cry "God save Richard, England's royal king!"

I did, along with his betrothal to Lady Lucy and his betrothal by proxy in France, the insatiable greed of his desires and his forcing of the citizens' wives, his tyranny over trifles, his own illegitimacy, since he was conceived while your father was in France, and the fact that he didn't look like the Duke. At the same time I pointed to your features, the true image of your father in both looks and nobility of mind. I laid out all your victories in Scotland, your discipline in war, your wisdom in peace, your generosity, virtue and fine humility. In fact I left nothing useful to your purpose untouched or lightly handled. And when my speech was coming to an end, I told those who loved their country's good to cry, "God save Richard, England's royal king!"

No, so God help me, they spake not a word; / But, like dumb statues or breathing stones, / Star'd each on other, and look'd deadly pale. / Which when I saw, I reprehended them; / And ask'd the mayor what meant this wilful silence: / His answer was--the people were not us'd / To be spoke to but by the recorder. / Then he was urg'd to tell my tale again,-- / "Thus saith the duke, thus hath the duke inferr'd;" / But nothing spoke in warrant from himself. / When he had done, some followers of mine own, / At lower end of the hall hurl'd up their caps, / And some ten voices cried, "God save King Richard!" / And thus I took the vantage of those few,-- / "Thanks, gentle citizens and friends," quoth I; / "This general applause and cheerful shout / Argues your wisdoms and your love to Richard:" / And even here brake off and came away.

No, so help me God, they didn't say a word. Like dumb statues or breathing stones they stared at each other and went deathly pale. When I saw that, I told them off and asked the Mayor what this stubborn silence meant. His answer was that the people weren't used to being addressed by anyone except the Recorder. Then the Recorder was pressed to repeat my speech: "This is what the Duke says, this is what the Duke argues," but said nothing on his own authority. When he'd finished, some of my own followers at the bottom of the hall threw their caps in the air, and about ten voices shouted, "God save King Richard!" So I took advantage of those few. "Thank you, gentle citizens and friends," I said. "This general applause and cheerful shout shows your wisdom and your love for Richard." And there I broke off and came away.
What, tongueless blocks were they! would they not speak? / Will not the mayor, then, and his brethren, come?
What tongueless blocks they were! Wouldn't they speak? Then won't the Mayor and his colleagues come?

The mayor is here at hand. Intend some fear; / Be not you spoke with but by mighty suit: / And look you get a prayer-book in your hand, / And stand between two churchmen, good my lord; / For on that ground I'll make a holy descant: / And be not easily won to our requests; / Play the maid's part,--still answer nay, and take it.

The Mayor is close by. Pretend to be afraid. Don't agree to talk to them except after strong pleading. Make sure you have a prayer book in your hand and stand between two churchmen, my good lord, because I'll compose a holy tune on that theme. And don't be easily won over by our requests. Play the girl's part: keep saying no, and take it.
I go; and if you plead as well for them / As I can say nay to thee for myself, / No doubt we bring it to a happy issue.
I'm going. If you plead as well for them as I say no to you for myself, no doubt we'll bring it to a happy end.
Go, go, up to the leads; the lord mayor knocks.
Go, go, up to the roof. The Lord Mayor is knocking.
Welcome, my lord. I dance attendance here; / I think the duke will not be spoke withal.
Welcome, my lord. I've been kept waiting here. I don't think the Duke will speak to anyone.
Now, Catesby,--what says your lord to my request?
Now, Catesby, what does your lord say to my request?

He doth entreat your grace, my noble lord, / To visit him to-morrow or next day: / He is within, with two right reverend fathers, / Divinely bent to meditation: / And in no worldly suit would he be mov'd, / To draw him from his holy exercise.

He begs your grace, my noble lord, to visit him tomorrow or the next day. He's inside with two very reverend fathers, devoutly given to meditation, and no worldly request will move him to leave his holy exercise.

Return, good Catesby, to the gracious duke; / Tell him, myself, the mayor and aldermen, / In deep designs, in matter of great moment, / No less importing than our general good, / Are come to have some conference with his grace.

Go back, good Catesby, to the gracious Duke. Tell him that I, the Mayor and the aldermen have come to talk with his grace about serious plans and matters of great importance, concerning nothing less than our common good.
I'll signify so much unto him straight.
I'll tell him so at once.

Ah, ha, my lord, this prince is not an Edward! / He is not lolling on a lewd day-bed, / But on his knees at meditation; / Not dallying with a brace of courtezans, / But meditating with two deep divines; / Not sleeping, to engross his idle body, / But praying, to enrich his watchful soul: / Happy were England would this virtuous prince / Take on his grace the sovereignty thereof: / But, sure, I fear, we shall not win him to it.

Ah ha, my lord, this prince is no Edward! He isn't lolling on a lewd couch but on his knees in meditation; not toying with a pair of courtesans but meditating with two deep theologians; not sleeping to fatten his idle body but praying to enrich his watchful soul. England would be happy if this virtuous prince would take on its sovereignty himself. But I'm afraid we won't win him to it.
Marry, God defend his grace should say us nay!
God forbid his grace should say no to us!
I fear he will. Here Catesby comes again.
I'm afraid he will. Here comes Catesby again.
Now, Catesby, what says his grace?
Now, Catesby, what does his grace say?
He wonders to what end you have assembled / Such troops of citizens to come to him: / His grace not being warn'd thereof before, / He fears, my lord, you mean no good to him.
He wonders why you have gathered such crowds of citizens to come to him. Since his grace wasn't warned of it in advance, he fears, my lord, you mean him no good.
Sorry I am my noble cousin should / Suspect me, that I mean no good to him: / By heaven, we come to him in perfect love; / And so once more return and tell his grace.
I'm sorry my noble cousin suspects I mean him no good. By heaven, we come to him in perfect love. Go back once more and tell his grace so.
When holy and devout religious men / Are at their beads, 'tis much to draw them thence,-- / So sweet is zealous contemplation.
When holy and devout religious men are at their prayers, it's hard to draw them away, contemplation is so sweet to them.
See where his grace stands 'tween two clergymen!
Look, there's his grace standing between two clergymen!

Two props of virtue for a Christian prince, / To stay him from the fall of vanity: / And, see, a book of prayer in his hand,-- / True ornaments to know a holy man.-- / Famous Plantagenet, most gracious prince, / Lend favourable ear to our requests; / And pardon us the interruption / Of thy devotion and right Christian zeal.

Two props of virtue for a Christian prince, to keep him from falling into vanity. And see, a prayer book in his hand, the true marks of a holy man. Famous Plantagenet, most gracious prince, listen kindly to our requests and forgive us for interrupting your devotion and true Christian zeal.

My lord, there needs no such apology: / I rather do beseech you pardon me, / Who, earnest in the service of my God, / Deferr'd the visitation of my friends. / But, leaving this, what is your grace's pleasure?

My lord, there's no need for such an apology. Rather, I beg you to forgive me for putting off my friends' visit while I was absorbed in the service of my God. But leaving that aside, what does your grace want?
Even that, I hope, which pleaseth God above, / And all good men of this ungovern'd isle.
What I hope pleases God above and all good men in this ungoverned island.
I do suspect I have done some offence / That seems disgracious in the city's eye; / And that you come to reprehend my ignorance.
I suspect I've done something that looks disgraceful in the city's eyes, and you've come to rebuke my ignorance.
You have, my lord: would it might please your grace, / On our entreaties, to amend your fault!
You have, my lord. If only your grace would agree, at our pleading, to correct your fault!
Else wherefore breathe I in a Christian land?
Why else do I live in a Christian country?

Know then, it is your fault that you resign / The supreme seat, the throne majestical, / The scepter'd office of your ancestors, / Your state of fortune and your due of birth, / The lineal glory of your royal house, / To the corruption of a blemish'd stock: / Whilst, in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts,-- / Which here we waken to our country's good,-- / The noble isle doth want her proper limbs; / Her face defac'd with scars of infamy, / Her royal stock graft with ignoble plants, / And almost shoulder'd in the swallowing gulf / Of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion. / Which to recure, we heartily solicit / Your gracious self to take on you the charge / And kingly government of this your land;-- / Not as protector, steward, substitute, / Or lowly factor for another's gain; / But as successively, from blood to blood, / Your right of birth, your empery, your own. / For this, consorted with the citizens, / Your very worshipful and loving friends, / And, by their vehement instigation, / In this just cause come I to move your grace.

Then know that your fault is giving up the supreme seat, the majestic throne, the sceptred office of your ancestors, your fortune and your birthright, the inherited glory of your royal house, to the corruption of a tainted family tree. Meanwhile, in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts, which we are waking here for our country's good, this noble island lacks its proper limbs. Its face is scarred with disgrace, its royal stock grafted with low-born plants, and it has almost been pushed into the swallowing pit of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion. To cure this, we earnestly ask your gracious self to take on the responsibility and kingly government of this land of yours, not as Protector, steward, deputy or humble agent for someone else's profit, but as your birthright passed down in your bloodline, your empire, your own. For this, together with the citizens, your very worshipful and loving friends, and at their urgent request, I come to move your grace in this just cause.

I cannot tell if to depart in silence / Or bitterly to speak in your reproof / Best fitteth my degree or your condition: / If not to answer, you might haply think / Tongue-tied ambition, not replying, yielded / To bear the golden yoke of sovereignty, / Which fondly you would here impose on me; / If to reprove you for this suit of yours, / So season'd with your faithful love to me, / Then, on the other side, I check'd my friends. / Therefore,--to speak, and to avoid the first, / And then, in speaking, not to incur the last,-- / Definitively thus I answer you. / Your love deserves my thanks; but my desert / Unmeritable shuns your high request. / First, if all obstacles were cut away, / And that my path were even to the crown, / As the ripe revenue and due of birth, / Yet so much is my poverty of spirit, / So mighty and so many my defects, / That I would rather hide me from my greatness,-- / Being a bark to brook no mighty sea,-- / Than in my greatness covet to be hid, / And in the vapour of my glory smother'd. / But, God be thank'd, there is no need of me,-- / And much I need to help you, were there need;-- / The royal tree hath left us royal fruit, / Which, mellow'd by the stealing hours of time, / Will well become the seat of majesty, / And make, no doubt, us happy by his reign. / On him I lay that you would lay on me,-- / The right and fortune of his happy stars; / Which God defend that I should wring from him!

I can't tell whether it better suits my rank or your position for me to leave in silence or to speak bitterly against you. If I don't answer, you might think that tongue-tied ambition, by not replying, agreed to bear the golden yoke of kingship that you foolishly want to put on me. If I rebuke you for this request, so full of your loyal love for me, then on the other hand I'd be scolding my friends. So, to speak and avoid the first, and in speaking not fall into the second, this is my definite answer. Your love deserves my thanks, but my unworthiness shrinks from your high request. First, even if every obstacle were cleared away and my path to the crown were level, as my ripe inheritance and birthright, my spirit is so poor and my defects so great and so many that I would rather hide from greatness, being a small boat that can't survive a mighty sea, than be swallowed up by greatness and smothered in the smoke of my own glory. But thank God there's no need for me, and I would lack much to help you if there were. The royal tree has left us royal fruit, which, ripened by the creeping hours of time, will suit the throne well and no doubt make us happy by his reign. On him I lay what you would lay on me: the right and fortune given by his lucky stars. God forbid I should wrench it from him!

My lord, this argues conscience in your grace; / But the respects thereof are nice and trivial, / All circumstances well considered. / You say that Edward is your brother's son: / So say we too, but not by Edward's wife; / For first was he contract to Lady Lucy,-- / Your mother lives a witness to his vow,-- / And afterward by substitute betroth'd / To Bona, sister to the King of France. / These both put off, a poor petitioner, / A care-craz'd mother to a many sons, / A beauty-waning and distressed widow, / Even in the afternoon of her best days, / Made prize and purchase of his wanton eye, / Seduc'd the pitch and height of his degree / To base declension and loath'd bigamy: / By her, in his unlawful bed, he got / This Edward, whom our manners call the prince. / More bitterly could I expostulate, / Save that, for reverence to some alive, / I give a sparing limit to my tongue. / Then, good my lord, take to your royal self / This proffer'd benefit of dignity; / If not to bless us and the land withal, / Yet to draw forth your noble ancestry / From the corruption of abusing time / Unto a lineal true-derived course.

My lord, this shows your grace has a conscience, but its scruples are fussy and trivial, when all the circumstances are considered. You say Edward is your brother's son. So do we, but not by Edward's wife. First he was betrothed to Lady Lucy, and your mother is alive to witness his vow; then he was betrothed by proxy to Bona, sister of the King of France. Both were set aside, and a poor petitioner, a mother worn out with caring for many sons, a widow in distress whose beauty was fading, in the afternoon of her best days, became the prize of his roving eye and seduced the height of his rank into a shameful fall and hateful bigamy. By her, in his unlawful bed, he fathered this Edward, whom we politely call the prince. I could argue more bitterly, except that out of respect for someone still alive I keep my tongue in check. So, my good lord, take to your royal self this offered dignity, if not to bless us and the country, then to draw your noble line out of the corruption of these degenerate times back into its true line of descent.
Do, good my lord; your citizens entreat you.
Do it, my good lord. Your citizens beg you.
Refuse not, mighty lord, this proffer'd love.
Don't refuse this offered love, mighty lord.
O, make them joyful, grant their lawful suit!
Oh, make them happy and grant their lawful request!
Alas, why would you heap those cares on me? / I am unfit for state and majesty:-- / I do beseech you, take it not amiss: / I cannot nor I will not yield to you.
Alas, why would you pile these cares on me? I'm not fit for government and majesty. Please don't take it badly: I cannot and will not give in to you.

If you refuse it,--as, in love and zeal, / Loath to depose the child, your brother's son-- / As well we know your tenderness of heart / And gentle, kind, effeminate remorse, / Which we have noted in you to your kindred, / And equally, indeed, to all estates,-- / Yet know, whe'er you accept our suit or no, / Your brother's son shall never reign our king; / But we will plant some other in the throne, / To the disgrace and downfall of your house: / And in this resolution here we leave you.-- / Come, citizens, we will entreat no more.

If you refuse it, out of loving reluctance to depose the child, your brother's son, as we know your tender heart and gentle, kind, womanly pity, which we've seen you show your relatives and indeed people of every rank, still know this: whether you accept our request or not, your brother's son will never reign as our king. We'll put someone else on the throne, to the disgrace and ruin of your house. And with that decision we leave you. Come, citizens, we'll plead no more.
Call them again, sweet prince, accept their suit: / If you deny them, all the land will rue it.
Call them back, sweet prince, and accept their request. If you refuse them, the whole country will regret it.
Will you enforce me to a world of cares? / Call them again.
Will you force me into a world of cares? Call them back.
I am not made of stone, / But penetrable to your kind entreaties, / Albeit against my conscience and my soul.
I'm not made of stone. I can be moved by your kind pleading, though it's against my conscience and my soul.

Cousin of Buckingham,--and sage grave men, / Since you will buckle fortune on my back, / To bear her burden, whe'er I will or no, / I must have patience to endure the load: / But if black scandal or foul-fac'd reproach / Attend the sequel of your imposition, / Your mere enforcement shall acquittance me / From all the impure blots and stains thereof; / For God doth know, and you may partly see, / How far I am from the desire of this.

Cousin Buckingham, and you wise, serious men, since you insist on strapping fortune on my back to carry its burden whether I want to or not, I must patiently bear the load. But if black scandal or ugly reproach follows from what you've forced on me, your compulsion alone will clear me of all its dirty stains and blots, because God knows, and you can partly see, how far I am from wanting this.
God bless your grace! we see it, and will say it.
God bless your grace! We see it, and we'll say so.
In saying so, you shall but say the truth.
In saying so, you'll only be telling the truth.
Then I salute you with this royal title,-- / Long live King Richard, England's worthy king!
Then I salute you with this royal title: long live King Richard, England's worthy king!
To-morrow may it please you to be crown'd?
Would it please you to be crowned tomorrow?
Even when you please, for you will have it so.
Whenever you like, since you insist on it.
To-morrow, then, we will attend your grace: / And so, most joyfully, we take our leave.
Tomorrow, then, we'll attend your grace. And so, most joyfully, we take our leave.
[To the BISHOPS] Come, let us to our holy work again.-- / Farewell, my cousin;--farewell, gentle friends.
(To the Bishops) Come, let's go back to our holy work. Farewell, my cousin; farewell, gentle friends.

Who meets us here?--my niece Plantagenet, / Led in the hand of her kind aunt of Gloster? / Now, for my life, she's wandering to the Tower, / On pure heart's love, to greet the tender princes.-- / Daughter, well met.

Who's this meeting us? My granddaughter Plantagenet, led by the hand of her kind aunt of Gloucester? I'll bet my life she's on her way to the Tower out of pure love, to greet the young princes. Daughter-in-law, well met.
God give your graces both / A happy and a joyful time of day!
God give both your graces a happy and joyful day!
As much to you, good sister! Whither away?
The same to you, good sister! Where are you going?
No farther than the Tower; and, as I guess, / Upon the like devotion as yourselves, / To gratulate the gentle princes there.
No further than the Tower, and I imagine on the same loving errand as you, to greet the young princes there.
Kind sister, thanks; we'll enter all together:-- / And in good time, here the lieutenant comes.
Thank you, kind sister. We'll all go in together. And here, just in time, comes the Lieutenant.
Master Lieutenant, pray you, by your leave, / How doth the prince, and my young son of York?
Master Lieutenant, if you please, how is the prince, and my young son of York?
Right well, dear madam. By your patience, / I may not suffer you to visit them. / The king hath strictly charg'd the contrary.
Very well, dear madam. Forgive me, but I can't allow you to visit them. The King has strictly ordered otherwise.
The Lord protect him from that kingly title! / Hath he set bounds between their love and me? / I am their mother; who shall bar me from them?
The Lord protect him from that kingly title! Has he put barriers between their love and me? I'm their mother. Who will keep me from them?
I am their father's mother; I will see them.
I'm their father's mother. I will see them.
Their aunt I am in law, in love their mother: / Then bring me to their sights; I'll bear thy blame, / And take thy office from thee on my peril.
I'm their aunt by law, their mother in love. So take me to see them. I'll take the blame and take over your duty at my own risk.
No, madam, no,--I may not leave it so: / I am bound by oath, and therefore pardon me.
No, madam, no, I can't give it up like that. I'm bound by an oath, so forgive me.
Let me but meet you, ladies, one hour hence, / And I'll salute your grace of York as mother / And reverend looker-on of two fair queens.--
Ladies, if I meet you an hour from now, I'll be greeting your grace of York as the mother and revered witness of two fair queens.
Come, madam, you must straight to Westminster, / There to be crowned Richard's royal queen.
Come, madam, you must go straight to Westminster, to be crowned as Richard's royal queen.
Ah, cut my lace asunder, / That my pent heart may have some scope to beat, / Or else I swoon with this dead-killing news!
Oh, cut my laces open so my squeezed heart has room to beat, or I'll faint at this deadly news!
Be of good cheer: mother, how fares your grace?
Cheer up. Mother, how is your grace?

O Dorset, speak not to me, get thee gone! / Death and destruction dog thee at thy heels; / Thy mother's name is ominous to children. / If thou wilt outstrip death, go cross the seas, / And live with Richmond, from the reach of hell: / Go, hie thee, hie thee from this slaughter-house, / Lest thou increase the number of the dead; / And make me die the thrall of Margaret's curse, / Nor mother, wife, nor England's counted queen.

Oh Dorset, don't speak to me, go away! Death and destruction are on your heels. Your mother's name is a bad omen for her children. If you want to outrun death, cross the sea and live with Richmond, out of hell's reach. Go, hurry, hurry from this slaughterhouse, so you don't add to the number of the dead and make me die a slave to Margaret's curse, neither mother, wife nor acknowledged Queen of England.

Full of wise care is this your counsel, madam.-- / Take all the swift advantage of the hours; / You shall have letters from me to my son / In your behalf, to meet you on the way: / Be not ta'en tardy by unwise delay.

This advice of yours is full of wise care, madam. Make quick use of every hour. You'll have letters from me to my stepson on your behalf, telling him to meet you on the way. Don't be caught out by foolish delay.
O ill-dispersing wind of misery!-- / O my accursed womb, the bed of death! / A cockatrice hast thou hatch'd to the world, / Whose unavoided eye is murderous.
Oh, evil wind that scatters misery! Oh, my cursed womb, the bed of death! You have hatched a cockatrice into the world, whose eye kills everyone it falls on.
Come, madam, come; I in all haste was sent.
Come, madam, come. I was sent in great haste.

And I with all unwillingness will go.-- / O, would to God that the inclusive verge / Of golden metal that must round my brow / Were red-hot steel, to sear me to the brain ! / Anointed let me be with deadly venom, / And die ere men can say God save the queen!

And I'll go with great unwillingness. I wish to God the golden ring of metal that must go round my head were red-hot steel, to burn me to the brain! Let me be anointed with deadly poison and die before men can say "God save the Queen"!
Go, go, poor soul; I envy not thy glory; / To feed my humour, wish thyself no harm.
Go, go, poor soul. I don't envy your glory. Don't wish yourself harm to please my mood.

No, why?--When he that is my husband now / Came to me, as I follow'd Henry's corse; / When scarce the blood was well wash'd from his hands / Which issued from my other angel husband, / And that dear saint which then I weeping follow'd; / O, when, I say, I look'd on Richard's face, / This was my wish,--"Be thou," quoth I, "accurs'd / For making me, so young, so old a widow! / And when thou wedd'st, let sorrow haunt thy bed; / And be thy wife,--if any be so mad,-- / More miserable by the life of thee / Than thou hast made me by my dear lord's death!" / Lo, ere I can repeat this curse again, / Within so small a time, my woman's heart / Grossly grew captive to his honey words, / And prov'd the subject of mine own soul's curse,-- / Which hitherto hath held my eyes from rest; / For never yet one hour in his bed / Did I enjoy the golden dew of sleep, / But with his timorous dreams was still awak'd. / Besides, he hates me for my father Warwick; / And will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me.

No? Why not? When the man who is now my husband came to me as I followed Henry's body, when the blood was hardly washed from his hands, blood that came from my other husband, an angel, and from that dear saint I was following in tears, when I looked at Richard's face, this was my wish: "May you be cursed," I said, "for making me so young and so old a widow! And when you marry, may sorrow haunt your bed, and may your wife, if anyone is mad enough, be made more miserable by your life than you have made me by my dear lord's death!" And look, before I could repeat that curse, in so short a time, my woman's heart was shamefully captured by his honeyed words and proved the target of my own soul's curse, which has kept my eyes from rest ever since. Not once in his bed have I enjoyed one hour of the golden dew of sleep without being woken by his frightened dreams. Besides, he hates me because of my father Warwick, and no doubt will soon be rid of me.
Poor heart, adieu! I pity thy complaining.
Poor heart, goodbye! I pity your sorrow.
No more than with my soul I mourn for yours.
No more than I mourn for yours with all my soul.
Farewell, thou woeful welcomer of glory!
Farewell, you who welcome glory with grief!
Adieu, poor soul, that tak'st thy leave of it!
Goodbye, poor soul, who are taking your leave of it!
[To DORSET] Go thou to Richmond, and good fortune guide thee!--
(To Dorset) You go to Richmond, and good fortune guide you!
Go thou to Richard, and good angels tend thee!--
(To Anne) You go to Richard, and good angels watch over you!
Go thou to sanctuary, and good thoughts possess thee! / I to my grave, where peace and rest lie with me! / Eighty odd years of sorrow have I seen, / And each hour's joy wreck'd with a week of teen.

(To Queen Elizabeth) You go to sanctuary, and may good thoughts fill you! And I go to my grave, where peace and rest will lie with me! I have seen eighty-odd years of sorrow, and every hour of joy wrecked by a week of grief.

Stay yet, look back with me unto the Tower.-- / Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes / Whom envy hath immur'd within your walls! / Rough cradle for such little pretty ones! / Rude ragged nurse, old sullen playfellow / For tender princes, use my babies well! / So foolish sorrows bids your stones farewell.

Wait, look back at the Tower with me. You ancient stones, pity those tender children whom hatred has walled up inside you! A rough cradle for such pretty little ones! Rough, ragged nurse, grim old playmate for tender princes, treat my babies well! So my foolish sorrow says goodbye to your stones.
Give me thy hand. Thus high, by thy advice / And thy assistance, is King Richard seated:-- / But shall we wear these glories for a day? / Or shall they last, and we rejoice in them?
Give me your hand. King Richard sits this high through your advice and help. But shall we wear these glories for just a day, or shall they last and we enjoy them?
Still live they, and for ever let them last!
Let them live always and last for ever!
Ah, Buckingham, now do I play the touch, / To try if thou be current gold indeed:-- / Young Edward lives;--think now what I would speak.
Ah, Buckingham, now I'll play the touchstone and test whether you're really genuine gold. Young Edward is alive. Now think what I mean to say.
Why, Buckingham, I say I would be king.
Why, Buckingham, I'm saying I want to be king.
Why, so you are, my thrice-renowned lord.
Why, so you are, my thrice-famous lord.
Ha! am I king? 'tis so: but Edward lives.
Ha! Am I king? So I am. But Edward is alive.

O bitter consequence, / That Edward still should live,--true, noble Prince!-- / Cousin, thou wast not wont to be so dull:-- / Shall I be plain?--I wish the bastards dead; / And I would have it suddenly perform'd. / What say'st thou now? speak suddenly, be brief.

What a bitter conclusion, that Edward should still be alive! "True, noble prince"! Cousin, you didn't used to be so slow. Shall I be plain? I want the bastards dead, and I want it done quickly. What do you say now? Speak quickly, be brief.
Your grace may do your pleasure.
Your grace may do as you please.
Tut, tut, thou art all ice, thy kindness freezes: / Say, have I thy consent that they shall die?
Tut, tut, you're all ice; your kindness is freezing. Tell me, do I have your agreement that they'll die?
Give me some little breath, some pause, dear lord, / Before I positively speak in this: / I will resolve your grace immediately.
Give me a little breathing space, a pause, dear lord, before I give you a definite answer. I'll give your grace my decision straight away.
[Aside] The king is angry: see, he gnaws his lip.
(Aside) The King is angry. Look, he's biting his lip.
I will converse with iron-witted fools
And unrespective boys; none are for me / That look into me with considerate eyes: / High-reaching Buckingham grows circumspect. / Boy!--
and careless boys. Nobody who looks into me with thoughtful eyes is any use to me. Ambitious Buckingham is growing cautious. Boy!
Know'st thou not any whom corrupting gold / Will tempt unto a close exploit of death?
Don't you know anyone whom corrupting gold would tempt to do a secret killing?
I know a discontented gentleman / Whose humble means match not his haughty spirit: / Gold were as good as twenty orators, / And will, no doubt, tempt him to anything.
I know a discontented gentleman whose humble means don't match his proud spirit. Gold would be as good as twenty orators to him and would no doubt tempt him to anything.
His name, my lord, is Tyrrel.
His name is Tyrrel, my lord.
I partly know the man: go, call him hither, boy.
I know the man a little. Go and call him here, boy.
The deep-revolving witty Buckingham / No more shall be the neighbour to my counsels: / Hath he so long held out with me untir'd, / And stops he now for breath?--well, be it so.
Deep-thinking, clever Buckingham will no longer share my secrets. Has he kept pace with me so long without tiring, and now stops for breath? Well, so be it.
How now, Lord Stanley! what's the news?
Well, Lord Stanley, what's the news?
Know, my loving lord, / The Marquis Dorset, as I hear, is fled / To Richmond, in the parts where he abides.
My loving lord, I hear the Marquis of Dorset has fled to Richmond, where he is living.

Come hither, Catesby: rumour it abroad / That Anne, my wife, is very grievous sick; / I will take order for her keeping close: / Inquire me out some mean poor gentleman, / Whom I will marry straight to Clarence' daughter;-- / The boy is foolish, and I fear not him.-- / Look how thou dream'st!--I say again, give out / That Anne, my queen, is sick and like to die: / About it; for it stands me much upon, / To stop all hopes whose growth may damage me.

Come here, Catesby. Spread the rumour that my wife Anne is very seriously ill. I'll give orders for her to be kept shut away. Find me some poor gentleman of low rank, whom I'll marry straight away to Clarence's daughter. The boy is simple, and I'm not afraid of him. Look how you're daydreaming! I tell you again, announce that Anne, my queen, is sick and likely to die. Get on with it, because it's vital for me to cut off any hopes whose growth might harm me.

I must be married to my brother's daughter, / Or else my kingdom stands on brittle glass:-- / Murder her brothers, and then marry her! / Uncertain way of gain! But I am in / So far in blood that sin will pluck on sin: / Tear-falling pity dwells not in this eye.

I must marry my brother's daughter, or my kingdom stands on brittle glass. Murder her brothers and then marry her! An uncertain way to profit! But I'm in so deep in blood that one sin will drag on another. Tearful pity doesn't live in this eye.
James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
Dar'st thou resolve to kill a friend of mine?
Would you dare to kill a friend of mine?
Please you. But I had rather kill two enemies.
If you like. But I'd rather kill two enemies.
Why, then thou hast it: two deep enemies, / Foes to my rest, and my sweet sleep's disturbers, / Are they that I would have thee deal upon:-- / Tyrell, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
Why, then you've got it: two deadly enemies, enemies of my peace who disturb my sweet sleep, are the ones I want you to deal with. Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
Let me have open means to come to them, / And soon I'll rid you from the fear of them.
Give me open access to them, and I'll soon rid you of the fear of them.

Thou sing'st sweet music. Hark, come hither, Tyrrel: / Go, by this token:--rise, and lend thine ear: / [Whispers] There is no more but so:--say it is done, / And I will love thee, and prefer thee for it.
You sing sweet music. Listen, come here, Tyrrel. Go with this token. Stand up and lend me your ear. (Whispers) That's all there is to it. Tell me it's done and I'll love you and promote you for it.
My lord, I have consider'd in my mind / The late request that you did sound me in.
My lord, I've thought over the request you sounded me on just now.
Well, let that rest. Dorset is fled to Richmond.
Well, never mind that. Dorset has fled to Richmond.
I hear the news, my lord.
I've heard the news, my lord.
Stanley, he is your wife's son:--well, look to it.
Stanley, he's your wife's son. Well, watch out.
My lord, I claim the gift, my due by promise, / For which your honour and your faith is pawn'd: / The earldom of Hereford, and the movables / Which you have promised I shall possess.
My lord, I claim the gift that's mine by promise, which your honour and word were pledged for: the earldom of Hereford and the movable property you promised I'd have.
Stanley, look to your wife: if she convey / Letters to Richmond, you shall answer it.
Stanley, watch your wife. If she sends letters to Richmond, you'll answer for it.
What says your highness to my just request?
What does your highness say to my just request?
I do remember me:--Henry the Sixth / Did prophesy that Richmond should be king, / When Richmond was a little peevish boy. / A king!--perhaps,--
I remember Henry VI prophesied that Richmond would be king, when Richmond was a peevish little boy. A king! Perhaps...
How chance the prophet could not at that time / Have told me, I being by, that I should kill him?
How is it the prophet couldn't have told me at the time, when I was standing by, that I would kill him?
My lord, your promise for the earldom,--
My lord, your promise of the earldom...

Richmond!--When last I was at Exeter, / The mayor in courtesy show'd me the castle / And call'd it Rougemount; at which name I started, / Because a bard of Ireland told me once / I should not live long after I saw Richmond.

Richmond! When I was last at Exeter, the Mayor politely showed me the castle and called it Rougemont, and at that name I jumped, because an Irish bard once told me I wouldn't live long after I saw Richmond.
I am thus bold to put your grace in mind / Of what you promis'd me.
I am bold enough to remind your grace of what you promised me.
Yes, but what time is it?
Because that, like a Jack, thou keep'st the stroke / Betwixt thy begging and my meditation. / I am not in the giving vein to-day.
Because, like the figure on a clock, you keep striking between your begging and my thinking. I'm not in a giving mood today.
Why then, resolve me whether you will or no.
Then tell me plainly whether you will or not.
Thou troublest me; I am not in the vein.
You're bothering me. I'm not in the mood.
And is it thus? repays he my deep service / With such contempt? made I him king for this? / O, let me think on Hastings, and be gone / To Brecknock while my fearful head is on!
Is this how it is? Does he repay my deep service with such contempt? Did I make him king for this? Oh, let me remember Hastings and be off to Brecknock while my frightened head is still on!

The tyrannous and bloody act is done,-- / The most arch deed of piteous massacre / That ever yet this land was guilty of. / Dighton and Forrest, who I did suborn / To do this piece of ruthless butchery, / Albeit they were flesh'd villains, bloody dogs, / Melted with tenderness and mild compassion, / Wept like two children in their deaths' sad story. / "O, thus," quoth Dighton, "lay the gentle babes,"-- / "Thus, thus," quoth Forrest, "girdling one another / Within their alabaster innocent arms: / Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, / And in their summer beauty kiss'd each other. / A book of prayers on their pillow lay; / Which once," quoth Forrest, "almost chang'd my mind; / But, O, the devil,"--there the villain stopp'd; / When Dighton thus told on:--"We smothered / The most replenished sweet work of nature / That from the prime creation e'er she framed."-- / Hence both are gone; with conscience and remorse / They could not speak; and so I left them both, / To bear this tidings to the bloody king:-- / And here he comes:--

The tyrannical, bloody act is done, the worst deed of pitiful massacre this country has ever been guilty of. Dighton and Forrest, whom I bribed to do this piece of ruthless butchery, though they were hardened villains and bloodthirsty dogs, melted with tenderness and gentle pity and wept like two children as they told the sad story of the deaths. "This is how the gentle children lay," said Dighton. "Like this, like this," said Forrest, "with their innocent white arms round each other. Their lips were four red roses on one stem, kissing each other in their summer beauty. A prayer book lay on their pillow, which almost changed my mind," said Forrest, "but oh, the devil..." There the villain stopped. Then Dighton went on: "We smothered the most perfect, sweet work nature ever made since the first creation." Then they both left, so full of conscience and remorse they couldn't speak, and so I left them to bring the news to the bloody King. And here he comes.
Good health to you, my royal lord!
Kind Tyrrel, am I happy in thy news?
Kind Tyrrel, does your news make me happy?
If to have done the thing you gave in charge / Beget your happiness, be happy then, / For it is done.
If having done what you ordered makes you happy, then be happy, because it's done.
But didst thou see them dead?
But did you see them dead?
The chaplain of the Tower hath buried them; / But where, to say the truth, I do not know.
The chaplain of the Tower has buried them, but to tell the truth I don't know where.
Come to me, Tyrrel, soon, at after supper, / When thou shalt tell the process of their death. / Meantime, but think how I may do thee good, / And be inheritor of thy desire. / Farewell till then.
Come to me soon, Tyrrel, after supper, and tell me how they died. Meanwhile, just think how I can do you good, and you'll get whatever you want. Goodbye until then.

The son of Clarence have I pent up close; / His daughter meanly have I match'd in marriage; / The sons of Edward sleep in Abraham's bosom, / And Anne my wife hath bid the world good-night. / Now, for I know the Britagne Richmond aims / At young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter, / And by that knot looks proudly on the crown, / To her go I, a jolly thriving wooer.

I've locked up Clarence's son. I've married his daughter to a nobody. Edward's sons sleep in Abraham's bosom, and my wife Anne has said goodnight to the world. Now, since I know Richmond in Brittany is aiming at young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter, and through that marriage is eyeing the crown proudly, I'll go to her as a jolly, prosperous suitor.
Good or bad news, that thou com'st in so bluntly?
Good news or bad, that you burst in so abruptly?
Bad news, my lord: Morton is fled to Richmond; / And Buckingham, back'd with the hardy Welshmen, / Is in the field, and still his power increaseth.
Bad news, my lord. Morton has fled to Richmond, and Buckingham, backed by the tough Welshmen, has taken the field, and his army keeps growing.

Ely with Richmond troubles me more near / Than Buckingham and his rash-levied strength. / Come,--I have learn'd that fearful commenting / Is leaden servitor to dull delay; / Delay leads impotent and snail-pac'd beggary: / Then fiery expedition be my wing, / Jove's Mercury, and herald for a king! / Go, muster men: my counsel is my shield; / We must be brief when traitors brave the field.

Ely joining Richmond worries me more than Buckingham and his hastily raised army. Come, I've learned that fearful talk is the sluggish servant of slow delay, and delay leads to helpless, snail-paced ruin. So let fiery speed be my wings, Jove's Mercury and a king's herald! Go, call up men. My shield is my plan. We must be quick when traitors challenge us in the field.

So, now prosperity begins to mellow, / And drop into the rotten mouth of death. / Here in these confines slily have I lurk'd / To watch the waning of mine enemies. / A dire induction am I witness to, / And will to France; hoping the consequence / Will prove as bitter, black, and tragical.-- / Withdraw thee, wretched Margaret: who comes here?

So now their prosperity is starting to over-ripen and drop into the rotten mouth of death. I've been lurking secretly around here to watch my enemies decline. I've witnessed a terrible first act, and I'll go to France, hoping what follows will be just as bitter, black and tragic. Step back, wretched Margaret. Who's coming?

Ah, my poor princes! ah, my tender babes! / My unblown flowers, new-appearing sweets! / If yet your gentle souls fly in the air / And be not fix'd in doom perpetual, / Hover about me with your airy wings / And hear your mother's lamentation!

Ah, my poor princes! Ah, my tender babies! My unopened flowers, newly budding sweets! If your gentle souls are still flying in the air and haven't yet been fixed in their eternal fate, hover round me on your airy wings and hear your mother's lament!
Hover about her; say that right for right / Hath dimm'd your infant morn to aged night.
Hover round her; tell her that justice for justice has darkened your childish morning into an old man's night.
So many miseries have craz'd my voice / That my woe-wearied tongue is still and mute.-- / Edward Plantagenet, why art thou dead?
So many miseries have cracked my voice that my grief-weary tongue is still and silent. Edward Plantagenet, why are you dead?
Plantagenet doth quit Plantagenet, / Edward for Edward pays a dying debt.
One Plantagenet pays for another Plantagenet; Edward pays Edward's debt of death.
Wilt thou, O God, fly from such gentle lambs, / And throw them in the entrails of the wolf? / When didst Thou sleep when such a deed was done?
God, will you desert such gentle lambs and throw them into the wolf's belly? When did you ever sleep while such a deed was done?
When holy Harry died, and my sweet son.
When holy Henry died, and my sweet son.
Dead life, blind sight, poor mortal living ghost, / Woe's scene, world's shame, grave's due by life usurp'd, / Brief abstract and record of tedious days, / Rest thy unrest on England's lawful earth,

Dead life, blind sight, poor living ghost of a mortal, stage of woe, shame of the world, owed to the grave but kept from it by life, brief summary and record of weary days: rest your restlessness on England's lawful earth,
Unlawfully made drunk with innocent blood.
which has been unlawfully made drunk with innocent blood.
Ah, that thou wouldst as soon afford a grave / As thou canst yield a melancholy seat! / Then would I hide my bones, not rest them here. / Ah, who hath any cause to mourn but we?
Ah, if only you would give me a grave as readily as you give me a gloomy seat! Then I'd bury my bones, not rest them here. Ah, who has any cause to mourn except us?
[Coming forward] If ancient sorrow be most reverent, / Give mine the benefit of seniory, / And let my griefs frown on the upper hand. / If sorrow can admit society,
(Coming forward) If the oldest sorrow deserves the most respect, give mine the privilege of seniority and let my griefs take the upper hand. If sorrow can bear company,

Tell o'er your woes again by viewing mine:-- / I had an Edward, till a Richard kill'd him; / I had a Henry, till a Richard kill'd him: / Thou hadst an Edward, till a Richard kill'd him; / Thou hadst a Richard, till a Richard kill'd him.

count your griefs over again by looking at mine. I had an Edward, until a Richard killed him. I had a Henry, until a Richard killed him. You had an Edward, until a Richard killed him. You had a Richard, until a Richard killed him.
I had a Richard too, and thou didst kill him; / I had a Rutland too, thou holp'st to kill him.
I had a Richard too, and you killed him. I had a Rutland too, and you helped kill him.

Thou hadst a Clarence too, and Richard kill'd him. / From forth the kennel of thy womb hath crept / A hell-hound that doth hunt us all to death: / That dog, that had his teeth before his eyes, / To worry lambs and lap their gentle blood; / That foul defacer of God's handiwork; / That excellent grand tyrant of the earth, / That reigns in galled eyes of weeping souls,-- / Thy womb let loose to chase us to our graves.-- / O upright, just, and true-disposing God, / How do I thank Thee that this carnal cur / Preys on the issue of his mother's body, / And makes her pew-fellow with others' moan!

You had a Clarence too, and Richard killed him. Out of the kennel of your womb has crept a hellhound that hunts us all to death: that dog who had teeth before his eyes were open, to savage lambs and lap their gentle blood; that foul spoiler of God's handiwork; that supreme tyrant of the earth, who reigns over the sore eyes of weeping souls. Your womb let him loose to chase us into our graves. O upright, just and fair-dealing God, how I thank you that this bloodthirsty cur preys on the children of his own mother's body and makes her share a pew with others in grief!
O Harry's wife, triumph not in my woes! / God witness with me, I have wept for thine.
Oh, Henry's wife, don't triumph over my sorrows! God is my witness, I have wept for yours.

Bear with me; I am hungry for revenge, / And now I cloy me with beholding it. / Thy Edward he is dead, that kill'd my Edward; / The other Edward dead to quit my Edward; / Young York he is but boot, because both they / Match not the high perfection of my loss: / Thy Clarence he is dead that stabb'd my Edward; / And the beholders of this frantic play, / The adulterate Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey, / Untimely smother'd in their dusky graves. / Richard yet lives, hell's black intelligencer; / Only reserv'd their factor to buy souls, / And send them thither: but at hand, at hand, / Ensues his piteous and unpitied end: / Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray, / To have him suddenly convey'd from hence.-- / Cancel his bond of life, dear God, I pray, / That I may live to say "The dog is dead."

Bear with me. I'm hungry for revenge, and now I'm stuffing myself by watching it. Your Edward is dead, who killed my Edward. The other Edward is dead to pay for my Edward. Young York is only a bonus, because both of them don't match the perfection of my loss. Your Clarence is dead, who stabbed my Edward, and the spectators of that mad play, adulterous Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan and Grey, are smothered too early in their dark graves. Richard is still alive, hell's black spy, kept only as its agent to buy souls and send them there. But near, near at hand comes his pitiful, unpitied end. The earth gapes, hell burns, devils roar, saints pray for him to be taken away from here quickly. Cancel his lease of life, dear God, I pray, so I may live to say, "The dog is dead."
O, thou didst prophesy the time would come / That I should wish for thee to help me curse / That bottled spider, that foul bunch-back'd toad!
Oh, you prophesied the time would come when I'd wish for you to help me curse that swollen spider, that foul hunchbacked toad!

I call'd thee then, vain flourish of my fortune; / I call'd thee then, poor shadow, painted queen; / The presentation of but what I was, / The flattering index of a direful pageant; / One heav'd a-high to be hurl'd down below, / A mother only mock'd with two fair babes; / A dream of what thou wast; a garish flag, / To be the aim of every dangerous shot; / A sign of dignity, a breath, a bubble; / A queen in jest, only to fill the scene. / Where is thy husband now? where be thy brothers? / Where be thy two sons? wherein dost thou joy? / Who sues, and kneels, and says, "God save the queen?" / Where be the bending peers that flatter'd thee? / Where be the thronging troops that follow'd thee? / Decline all this, and see what now thou art: / For happy wife, a most distressed widow; / For joyful mother, one that wails the name; / For one being su'd to, one that humbly sues; / For queen, a very caitiff crown'd with care; / For she that scorn'd at me, now scorn'd of me; / For she being fear'd of all, now fearing one; / For she commanding all, obey'd of none. / Thus hath the course of justice wheel'd about / And left thee but a very prey to time; / Having no more but thought of what thou wast, / To torture thee the more, being what thou art. / Thou didst usurp my place, and dost thou not / Usurp the just proportion of my sorrow? / Now thy proud neck bears half my burden'd yoke; / From which even here I slip my weary head, / And leave the burden of it all on thee. / Farewell, York's wife, and queen of sad mischance:-- / These English woes shall make me smile in France.

I called you then an empty imitation of my fortune; I called you a poor shadow, a painted queen, only a copy of what I was, the flattering preview of a dreadful show, someone raised high to be hurled down, a mother only mocked with two fine babies, a dream of what you were, a gaudy flag to draw every dangerous shot, a mere sign of rank, a breath, a bubble, a pretend queen just to fill the stage. Where is your husband now? Where are your brothers? Where are your two sons? What do you have to enjoy? Who petitions you, kneels and says "God save the Queen"? Where are the bowing lords who flattered you? Where are the crowds who followed you? Go through all this and see what you are now: instead of a happy wife, a desperate widow; instead of a joyful mother, one who weeps at the name; instead of being petitioned, one who humbly petitions; instead of a queen, a wretch crowned with cares; instead of scorning me, scorned by me; instead of being feared by all, fearing one; instead of commanding all, obeyed by none. So justice's wheel has come full circle and left you a mere victim of time, with nothing but the memory of what you were to torture you more for what you are. You took my place, so don't you take your fair share of my sorrow too? Now your proud neck carries half my heavy yoke, and here I slip my weary head out of it and leave the whole burden on you. Farewell, York's wife, and queen of sad misfortune. These English woes will make me smile in France.
O thou well skill'd in curses, stay awhile, / And teach me how to curse mine enemies!
You who are so skilled in curses, stay a while and teach me how to curse my enemies!

Forbear to sleep the night, and fast the day; / Compare dead happiness with living woe; / Think that thy babes were sweeter than they were, / And he that slew them fouler than he is; / Bettering thy loss makes the bad-causer worse; / Revolving this will teach thee how to curse.

Don't sleep at night and fast by day. Compare your dead happiness with your living sorrow. Imagine your babies were sweeter than they were and their killer fouler than he is. Making your loss greater makes the one who caused it worse. Turning this over will teach you how to curse.
My words are dull; O, quicken them with thine!
My words are dull; oh, sharpen them with yours!
Thy woes will make them sharp, and pierce like mine.
Your sorrows will make them sharp, and they'll pierce like mine.
Why should calamity be full of words?
Why should disaster be so full of words?

Windy attorneys to their client woes, / Airy succeeders of intestate joys, / Poor breathing orators of miseries! / Let them have scope: though what they do impart / Help nothing else, yet do they ease the heart.

Words are long-winded lawyers for their clients' sorrows, empty heirs to joys that left no will, poor breathing speakers for misery! Let them have room. Though what they say helps nothing else, it eases the heart.
If so, then be not tongue-tied: go with me, / And in the breath of bitter words let's smother / My damned son, that thy two sweet sons smother'd.
If so, don't be tongue-tied. Come with me, and let's smother my damned son, who smothered your two sweet sons, in a blast of bitter words.
I hear his drum:--be copious in exclaims.
I hear his drum. Be generous with your outcries.
Who intercepts me in my expedition?
O, she that might have intercepted thee, / By strangling thee in her accursed womb, / From all the slaughters, wretch, that thou hast done!
Oh, she who could have blocked you from all the slaughters you've committed, wretch, by strangling you in her cursed womb!

Hidest thou that forehead with a golden crown, / Where should be branded, if that right were right, / The slaughter of the prince that ow'd that crown, / And the dire death of my poor sons and brothers? / Tell me, thou villain-slave, where are my children?

Are you hiding under a golden crown that forehead which should be branded, if justice were done, with the murder of the prince who owned that crown and the terrible deaths of my poor sons and brothers? Tell me, you villainous slave, where are my children?
Thou toad, thou toad, where is thy brother Clarence? / And little Ned Plantagenet, his son?
You toad, you toad, where is your brother Clarence, and little Ned Plantagenet, his son?
Where is the gentle Rivers, Vaughan, Grey?
Where are gentle Rivers, Vaughan and Grey?
A flourish, trumpets! strike alarum, drums! / Let not the heavens hear these tell-tale women / Rail on the Lord's anointed: strike, I say!
Sound a flourish, trumpets! Beat the alarm, drums! Don't let the heavens hear these tale-telling women abuse the Lord's anointed king. Sound, I say!
Either be patient and entreat me fair, / Or with the clamorous report of war / Thus will I drown your exclamations.
Either be calm and speak to me politely, or I'll drown your cries like this with the noisy sound of war.
Ay, I thank God, my father, and yourself.
Yes, thanks to God, my father and you.
Then listen patiently to my impatience.
Madam, I have a touch of your condition / That cannot brook the accent of reproof.
Madam, I have a touch of your temperament, which can't stand the tone of a rebuke.
Do, then; but I'll not hear.
Do, then, but I won't listen.
I will be mild and gentle in my words.
I'll be mild and gentle in my words.
And brief, good mother; for I am in haste.
And brief, good mother, because I'm in a hurry.
Art thou so hasty? I have stay'd for thee, / God knows, in torment and in agony.
Are you in such a hurry? God knows I waited for you in torment and agony.
And came I not at last to comfort you?
And didn't I come at last to comfort you?

No, by the holy rood, thou know'st it well / Thou cam'st on earth to make the earth my hell. / A grievous burden was thy birth to me; / Tetchy and wayward was thy infancy; / Thy school-days frightful, desperate, wild, and furious; / Thy prime of manhood daring, bold, and venturous; / Thy age confirm'd, proud, subtle, sly, and bloody, / More mild, but yet more harmful, kind in hatred: / What comfortable hour canst thou name / That ever grac'd me with thy company?

No, by the holy cross, you know very well you came into the world to make the world my hell. Your birth was a painful burden to me; your infancy irritable and difficult; your schooldays frightening, reckless, wild and violent; your early manhood daring, bold and venturesome; your maturity proud, subtle, sly and bloody, milder but more harmful, kind while hating. What comforting hour can you name that you ever blessed me with your company?

Faith, none but Humphrey Hour, that call'd your grace / To breakfast once forth of my company. / If I be so disgracious in your eye, / Let me march on and not offend you, madam.-- / Strike up the drum.
Honestly, none, except the hour that once called your grace away from my company to breakfast. If I'm so displeasing in your eyes, let me march on and stop offending you, madam. Beat the drum.
Hear me a word; / For I shall never speak to thee again.
Hear one word, because I'll never speak to you again.

Either thou wilt die by God's just ordinance / Ere from this war thou turn a conqueror; / Or I with grief and extreme age shall perish / And never more behold thy face again. / Therefore take with thee my most grievous curse; / Which in the day of battle tire thee more / Than all the complete armour that thou wear'st! / My prayers on the adverse party fight; / And there the little souls of Edward's children / Whisper the spirits of thine enemies, / And promise them success and victory. / Bloody thou art; bloody will be thy end: / Shame serves thy life and doth thy death attend.

Either you'll die by God's just decree before you come back a winner from this war, or I'll die of grief and old age and never see your face again. So take my most grievous curse with you, and may it tire you more on the day of battle than all the armour you wear! My prayers will fight on the other side, and there the little souls of Edward's children will whisper to your enemies' spirits and promise them success and victory. You are bloody; your end will be bloody. Shame serves your life and will attend your death.
Though far more cause, yet much less spirit to curse / Abides in me; I say amen to her.
Though I have far more cause, I have much less spirit to curse. I say amen to her.
Stay, madam, I must talk a word with you.
Wait, madam, I need a word with you.
I have no more sons of the royal blood / For thee to slaughter: for my daughters, Richard,-- / They shall be praying nuns, not weeping queens; / And therefore level not to hit their lives.
I have no more sons of royal blood for you to slaughter. As for my daughters, Richard, they'll be nuns at their prayers, not weeping queens. So don't aim at their lives.
You have a daughter call'd Elizabeth. / Virtuous and fair, royal and gracious.
You have a daughter called Elizabeth, virtuous and beautiful, royal and gracious.

And must she die for this? O, let her live, / And I'll corrupt her manners, stain her beauty: / Slander myself as false to Edward's bed; / Throw over her the veil of infamy: / So she may live unscarr'd of bleeding slaughter, / I will confess she was not Edward's daughter.

And must she die for that? Oh, let her live, and I'll corrupt her morals and spoil her beauty. I'll slander myself as unfaithful to Edward and throw a veil of disgrace over her. To let her live safe from bloody slaughter, I'll confess she wasn't Edward's daughter.
Wrong not her birth; she is of royal blood.
Don't slander her birth. She is of royal blood.
To save her life I'll say she is not so.
To save her life I'll say she isn't.
Her life is safest only in her birth.
Her life is safest only because of her birth.
And only in that safety died her brothers.
And her brothers died of that same safety.
Lo, at their births good stars were opposite.
Why, the stars at their birth were against them.
No, to their lives bad friends were contrary.
No, bad friends were against their lives.
All unavoided is the doom of destiny.
The decree of destiny can't be avoided.
True, when avoided grace makes destiny: / My babes were destined to a fairer death, / If grace had bless'd thee with a fairer life.
True, when someone who has avoided God's grace makes the destiny. My babies were destined for a better death if grace had blessed you with a better life.
You speak as if that I had slain my cousins.
You talk as if I had killed my nephews.

Cousins, indeed; and by their uncle cozen'd / Of comfort, kingdom, kindred, freedom, life. / Whose hand soever lanc'd their tender hearts, / Thy head, all indirectly, gave direction: / No doubt the murderous knife was dull and blunt / Till it was whetted on thy stone-hard heart, / To revel in the entrails of my lambs. / But that still use of grief makes wild grief tame, / My tongue should to thy ears not name my boys / Till that my nails were anchor'd in thine eyes; / And I, in such a desperate bay of death, / Like a poor bark, of sails and tackling reft, / Rush all to pieces on thy rocky bosom.

Nephews indeed, and cheated by their uncle of comfort, kingdom, family, freedom and life. Whoever's hand pierced their tender hearts, your head gave the orders, however indirectly. No doubt the murderous knife was dull and blunt until it was sharpened on your stone-hard heart to revel in my lambs' insides. If constant grief didn't make wild grief tame, my tongue wouldn't name my boys to your ears until my nails were anchored in your eyes, and I, in that desperate bay of death, like a poor boat stripped of sails and rigging, would smash myself to pieces on your rocky heart.
Madam, so thrive I in my enterprise / And dangerous success of bloody wars, / As I intend more good to you and yours / Than ever you or yours by me were harm'd!
Madam, I swear by my success in my enterprise and the dangerous outcome of bloody wars that I intend more good to you and yours than you or yours were ever harmed by me!
What good is cover'd with the face of heaven, / To be discover'd, that can do me good?
What good is hidden under the face of heaven, waiting to be found, that can do me good?
Advancement of your children, gentle lady.
The advancement of your children, gentle lady.
Up to some scaffold, there to lose their heads?
Up to some scaffold, to lose their heads?
Unto the dignity and height of honour, / The high imperial type of this earth's glory.
Up to the dignity and height of honour, the high imperial symbol of earthly glory.
Flatter my sorrows with report of it; / Tell me what state, what dignity, what honour, / Canst thou demise to any child of mine?
Flatter my sorrows by telling me about it. Tell me what rank, what dignity, what honour you can hand over to any child of mine.

Even all I have; ay, and myself and all / Will I withal endow a child of thine; / So in the Lethe of thy angry soul / Thou drown the sad remembrance of those wrongs / Which thou supposest I have done to thee.
All I have, yes, and myself as well, I'll give to a child of yours, if you'll drown in the river of forgetfulness of your angry soul the sad memory of the wrongs you think I've done you.
Be brief, lest that the process of thy kindness / Last longer telling than thy kindness' date.
Be brief, in case the telling of your kindness lasts longer than your kindness itself.
Then know, that from my soul I love thy daughter.
Then know that I love your daughter with all my soul.
My daughter's mother thinks it with her soul.
Her mother thinks so with all her soul.
That thou dost love my daughter from thy soul: / So from thy soul's love didst thou love her brothers; / And from my heart's love I do thank thee for it.
That you love my daughter with all your soul, just as with your soul's love you loved her brothers, and with my heart's love I thank you for it.
Be not so hasty to confound my meaning: / I mean that with my soul I love thy daughter, / And do intend to make her Queen of England.
Don't be so quick to twist my meaning. I mean that I love your daughter with my soul and intend to make her Queen of England.
Well, then, who dost thou mean shall be her king?
Well then, who do you intend to be her king?
Even he that makes her queen: who else should be?
The man who makes her queen. Who else should it be?
I, even I: what think you of it, madam?
I, yes, I. What do you think of it, madam?
That would I learn of you, / As one being best acquainted with her humour.
That's what I'd like to learn from you, as the person who knows her temperament best.
And wilt thou learn of me?
And will you learn from me?

Send to her, by the man that slew her brothers, / A pair of bleeding hearts; thereon engrave / "Edward" and "York." Then haply will she weep: / Therefore present to her,--as sometimes Margaret / Did to thy father, steep'd in Rutland's blood,-- / A handkerchief; which, say to her, did drain / The purple sap from her sweet brothers' bodies, / And bid her wipe her weeping eyes withal. / If this inducement move her not to love, / Send her a letter of thy noble deeds; / Tell her thou mad'st away her uncle Clarence, / Her uncle Rivers; ay, and for her sake / Mad'st quick conveyance with her good aunt Anne.

Send her, by the man who killed her brothers, a pair of bleeding hearts engraved "Edward" and "York". Then perhaps she'll weep. So give her a handkerchief, as Margaret once gave your father one soaked in Rutland's blood, and tell her it soaked up the red sap from her sweet brothers' bodies, and tell her to wipe her weeping eyes with it. If that doesn't move her to love, send her a list of your noble deeds. Tell her you did away with her uncle Clarence, her uncle Rivers, yes, and for her sake quickly disposed of her good aunt Anne.
You mock me, madam; this is not the way / To win your daughter.
You're mocking me, madam. This isn't the way to win your daughter.
There is no other way; / Unless thou couldst put on some other shape, / And not be Richard that hath done all this.
There's no other way, unless you could take on some other shape and not be the Richard who has done all this.
Say that I did all this for love of her?
What if I said I did all this for love of her?
Nay, then indeed she cannot choose but hate thee, / Having bought love with such a bloody spoil.
Then she'd have no choice but to hate you, since you bought love with such bloody plunder.

Look, what is done cannot be now amended: / Men shall deal unadvisedly sometimes, / Which after-hours gives leisure to repent. / If I did take the kingdom from your sons, / To make amends I'll give it to your daughter. / If I have kill'd the issue of your womb, / To quicken your increase I will beget / Mine issue of your blood upon your daughter. / A grandam's name is little less in love / Than is the doating title of a mother; / They are as children but one step below, / Even of your mettle, of your very blood; / Of all one pain,--save for a night of groans / Endur'd of her, for whom you bid like sorrow. / Your children were vexation to your youth; / But mine shall be a comfort to your age. / The loss you have is but a son being king, / And by that loss your daughter is made queen. / I cannot make you what amends I would, / Therefore accept such kindness as I can. / Dorset your son, that with a fearful soul / Leads discontented steps in foreign soil, / This fair alliance quickly shall call home / To high promotions and great dignity: / The king, that calls your beauteous daughter wife, / Familiarly shall call thy Dorset brother; / Again shall you be mother to a king, / And all the ruins of distressful times / Repair'd with double riches of content. / What! we have many goodly days to see: / The liquid drops of tears that you have shed / Shall come again, transform'd to orient pearl, / Advantaging their loan with interest / Of ten times double gain of happiness. / Go, then, my mother, to thy daughter go; / Make bold her bashful years with your experience; / Prepare her ears to hear a wooer's tale: / Put in her tender heart the aspiring flame / Of golden sovereignty; acquaint the princess / With the sweet silent hours of marriage joys: / And when this arm of mine hath chastised / The petty rebel, dull-brain'd Buckingham, / Bound with triumphant garlands will I come, / And lead thy daughter to a conqueror's bed; / To whom I will retail my conquest won, / And she shall be sole victoress, Caesar's Caesar.

Look, what's done can't be undone now. Men sometimes act rashly and later have time to repent. If I took the kingdom from your sons, to make amends I'll give it to your daughter. If I killed the children of your womb, to bring your family back to life I'll father children of your blood on your daughter.
