A grandmother's name is hardly less loving than the doting title of mother. Grandchildren are like children, only one step down, of your own spirit and very blood, all from the same pain, except for one night of groans endured by her for whom you suffered the same. Your children troubled your youth, but mine will comfort your old age. All you lose is a son as king, and by that loss your daughter becomes queen. I can't make all the amends I'd like, so accept what kindness I can give. Your son Dorset, who wanders discontented and afraid in foreign lands, will quickly be called home by this fine marriage to high promotion and great dignity. The king who calls your beautiful daughter wife will call your Dorset brother. You'll be the mother of a king again, and all the ruins of these troubled times will be repaired with double riches of happiness. Why, we have many good days ahead! The tears you've shed will come back transformed into shining pearls, repaying their loan with interest of ten times double happiness. So go, my mother, go to your daughter. Make her shy youth bold with your experience. Prepare her ears to hear a suitor's story. Put the aspiring flame of golden sovereignty into her tender heart. Introduce the princess to the sweet silent hours of married joy. And when this arm of mine has punished the petty rebel, thick-headed Buckingham, I'll come crowned with victory garlands and lead your daughter to a conqueror's bed. I'll hand over my conquest to her, and she'll be the sole victor, Caesar's Caesar.

What were I best to say? her father's brother / Would be her lord? or shall I say her uncle? / Or he that slew her brothers and her uncles? / Under what title shall I woo for thee, / That God, the law, my honour, and her love / Can make seem pleasing to her tender years?

What would be best to say? That her father's brother wants to be her husband? Or should I say her uncle? Or the man who killed her brothers and her uncles? Under what title can I woo for you that God, the law, my honour and her love could make pleasing to her young years?
Infer fair England's peace by this alliance.
Point out that this marriage will bring peace to fair England.
Which she shall purchase with still-lasting war.
Which she'll pay for with never-ending war.
Tell her the king, that may command, entreats.
Tell her the King, who could command, begs.
That at her hands which the king's King forbids.
Begs for something from her that the King of kings forbids.
Say she shall be a high and mighty queen.
Tell her she'll be a high and mighty queen.
To wail the title, as her mother doth.
To mourn the title, as her mother does.
Say I will love her everlastingly.
Tell her I'll love her for ever.
But how long shall that title, "ever," last?
But how long will that word "ever" last?
Sweetly in force unto her fair life's end.
Sweetly in force until her fair life ends.
But how long fairly shall her sweet life last?
But how long will her sweet life fairly last?
As long as heaven and nature lengthens it.
As long as heaven and nature let it.
As long as hell and Richard likes of it.
As long as hell and Richard like it to.
Say I, her sovereign, am her subject low.
Tell her that I, her sovereign, am her humble subject.
But she, your subject, loathes such sovereignty.
But she, your subject, hates such sovereignty.
Be eloquent in my behalf to her.
Be eloquent to her on my behalf.
An honest tale speeds best being plainly told.
An honest story does best when it's told plainly.
Then plainly to her tell my loving tale.
Then tell her my loving story plainly.
Plain and not honest is too harsh a style.
Plain and dishonest is too harsh a style.
Your reasons are too shallow and too quick.
Your arguments are too shallow and too quick.
O, no, my reasons are too deep and dead;-- / Too deep and dead, poor infants, in their graves.
Oh no, my arguments are too deep and dead: too deep and dead, poor children, in their graves.
Harp not on that string, madam; that is past.
Don't harp on that string, madam. That's in the past.
Harp on it still shall I till heartstrings break.
I'll keep harping on it until my heartstrings break.
Now, by my George, my garter, and my crown,--
Now, by my George, my Garter and my crown...
Profan'd, dishonour'd, and the third usurp'd.
The first profaned, the second dishonoured, the third stolen.

By nothing; for this is no oath: / Thy George, profan'd, hath lost his lordly honour; / Thy garter, blemish'd, pawn'd his knightly virtue; / Thy crown, usurp'd, disgrac'd his kingly glory. / If something thou wouldst swear to be believ'd, / Swear then by something that thou hast not wrong'd.

By nothing, because that's no oath. Your George, profaned, has lost its lordly honour; your Garter, stained, has pawned its knightly virtue; your crown, stolen, has disgraced its kingly glory. If you want to swear something that will be believed, swear by something you haven't wronged.
It's full of your foul wrongs.

God's wrong is most of all. / If thou hadst fear'd to break an oath by Him, / The unity the king thy brother made / Had not been broken, nor my brother slain: / If thou hadst fear'd to break an oath by Him, / The imperial metal, circling now thy head, / Had grac'd the tender temples of my child; / And both the princes had been breathing here, / Which now, two tender bedfellows for dust, / Thy broken faith hath made a prey for worms. / What canst thou swear by now?

You've wronged God most of all. If you had been afraid to break an oath sworn by him, the union your brother the King made wouldn't have been broken, nor my brother killed. If you had been afraid to break an oath sworn by him, the royal metal now circling your head would have graced the tender temples of my child, and both princes would be alive here, who now, two tender bedfellows for the dust, your broken faith has made food for worms. What can you swear by now?

That thou hast wronged in the time o'erpast; / For I myself have many tears to wash / Hereafter time, for time past wronged by thee. / The children live whose fathers thou hast slaughter'd, / Ungovern'd youth, to wail it in their age; / The parents live whose children thou hast butcher'd, / Old barren plants, to wail it with their age. / Swear not by time to come: for that thou hast / Misus'd ere used, by times ill-us'd o'erpast.

You've wronged that in the time gone by, because I myself have many tears to wash the future with, for the past you've wronged. Children are alive whose fathers you slaughtered, young and without guidance, to weep for it in their old age. Parents are alive whose children you butchered, old barren plants, to weep for it in their old age. Don't swear by the future, because you've misused it before you've used it, by your misused past.

As I intend to prosper and repent! / So thrive I in my dangerous attempt / Of hostile arms! myself myself confound! / Heaven and fortune bar me happy hours! / Day, yield me not thy light; nor, night, thy rest! / Be opposite all planets of good luck / To my proceeding!--if, with pure heart's love, / Immaculate devotion, holy thoughts, / I tender not thy beauteous princely daughter! / In her consists my happiness and thine; / Without her, follows to myself and thee, / Herself, the land, and many a Christian soul, / Death, desolation, ruin, and decay: / It cannot be avoided but by this; / It will not be avoided but by this. / Therefore, dear mother,--I must call you so,-- / Be the attorney of my love to her: / Plead what I will be, not what I have been; / Not my deserts, but what I will deserve: / Urge the necessity and state of times, / And be not peevish found in great designs.

As I intend to prosper and repent, so may I succeed in my dangerous military venture! May I destroy myself! May heaven and fortune deny me happy hours! Day, don't give me your light, nor night your rest! May all the lucky planets oppose my actions, if I don't offer your beautiful princely daughter pure heartfelt love, spotless devotion and holy thoughts! My happiness and yours depend on her. Without her, death, desolation, ruin and decay will follow for me and you, for her, for the country and for many Christian souls. It can't be avoided except by this. It won't be avoided except by this. So, dear mother, I must call you that, be the advocate of my love to her. Plead what I will be, not what I have been; not what I deserve now, but what I will deserve. Stress the necessity and condition of the times, and don't be found childish in great plans.
Shall I be tempted of the devil thus?
Shall I be tempted by the devil like this?
Ay, if the devil tempt you to do good.
Yes, if the devil tempts you to do good.
Shall I forget myself to be myself?
Shall I forget who I am to be myself?
Ay, if your self's remembrance wrong yourself.
Yes, if remembering who you are harms you.
Yet thou didst kill my children.
But in your daughter's womb I bury them: / Where, in that nest of spicery, they shall breed / Selves of themselves, to your recomforture.
But I'll bury them in your daughter's womb, where in that sweet-scented nest they'll breed new selves of themselves, to comfort you.
Shall I go win my daughter to thy will?
Shall I go and win my daughter over to what you want?
And be a happy mother by the deed.
And be a happy mother by doing it.
I go.--Write to me very shortly, / And you shall understand from me her mind.
I'm going. Write to me very soon, and you'll hear from me what she thinks.
Bear her my true love's kiss; and so, farewell.
Take her my true love's kiss, and so, farewell.
Relenting fool, and shallow, changing woman!

Most mighty sovereign, on the western coast / Rideth a puissant navy; to the shore / Throng many doubtful hollow-hearted friends, / Unarm'd, and unresolv'd to beat them back: / 'Tis thought that Richmond is their admiral; / And there they hull, expecting but the aid / Of Buckingham to welcome them ashore.

Most mighty sovereign, a powerful fleet is riding off the west coast. Many doubtful, hollow-hearted friends crowd to the shore, unarmed and with no intention of beating them back. It's thought Richmond is their admiral, and they're lying at anchor there, only waiting for Buckingham's help to welcome them ashore.
Some light-foot friend post to the Duke of Norfolk:-- / Ratcliff, thyself,--or Catesby; where is he?
Some quick-footed friend ride to the Duke of Norfolk. Ratcliff, you, or Catesby. Where is he?
I will my lord, with all convenient haste.
I will, my lord, as fast as I can.
Ratcliff, come hither: post to Salisbury: / When thou com'st thither,-- / [To CATESBY] Dull, unmindful villain, / Why stay'st thou here, and go'st not to the duke?
Ratcliff, come here. Ride to Salisbury. When you get there... (To Catesby) Slow, careless villain, why are you still standing here instead of going to the Duke?
First, mighty liege, tell me your highness' pleasure, / What from your grace I shall deliver to him.
First, mighty lord, tell me your highness's wishes, what message I'm to give him from your grace.
O, true, good Catesby:--bid him levy straight / The greatest strength and power that he can make, / And meet me suddenly at Salisbury.
Oh, true, good Catesby. Tell him to raise at once the biggest army he can and meet me quickly at Salisbury.
What, may it please you, shall I do at Salisbury?
What do you want me to do at Salisbury, if you please?
Why, what wouldst thou do there before I go?
Why, what would you do there before I go?
Your highness told me I should post before.
Your highness told me to ride ahead.
My mind is chang'd.--Stanley, what news with you?
I've changed my mind. Stanley, what news do you have?
None good, my liege, to please you with the hearing; / Nor none so bad but well may be reported.
None good enough to please you to hear, my lord, and none so bad it can't be reported.
Hoyday, a riddle! neither good nor bad! / What need'st thou run so many miles about, / When thou mayest tell thy tale the nearest way? / Once more, what news?
Well, a riddle! Neither good nor bad! Why go so many miles round when you could tell your story the shortest way? Once more, what's the news?
There let him sink, and be the seas on him! / White-liver'd runagate, what doth he there?
Let him sink there, and the seas cover him! Cowardly runaway, what's he doing there?
I know not, mighty sovereign, but by guess.
I don't know, mighty sovereign, except by guessing.
Stirr'd up by Dorset, Buckingham, and Morton, / He makes for England here, to claim the crown.
Stirred up by Dorset, Buckingham and Morton, he's heading here to England to claim the crown.

Is the chair empty? is the sword unsway'd? / Is the king dead? the empire unpossess'd? / What heir of York is there alive but we? / And who is England's king but great York's heir? / Then tell me, what makes he upon the seas?

Is the throne empty? Is the sword of state unwielded? Is the King dead? Is the kingdom unowned? What heir of York is alive except me? And who is England's king except great York's heir? Then tell me, what's he doing at sea?
Unless for that, my liege, I cannot guess.
Unless for that, my lord, I can't guess.
Unless for that he comes to be your liege, / You cannot guess wherefore the Welshman comes. / Thou wilt revolt and fly to him, I fear.
Unless he's coming to be your lord, you can't guess why the Welshman is coming. You'll rebel and run to him, I'm afraid.
No, mighty leige; therefore mistrust me not.
No, mighty lord, so don't distrust me.
Where is thy power, then, to beat him back? / Where be thy tenants and thy followers? / Are they not now upon the western shore, / Safe-conducting the rebels from their ships?
Then where's your army to beat him back? Where are your tenants and followers? Aren't they on the west coast now, escorting the rebels safely off their ships?
No, my good lord, my friends are in the north.
No, my good lord, my friends are in the north.
Cold friends to me: what do they in the north, / When they should serve their sovereign in the west?
Cold friends to me. What are they doing in the north when they should be serving their king in the west?
They have not been commanded, mighty king: / Pleaseth your majesty to give me leave, / I'll muster up my friends, and meet your grace / Where and what time your majesty shall please.
They haven't been ordered to, mighty king. If your majesty gives me permission, I'll call up my friends and meet your grace wherever and whenever your majesty likes.
Ay, ay, thou wouldst be gone to join with Richmond; / But I'll not trust thee.
Yes, yes, you'd like to go off and join Richmond. But I won't trust you.
Most mighty sovereign, / You have no cause to hold my friendship doubtful: / I never was nor never will be false.
Most mighty sovereign, you have no reason to doubt my friendship. I never was and never will be false.
Go, then, and muster men. But leave behind / Your son, George Stanley: look your heart be firm, / Or else his head's assurance is but frail.
Go, then, and raise men. But leave your son George Stanley behind. Make sure your heart stays firm, or his head isn't very safe.
So deal with him as I prove true to you.
Treat him according to how loyal I prove to you.

My gracious sovereign, now in Devonshire, / As I by friends am well advertised, / Sir Edward Courtney, and the haughty prelate, / Bishop of Exeter, his elder brother, / With many more confederates, are in arms.
My gracious sovereign, my friends inform me that in Devonshire Sir Edward Courtney and the proud churchman the Bishop of Exeter, his elder brother, have taken up arms with many more allies.
In Kent, my liege, the Guilfords are in arms; / And every hour more competitors / Flock to the rebels, and their power grows strong.
In Kent, my lord, the Guildfords have taken up arms, and every hour more supporters flock to the rebels, and their army grows strong.
My lord, the army of great Buckingham,--
My lord, the army of great Buckingham...
Out on you, owls! Nothing but songs of death?
Away with you, owls! Nothing but songs of death?
There, take thou that till thou bring better news.
There, take that until you bring better news.
The news I have to tell your majesty / Is, that by sudden floods and fall of waters, / Buckingham's army is dispers'd and scatter'd; / And he himself wander'd away alone, / No man knows whither.
The news I have for your majesty is that sudden floods and rising waters have broken up and scattered Buckingham's army, and he himself has wandered off alone, nobody knows where.
I cry you mercy: / There is my purse to cure that blow of thine. / Hath any well-advised friend proclaim'd / Reward to him that brings the traitor in?
I beg your pardon. There's my purse to heal that blow I gave you. Has any sensible friend proclaimed a reward for whoever brings the traitor in?
Such proclamation hath been made, my liege.
That proclamation has been made, my lord.

Sir Thomas Lovel and Lord Marquis Dorset, / 'Tis said, my liege, in Yorkshire are in arms. / But this good comfort bring I to your highness,-- / The Britagne navy is dispers'd by tempest: / Richmond, in Dorsetshire, sent out a boat / Unto the shore, to ask those on the banks / If they were his assistants, yea or no; / Who answer'd him they came from Buckingham / Upon his party. He, mistrusting them, / Hois'd sail, and made his course again for Britagne.

It's said, my lord, that Sir Thomas Lovel and the Marquis of Dorset have taken up arms in Yorkshire. But I bring your highness this good comfort: the Breton fleet has been scattered by a storm. Off Dorset, Richmond sent a boat to the shore to ask the people on the banks whether they were his supporters or not. They answered that they came from Buckingham to join his side. He didn't trust them, raised sail and headed back to Brittany.
March on, march on, since we are up in arms; / If not to fight with foreign enemies, / Yet to beat down these rebels here at home.
March on, march on, since we're armed, if not to fight foreign enemies, then to crush these rebels here at home.
My liege, the Duke of Buckingham is taken,-- / That is the best news: that the Earl of Richmond / Is with a mighty power landed at Milford / Is colder tidings, yet they must be told.
My lord, the Duke of Buckingham has been captured. That's the good news. That the Earl of Richmond has landed at Milford with a powerful army is less welcome news, but it must be told.
Away towards Salisbury! while we reason here / A royal battle might be won and lost:-- / Some one take order Buckingham be brought / To Salisbury; the rest march on with me.
Off towards Salisbury! While we stand talking here, a royal battle could be won and lost. Someone give orders for Buckingham to be brought to Salisbury. The rest of you, march on with me.

Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me:-- / That in the sty of the most deadly boar / My son George Stanley is frank'd up in hold: / If I revolt, off goes young George's head; / The fear of that holds off my present aid. / So, get thee gone: commend me to thy lord; / Withal say that the queen hath heartily consented / He should espouse Elizabeth her daughter. / But tell me, where is princely Richmond now?

Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me: my son George Stanley is penned up in the sty of the deadly boar. If I rebel, off goes young George's head. Fear of that holds back my help for now. So go, give my regards to your lord, and tell him too that the Queen has heartily agreed that he should marry her daughter Elizabeth. But tell me, where is princely Richmond now?
At Pembroke, or at Ha'rford-west in Wales.
At Pembroke, or at Haverfordwest in Wales.
What men of name resort to him?
What men of rank are joining him?

Sir Walter Herbert, a renowned soldier; / Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley; / Oxford, redoubted Pembroke, Sir James Blunt, / And Rice ap Thomas, with a valiant crew; / And many other of great name and worth: / And towards London do they bend their power, / If by the way they be not fought withal.

Sir Walter Herbert, a famous soldier; Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley, Oxford, feared Pembroke, Sir James Blunt and Rhys ap Thomas with a brave band, and many others of great name and worth. They're heading their army towards London, unless they're attacked on the way.
Well, hie thee to thy lord; I kiss his hand; / My letter will resolve him of my mind. / Farewell.
Well, hurry to your lord. I kiss his hand. My letter will tell him my mind. Farewell.
Will not King Richard let me speak with him?
Won't King Richard let me speak with him?
No, my good lord; therefore be patient.
No, my good lord, so be patient.

Hastings, and Edward's children, Grey, and Rivers, / Holy King Henry, and thy fair son Edward, / Vaughan, and all that have miscarried / By underhand corrupted foul injustice,-- / If that your moody discontented souls / Do through the clouds behold this present hour, / Even for revenge mock my destruction!-- / This is All-Souls' day, fellow, is it not?

Hastings, and Edward's children, Grey and Rivers, holy King Henry and your fair son Edward, Vaughan, and all who have died through secret, corrupt, foul injustice: if your angry, unsatisfied souls are looking down through the clouds at this moment, mock my destruction to get your revenge! This is All Souls' Day, fellow, isn't it?

Why, then All-Souls' day is my body's doomsday. / This is the day which in King Edward's time / I wish'd might fall on me, when I was found / False to his children and his wife's allies; / This is the day wherein I wish'd to fall / By the false faith of him whom most I trusted; / This, this All-Souls' day to my fearful soul / Is the determin'd respite of my wrongs: / That high All-Seer which I dallied with / Hath turn'd my feigned prayer on my head / And given in earnest what I begg'd in jest. / Thus doth He force the swords of wicked men / To turn their own points in their masters' bosoms: / Thus Margaret's curse falls heavy on my neck,-- / "When he," quoth she, "shall split thy heart with sorrow, / Remember Margaret was a prophetess."-- / Come lead me, officers, to the block of shame; / Wrong hath but wrong, and blame the due of blame.

Why, then All Souls' Day is my body's doomsday. This is the day that I wished, in King Edward's time, would fall on me if I were found false to his children and his wife's family. This is the day on which I wished to fall through the treachery of the man I trusted most. This, this All Souls' Day is the appointed deadline for my fearful soul's wrongs. The all-seeing God on high whom I trifled with has turned my false prayer back on my head and given me in earnest what I asked for in jest. So he forces wicked men's swords to turn their points into their masters' chests. So Margaret's curse falls heavily on my neck: "When he splits your heart with sorrow," she said, "remember Margaret was a prophet." Come, officers, lead me to the block of shame. Wrong gets only wrong, and blame what blame deserves.

Fellows in arms, and my most loving friends, / Bruis'd underneath the yoke of tyranny, / Thus far into the bowels of the land / Have we march'd on without impediment; / And here receive we from our father Stanley / Lines of fair comfort and encouragement. / The wretched, bloody, and usurping boar / That spoil'd your summer fields and fruitful vines, / Swills your warm blood like wash, and makes his trough / In your embowell'd bosoms,--this foul swine / Lies now even in the centre of this isle, / Near to the town of Leicester, as we learn: / From Tamworth thither is but one day's march. / In God's name cheerly on, courageous friends, / To reap the harvest of perpetual peace / By this one bloody trial of sharp war.

Comrades in arms and my most loving friends, bruised under the yoke of tyranny, we have marched this far into the heart of the country without hindrance, and here we receive from my stepfather Stanley letters of real comfort and encouragement. The wretched, bloody, usurping boar who spoiled your summer fields and fruitful vines, swills your warm blood like pigswill and makes a trough of your ripped-open bodies: this foul swine now lies right in the middle of this island, near the town of Leicester, we hear. From Tamworth it's only one day's march. In God's name, on with good cheer, brave friends, to reap the harvest of lasting peace through this one bloody test of sharp war.
Every man's conscience is a thousand swords, / To fight against that bloody homicide.
Every man's conscience is worth a thousand swords against that bloody murderer.
I doubt not but his friends will turn to us.
I'm sure his friends will come over to us.
He hath no friends but what are friends for fear, / Which in his dearest need will fly from him.
He has no friends except those who are friends out of fear, and they'll run from him when he needs them most.
All for our vantage. Then in God's name, march: / True hope is swift, and flies with swallow's wings; / Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings.
All to our advantage. Then in God's name, march. True hope is swift and flies on swallow's wings. It makes kings into gods and lesser men into kings.
Here pitch our tents, even here in Bosworth field.-- / My Lord of Surrey, why look you so sad?
Pitch our tents here, right here in Bosworth Field. My lord of Surrey, why do you look so sad?
My heart is ten times lighter than my looks.
My heart is ten times lighter than my face.
Norfolk, we must have knocks; ha! must we not?
Norfolk, there'll be blows, won't there?
We must both give and take, my loving lord.
We must both give and take them, my loving lord.
Up With my tent! Here will I lie to-night;
Put up my tent! I'll sleep here tonight.
But where to-morrow? Well, all's one for that.-- / Who hath descried the number of the traitors?
But where tomorrow? Well, it's all the same. Who has found out the traitors' numbers?
Six or seven thousand is their utmost power.
Six or seven thousand at most.

Why, our battalia trebles that account: / Besides, the king's name is a tower of strength, / Which they upon the adverse faction want.-- / Up with the tent!--Come, noble gentlemen, / Let us survey the vantage of the ground;-- / Call for some men of sound direction:-- / Let's lack no discipline, make no delay; / For, lords, to-morrow is a busy day.

Why, our army is three times that. Besides, the King's name is a tower of strength, which the other side lacks. Put up the tent! Come, noble gentlemen, let's survey the advantages of the ground. Call for some men with good judgement. Let's not lack discipline or delay, because, lords, tomorrow is a busy day.

The weary sun hath made a golden set, / And by the bright tract of his fiery car / Gives token of a goodly day to-morrow. / Sir William Brandon, you shall bear my standard.-- / Give me some ink and paper in my tent: / I'll draw the form and model of our battle, / Limit each leader to his several charge, / And part in just proportion our small power.-- / My Lord of Oxford,--you, Sir William Brandon,-- / And you, Sir Walter Herbert,--stay with me.-- / The Earl of Pembroke keeps his regiment:-- / Good Captain Blunt, bear my good night to him, / And by the second hour in the morning / Desire the earl to see me in my tent: / Yet one thing more, good captain, do for me,-- / Where is Lord Stanley quarter'd, do you know?

The weary sun has set in gold, and the bright track of his fiery chariot promises a fine day tomorrow. Sir William Brandon, you'll carry my standard. Bring me ink and paper in my tent. I'll draw up the plan and formation of our battle, assign each commander his own unit and divide our small army fairly. My lord of Oxford, you, Sir William Brandon, and you, Sir Walter Herbert, stay with me. The Earl of Pembroke stays with his regiment. Good Captain Blunt, take him my good night, and ask the Earl to see me in my tent by two in the morning. One more thing, good captain, do for me: do you know where Lord Stanley is camped?
Unless I have mista'en his colours much,-- / Which well I am assur'd I have not done,-- / His regiment lies half a mile at least / South from the mighty power of the king.
Unless I've badly mistaken his banners, which I'm sure I haven't, his regiment is at least half a mile south of the King's mighty army.
If without peril it be possible, / Sweet Blunt, make some good means to speak with him / And give him from me this most needful note.
If it can be done without danger, sweet Blunt, find some good way to speak with him and give him this vital note from me.
Upon my life, my lord, I'll undertake it; / And so, God give you quiet rest to-night!
On my life, my lord, I'll do it. And so, God give you quiet rest tonight!
Good night, good Captain Blunt.--Come, gentlemen, / Let us consult upon to-morrow's business: / In to my tent; the air is raw and cold.
Good night, good Captain Blunt. Come, gentlemen, let's discuss tomorrow's business. Into my tent; the air is raw and cold.
It's supper-time, my lord; It's six o'clock.
It's supper time, my lord. It's six o'clock.
I will not sup to-night.-- / Give me some ink and paper.-- / What, is my beaver easier than it was? / And all my armour laid into my tent?
I won't have supper tonight. Give me some ink and paper. Well, does my visor move more easily than it did? And is all my armour laid out in my tent?
It is, my liege; and all things are in readiness.
It is, my lord, and everything is ready.
Good Norfolk, hie thee to thy charge; / Use careful watch, choose trusty sentinels.
Good Norfolk, hurry to your post. Keep a careful watch and choose reliable sentries.
Stir with the lark to-morrow, gentle Norfolk.
Get up with the lark tomorrow, gentle Norfolk.
I promise you I will, my lord.

Send out a pursuivant-at-arms / To Stanley's regiment; bid him bring his power / Before sunrising, lest his son George fall / Into the blind cave of eternal night.-- / Fill me a bowl of wine.--Give me a watch.-- / Saddle white Surrey for the field to-morrow.-- / Look that my staves be sound, and not too heavy.-- / Ratcliff,--

Send a herald to Stanley's regiment. Tell him to bring his army before sunrise, or his son George will fall into the blind cave of eternal night. Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a candle. Saddle white Surrey for the battle tomorrow. Make sure my lances are sound and not too heavy. Ratcliff...
Saw'st thou the melancholy Lord Northumberland?
Did you see the gloomy Lord Northumberland?
Thomas the Earl of Surrey and himself, / Much about cock-shut time, from troop to troop / Went through the army, cheering up the soldiers.
He and Thomas, Earl of Surrey, went through the army from troop to troop around twilight, cheering up the soldiers.
So, I am satisfied.--Give me a bowl of wine: / I have not that alacrity of spirit / Nor cheer of mind that I was wont to have. / Set it down.--Is ink and paper ready?
Good, I'm satisfied. Give me a bowl of wine. I don't have the eagerness of spirit or cheerfulness of mind I used to have. Put it down. Are the ink and paper ready?
Bid my guard watch; leave me. / Ratcliff, about the mid of night come to my tent / And help to arm me. Leave me, I say.
Tell my guard to keep watch. Leave me. Ratcliff, come to my tent around midnight and help me put on my armour. Leave me, I say.
Fortune and victory sit on thy helm!
May fortune and victory sit on your helmet!
All comfort that the dark night can afford / Be to thy person, noble father-in-law! / Tell me, how fares our loving mother?
All the comfort the dark night can give be with you, noble stepfather! Tell me, how is our loving mother?

I, by attorney, bless thee from thy mother, / Who prays continually for Richmond's good. / So much for that.--The silent hours steal on, / And flaky darkness breaks within the east. / In brief,--for so the season bids us be,-- / Prepare thy battle early in the morning, / And put thy fortune to the arbitrement / Of bloody strokes and mortal-staring war. / I, as I may,--that which I would I cannot,-- / With best advantage will deceive the time, / And aid thee in this doubtful stroke of arms: / But on thy side I may not be too forward, / Lest, being seen, thy brother, tender George, / Be executed in his father's sight. / Farewell: the leisure and the fearful time / Cuts off the ceremonious vows of love / And ample interchange of sweet discourse, / Which so-long-sunder'd friends should dwell upon: / God give us leisure for these rites of love! / Once more, adieu: be valiant, and speed well!

I bless you on your mother's behalf; she prays constantly for Richmond's good. So much for that. The silent hours are slipping by and the darkness is breaking up in the east. In short, because the time demands it, prepare your army early in the morning and put your fortune to the judgement of bloody blows and deadly war. I'll do what I can, though not what I'd like: I'll play for time as best I can and help you in this uncertain battle. But I can't be too openly on your side, or if I'm seen, your young half-brother George will be executed in front of his father. Farewell. The lack of time and the dangerous moment cut short the formal vows of love and long exchange of sweet conversation that friends parted so long should linger over. God give us time for these rites of love! Once more, goodbye. Be brave, and succeed!

Good lords, conduct him to his regiment: / I'll strive with troubled thoughts to take a nap, / Lest leaden slumber peise me down to-morrow, / When I should mount with wings of victory: / Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.

Good lords, escort him to his regiment. Despite my troubled thoughts I'll try to take a nap, so heavy sleepiness doesn't weigh me down tomorrow when I should rise on wings of victory. Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.

O Thou Whose captain I account myself, / Look on my forces with a gracious eye; / Put in their hands Thy bruising irons of wrath, / That they may crush down with a heavy fall / The usurping helmets of our adversaries! / Make us Thy ministers of chastisement, / That we may praise Thee in Thy victory! / To Thee I do commend my watchful soul / Ere I let fall the windows of mine eyes: / Sleeping and waking, O, defend me still!

You whose captain I consider myself, look on my army with a gracious eye. Put into their hands your crushing weapons of anger, so that they may smash down with a heavy blow the usurping helmets of our enemies! Make us your agents of punishment, so that we may praise you in your victory! To you I commend my watchful soul before I close the windows of my eyes. Sleeping and waking, oh, keep defending me!

[To KING RICHARD] Let me sit heavy on thy soul to-morrow! / Think how thou stabb'dst me in my prime of youth / At Tewksbury: despair, therefore, and die!-- / [To RICHMOND] Be cheerful, Richmond; for the wronged souls / Of butcher'd princes fight in thy behalf: / King Henry's issue, Richmond, comforts thee.

(To King Richard) Let me sit heavy on your soul tomorrow! Remember how you stabbed me in the prime of my youth at Tewkesbury. So despair and die! (To Richmond) Be cheerful, Richmond, because the wronged souls of butchered princes fight for you. King Henry's son, Richmond, comforts you.

[To KING RICHARD] When I was mortal, my anointed body / By thee was punched full of deadly holes: / Think on the Tower and me: despair, and die,-- / Harry the Sixth bids thee despair and die.-- / [To RICHMOND] Virtuous and holy, be thou conqueror! / Harry, that prophesied thou shouldst be king, / Doth comfort thee in thy sleep: live, and flourish!

(To King Richard) When I was alive, you punched my anointed body full of deadly holes. Think of the Tower and me. Despair and die! Henry VI tells you to despair and die. (To Richmond) Virtuous and holy one, be the conqueror! Henry, who prophesied you would be king, comforts you in your sleep. Live and flourish!

[To KING RICHARD] Let me sit heavy in thy soul to-morrow! / I that was wash'd to death with fulsome wine, / Poor Clarence, by thy guile betray'd to death! / To-morrow in the battle think on me, / And fall thy edgeless sword: despair, and die!-- / [To RICHMOND] Thou offspring of the house of Lancaster, / The wronged heirs of York do pray for thee: / Good angels guard thy battle! live, and flourish!

(To King Richard) Let me sit heavy on your soul tomorrow! I, who was washed to death in sickly wine, poor Clarence, betrayed to death by your trickery! Tomorrow in the battle think of me, and drop your blunted sword. Despair and die! (To Richmond) You descendant of the house of Lancaster, the wronged heirs of York pray for you. Good angels guard your army! Live and flourish!
[To KING RICHARD] Let me sit heavy in thy soul to-morrow, / Rivers that died at Pomfret! despair and die!
(To King Richard) Let me sit heavy on your soul tomorrow, Rivers, who died at Pomfret! Despair and die!
[To KING RICHARD] Think upon Grey, and let thy soul despair!
(To King Richard) Think of Grey, and let your soul despair!
[To KING RICHARD] Think upon Vaughan, and, with guilty fear, / Let fall thy lance: despair and die!--
(To King Richard) Think of Vaughan, and in guilty fear drop your lance. Despair and die!
Ghosts Of Rivers, Grey And Vaughan
[To RICHMOND] Awake, and think our wrongs in Richard's bosom / Will conquer him!--awake, and win the day!
(To Richmond) Wake up, and know that our wrongs lodged in Richard's heart will defeat him! Wake up and win the day!

[To KING RICHARD] Bloody and guilty, guiltily awake, / And in a bloody battle end thy days! / Think on Lord Hastings: despair and die!-- / [To RICHMOND] Quiet untroubled soul, awake, awake! / Arm, fight, and conquer, for fair England's sake!

(To King Richard) Bloody and guilty, wake up in guilt and end your days in a bloody battle! Think of Lord Hastings. Despair and die! (To Richmond) Quiet, untroubled soul, wake up, wake up! Arm, fight and conquer for fair England's sake!

[To KING RICHARD] Dream on thy cousins smothered in the Tower: / Let us be lead within thy bosom, Richard, / And weigh thee down to ruin, shame, and death! / Thy nephews' souls bid thee despair and die!-- / [To RICHMOND] Sleep, Richmond, sleep in peace, and wake in joy; / Good angels guard thee from the boar's annoy! / Live, and beget a happy race of kings! / Edward's unhappy sons do bid thee flourish.

(To King Richard) Dream of your nephews smothered in the Tower. Let us be lead inside your chest, Richard, and weigh you down to ruin, shame and death! Your nephews' souls tell you to despair and die! (To Richmond) Sleep, Richmond, sleep in peace and wake in joy. Good angels guard you from the boar's harm! Live and father a happy line of kings! Edward's unhappy sons wish you well.

[To KING RICHARD] Richard, thy wife, that wretched Anne thy wife, / That never slept a quiet hour with thee, / Now fills thy sleep with perturbations: / To-morrow in the battle think on me, / And fall thy edgeless sword: despair and die!-- / [To RICHMOND] Thou quiet soul, sleep thou a quiet sleep; / Dream of success and happy victory: / Thy adversary's wife doth pray for thee.

(To King Richard) Richard, your wife, that wretched Anne your wife, who never slept a quiet hour with you, now fills your sleep with disturbances. Tomorrow in the battle think of me, and drop your blunted sword. Despair and die! (To Richmond) You quiet soul, sleep a quiet sleep. Dream of success and happy victory. Your enemy's wife prays for you.

[To KING RICHARD] The first was I that help'd thee to the crown; / The last was I that felt thy tyranny: / O, in the battle think on Buckingham, / And die in terror of thy guiltiness! / Dream on, dream on of bloody deeds and death: / Fainting, despair; despairing, yield thy breath!-- / [To RICHMOND] I died for hope ere I could lend thee aid: / But cheer thy heart and be thou not dismay'd: / God and good angels fight on Richmond's side; / And Richard falls in height of all his pride.

(To King Richard) I was the first to help you to the crown, and the last to feel your tyranny. In the battle, think of Buckingham and die in terror of your guilt! Dream on, dream on, of bloody deeds and death. Fainting, despair; despairing, give up your breath! (To Richmond) I died hoping to help you before I could. But cheer up and don't be dismayed. God and good angels fight on Richmond's side, and Richard will fall at the height of his pride.

Give me another horse,--bind up my wounds,-- / Have mercy, Jesu!--Soft! I did but dream.-- / O coward conscience, how dost thou afflict me!-- / The lights burn blue.--It is now dead midnight. / Cold fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh. / What, do I fear myself? there's none else by: / Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I. / Is there a murderer here? No;--yes, I am: / Then fly. What, from myself? Great reason why,-- / Lest I revenge. What,--myself upon myself! / Alack, I love myself. Wherefore? for any good / That I myself have done unto myself? / O, no! alas, I rather hate myself / For hateful deeds committed by myself! / I am a villain: yet I lie, I am not. / Fool, of thyself speak well:--fool, do not flatter. / My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, / And every tongue brings in a several tale, / And every tale condemns me for a villain. / Perjury, perjury, in the high'st degree; / Murder, stern murder, in the dir'st degree; / All several sins, all us'd in each degree, / Throng to the bar, crying all "Guilty! guilty!" / I shall despair. There is no creature loves me; / And if I die no soul will pity me: / And wherefore should they,--since that I myself / Find in myself no pity to myself? / Methought the souls of all that I had murder'd / Came to my tent; and every one did threat / To-morrow's vengeance on the head of Richard.

Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds! Have mercy, Jesus! Wait, I was only dreaming. Oh, cowardly conscience, how you torment me! The candles are burning blue. It's dead midnight. Cold drops of fear stand on my trembling skin. What, am I afraid of myself? There's no one else here. Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am. Then run. What, from myself? A good reason: in case I take revenge. What, on myself? Alas, I love myself. Why? For any good I have done myself? Oh no, alas, I'd rather hate myself for hateful deeds I've committed myself. I'm a villain. But I'm lying, I'm not. Fool, speak well of yourself. Fool, don't flatter. My conscience has a thousand separate tongues, and every tongue tells a separate story, and every story condemns me as a villain. Perjury, perjury of the worst kind; murder, cruel murder of the most dreadful kind; all kinds of sins, each committed to the full, crowd into the courtroom, all crying "Guilty! Guilty!" I'll despair. No creature loves me, and if I die no soul will pity me. And why should they, since I myself find no pity in myself for myself? I dreamed the souls of everyone I had murdered came to my tent, and every one of them threatened tomorrow's vengeance on Richard's head.
Ratcliff, my lord; 'tis I. The early village-cock / Hath twice done salutation to the morn; / Your friends are up, and buckle on their armour.
Ratcliff, my lord, it's me. The early village cock has crowed twice to greet the morning. Your friends are up and buckling on their armour.
O Ratcliff, I have dream'd a fearful dream!-- / What think'st thou,--will our friends prove all true?
Oh Ratcliff, I've had a terrible dream! What do you think, will all our friends prove loyal?
O Ratcliff, I fear, I fear,--
Oh Ratcliff, I'm afraid, I'm afraid...
Nay, good my lord, be not afraid of shadows.
No, my good lord, don't be afraid of shadows.

By the apostle Paul, shadows to-night / Have stuck more terror to the soul of Richard / Than can the substance of ten thousand soldiers / Armed in proof and led by shallow Richmond. / It is not yet near day. Come, go with me; / Under our tents I'll play the eaves-dropper, / To see if any mean to shrink from me.

By the apostle Paul, shadows tonight have struck more terror into Richard's soul than ten thousand real soldiers could, in tested armour and led by shallow Richmond. It isn't near daybreak yet. Come with me. I'll eavesdrop outside the tents to see if anyone means to desert me.
Cry mercy, lords and watchful gentlemen, / That you have ta'en a tardy sluggard here.
I beg your pardon, lords and watchful gentlemen, for catching a late sleepyhead here.
How have you slept, my lord?
How did you sleep, my lord?

The sweetest sleep and fairest-boding dreams / That ever enter'd in a drowsy head / Have I since your departure had, my lords. / Methought their souls whose bodies Richard murder'd / Came to my tent and cried on victory: / I promise you, my heart is very jocund / In the remembrance of so fair a dream. / How far into the morning is it, lords?

I've had the sweetest sleep and most hopeful dreams that ever entered a drowsy head since you left, my lords. I dreamed the souls of those whose bodies Richard murdered came to my tent and cried "Victory!" I promise you, my heart is very cheerful remembering such a good dream. How far into the morning is it, lords?
Why, then 'tis time to arm and give direction.--
Why, then it's time to arm and give orders.

More than I have said, loving countrymen, / The leisure and enforcement of the time / Forbids to dwell on: yet remember this,-- / God and our good cause fight upon our side; / The prayers of holy saints and wronged souls, / Like high-rear'd bulwarks, stand before our faces; / Richard except, those whom we fight against / Had rather have us win than him they follow: / For what is he they follow? truly, gentlemen, / A bloody tyrant and a homicide; / One rais'd in blood, and one in blood establish'd; / One that made means to come by what he hath, / And slaughter'd those that were the means to help him; / A base foul stone, made precious by the foil / Of England's chair, where he is falsely set; / One that hath ever been God's enemy. / Then, if you fight against God's enemy, / God will, in justice, ward you as His soldiers; / If you do sweat to put a tyrant down, / You sleep in peace, the tyrant being slain; / If you do fight against your country's foes, / Your country's fat shall pay your pains the hire; / If you do fight in safeguard of your wives, / Your wives shall welcome home the conquerors; / If you do free your children from the sword, / Your children's children quit it in your age. / Then, in the name of God and all these rights, / Advance your standards, draw your willing swords. / For me, the ransom of my bold attempt / Shall be this cold corpse on the earth's cold face; / But if I thrive, the gain of my attempt / The least of you shall share his part thereof. / Sound drums and trumpets boldly and cheerfully; / God and Saint George! Richmond and victory!

The lack of time and the pressure of the moment won't let me dwell on more than I've said, loving countrymen. But remember this: God and our good cause fight on our side. The prayers of holy saints and wronged souls stand before us like high fortifications. Except for Richard, the men we fight against would rather we won than the man they follow. For who is it they follow? Truly, gentlemen, a bloody tyrant and a murderer; a man raised up in blood and established in blood; a man who schemed to get what he has and slaughtered those who helped him get it; a cheap, dirty stone made to look precious by its setting in England's throne, where he sits falsely; a man who has always been God's enemy. So if you fight against God's enemy, God will justly protect you as his soldiers. If you sweat to bring down a tyrant, you'll sleep in peace when the tyrant is dead. If you fight against your country's enemies, your country's wealth will pay you for your pains. If you fight to protect your wives, your wives will welcome you home as conquerors. If you free your children from the sword, your children's children will repay you in your old age. So in the name of God and all these rights, raise your banners and draw your willing swords. As for me, the price of my bold attempt, if I fail, will be this body lying cold on the earth's cold face. But if I succeed, the least of you will share in the gain. Sound the drums and trumpets boldly and cheerfully. God and Saint George! Richmond and victory!
What said Northumberland as touching Richmond?
What did Northumberland say about Richmond?
That he was never trained up in arms.
That he was never trained as a soldier.
He said the truth; and what said Surrey then?
He told the truth. And what did Surrey say?
He smil'd, and said, "the better for our purpose."
He smiled and said, "So much the better for us."
He was in the right; and so indeed it is.
He was right, and so it is.
Tell the clock there.--Give me a calendar.-- / Who saw the sun to-day?
Count the strokes. Give me an almanac. Who has seen the sun today?
Then he disdains to shine; for by the book / He should have brav'd the east an hour ago: / A black day will it be to somebody.-- / Ratcliff,--
Then it refuses to shine, because by the book it should have lit up the east an hour ago. It will be a black day for somebody. Ratcliff...

The sun will not be seen to-day; / The sky doth frown and lower upon our army. / I would these dewy tears were from the ground. / Not shine to-day! Why, what is that to me / More than to Richmond? for the selfsame heaven / That frowns on me looks sadly upon him.

The sun won't be seen today. The sky frowns and scowls on our army. I wish these dewy tears were gone from the ground. Won't shine today! Why, what's that to me more than to Richmond? The same heaven that frowns on me looks gloomily on him too.
Arm, arm, my lord; the foe vaunts in the field.
Arm, arm, my lord! The enemy is parading on the field.

Come, bustle, bustle; caparison my horse;-- / Call up Lord Stanley, bid him bring his power: / I will lead forth my soldiers to the plain, / And thus my battle shall be ordered:-- / My foreward shall be drawn out all in length, / Consisting equally of horse and foot; / Our archers shall be placed in the midst: / John Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Earl of Surrey, / Shall have the leading of this foot and horse. / They thus directed, we will follow / In the main battle; whose puissance on either side / Shall be well winged with our chiefest horse. / This, and Saint George to boot!--What think'st thou, / Norfolk?

Come, hurry, hurry. Put the armour on my horse. Call Lord Stanley and tell him to bring his army. I'll lead my soldiers out on to the plain, and this is how my battle will be arranged. My vanguard will be drawn out in a long line, made up equally of cavalry and infantry, with our archers in the middle. John, Duke of Norfolk, and Thomas, Earl of Surrey, will command these foot and horse. Once they're positioned, we'll follow with the main army, whose strength will be protected on both flanks by our best cavalry. This, and Saint George as well! What do you think, Norfolk?
A good direction, warlike sovereign.-- / This found I on my tent this morning.
A good plan, warlike sovereign. I found this on my tent this morning.

[Reads] "Jockey of Norfolk, be not too bold, / For Dickon thy master is bought and sold." / A thing devised by the enemy.-- / Go, gentlemen, every man unto his charge: / Let not our babbling dreams affright our souls; / Conscience is but a word that cowards use, / Devis'd at first to keep the strong in awe: / Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law. / March on, join bravely, let us to't pell-mell; / If not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.-- / What shall I say more than I have inferr'd? / Remember whom you are to cope withal;-- / A sort of vagabonds, rascals, and runaways, / A scum of Britagnes, and base lackey peasants, / Whom their o'er-cloyed country vomits forth / To desperate adventures and assur'd destruction. / You sleeping safe, they bring to you unrest; / You having lands, and bless'd with beauteous wives, / They would restrain the one, distain the other. / And who doth lead them but a paltry fellow, / Long kept in Britagne at our mother's cost? / A milk-sop, one that never in his life / Felt so much cold as over shoes in snow? / Let's whip these stragglers o'er the seas again; / Lash hence these over-weening rags of France, / These famish'd beggars, weary of their lives; / Who, but for dreaming on this fond exploit, / For want of means, poor rats, had hang'd themselves: / If we be conquered, let men conquer us, / And not these bastard Britagnes, whom our fathers / Have in their own land beaten, bobb'd, and thump'd, / And, on record, left them the heirs of shame. / Shall these enjoy our lands? lie with our wives, / Ravish our daughters?--Hark! I hear their drum.

(Reads) "Jockey of Norfolk, don't be too bold, because Dickon your master is bought and sold." A trick devised by the enemy. Go, gentlemen, every man to his post. Don't let our babbling dreams frighten our souls. Conscience is only a word cowards use, invented in the first place to keep the strong in awe. Let our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law. March on, charge bravely, let's get to it pell-mell, if not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell. What more can I say than I've already said? Remember who you're dealing with: a bunch of vagabonds, rascals and runaways, the scum of Brittany and low-born servant peasants, whom their overfed country vomits out on desperate adventures and certain destruction. You sleep safely; they bring you unrest. You have lands and are blessed with beautiful wives; they want to seize the one and defile the other. And who leads them but a worthless fellow kept for years in Brittany at our mother's expense? A milksop, who never in his life felt colder than snow over his shoes? Let's whip these stragglers back over the sea. Lash away these arrogant French rags, these starving beggars tired of their lives, who, if they hadn't been dreaming of this foolish exploit, would have hanged themselves for lack of money, poor rats. If we're conquered, let men conquer us, not these bastard Bretons, whom our fathers beat, battered and thumped in their own land and left, on record, the heirs of shame. Shall these men enjoy our lands, sleep with our wives, rape our daughters? Listen! I hear their drum.
Fight, gentlemen of England! fight, bold yeomen! / Draw, archers, draw your arrows to the head! / Spur your proud horses hard, and ride in blood; / Amaze the welkin with your broken staves!
Fight, gentlemen of England! Fight, bold yeomen! Draw, archers, draw your arrows back to the head! Spur your proud horses hard and ride through blood. Astonish the sky with your splintered lances!
What says Lord Stanley? will he bring his power?
What does Lord Stanley say? Will he bring his army?
My lord, he doth deny to come.
My lord, he refuses to come.
Off with his son George's head!
Off with his son George's head!
My lord, the enemy is pass'd the marsh: / After the battle let George Stanley die.
My lord, the enemy is past the marsh. Let George Stanley die after the battle.

A thousand hearts are great within my bosom: / Advance our standards, set upon our foes; / Our ancient word of courage, fair Saint George, / Inspire us with the spleen of fiery dragons! / Upon them! Victory sits on our helms.

A thousand hearts swell in my chest. Raise our banners and charge our enemies! May our ancient battle cry, fair Saint George, fill us with the fury of fiery dragons! At them! Victory sits on our helmets.

Rescue, my Lord of Norfolk, rescue, rescue! / The king enacts more wonders than a man, / Daring an opposite to every danger: / His horse is slain, and all on foot he fights, / Seeking for Richmond in the throat of death. / Rescue, fair lord, or else the day is lost!

Help, my lord of Norfolk, help, help! The King is doing more wonders than a man could, facing every danger. His horse is killed, and he's fighting on foot, looking for Richmond in the jaws of death. Help, fair lord, or the day is lost!
A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
Withdraw, my lord! I'll help you to a horse.
Withdraw, my lord! I'll help you find a horse.

Slave, I have set my life upon a cast, / And I will stand the hazard of the die: / I think there be six Richmonds in the field: / Five have I slain to-day instead of him.-- / A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!

Slave, I've staked my life on one throw, and I'll take the chance of the dice. I think there are six Richmonds on the field. I've killed five today instead of him. A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!
God and your arms be prais'd, victorious friends; / The day is ours, the bloody dog is dead.
God and your weapons be praised, victorious friends. The day is ours; the bloody dog is dead.

Courageous Richmond, well hast thou acquit thee! / Lo, here, this long-usurped royalty / From the dead temples of this bloody wretch / Have I pluck'd off, to grace thy brows withal. / Wear it, enjoy it, and make much of it.

Brave Richmond, you've done well! Look, here is the royal crown, usurped so long, which I have pulled from the dead head of this bloody wretch to decorate your brows. Wear it, enjoy it and make the most of it.
Great God of heaven, say Amen to all!-- / But, tell me is young George Stanley living?
Great God of heaven, say amen to all of it! But tell me, is young George Stanley alive?
He is, my lord, and safe in Leicester town, / Whither, if it please you, we may now withdraw us.
He is, my lord, and safe in the town of Leicester, where, if you please, we can now go.
What men of name are slain on either side?
What men of rank have been killed on either side?
John Duke of Norfolk, Walter Lord Ferrers, / Sir Robert Brakenbury, and Sir William Brandon.
John, Duke of Norfolk; Walter, Lord Ferrers; Sir Robert Brakenbury and Sir William Brandon.

Inter their bodies as becomes their births: / Proclaim a pardon to the soldiers fled / That in submission will return to us: / And then, as we have ta'en the sacrament, / We will unite the white rose and the red:-- / Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction, / That long have frown'd upon their emnity! / What traitor hears me, and says not Amen? / England hath long been mad, and scarr'd herself; / The brother blindly shed the brother's blood, / The father rashly slaughter'd his own son, / The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire: / All this divided York and Lancaster, / Divided in their dire division,-- / O, now let Richmond and Elizabeth, / The true succeeders of each royal house, / By God's fair ordinance conjoin together! / And let their heirs,--God, if Thy will be so,-- / Enrich the time to come with smooth'd-fac'd peace, / With smiling plenty, and fair prosperous days! / Abate the edge of traitors, gracious Lord, / That would reduce these bloody days again, / And make poor England weep in streams of blood! / Let them not live to taste this land's increase / That would with treason wound this fair land's peace! / Now civil wounds are stopp'd, peace lives again: / That she may long live here, God say Amen!

Bury their bodies as suits their rank. Proclaim a pardon for the soldiers who fled, if they'll submit and come back to us. And then, as we have sworn on the sacrament, we'll unite the white rose and the red. May heaven, which has long frowned on their hostility, smile on this fair union! What traitor hears me and doesn't say amen? England has long been mad and scarred herself. The brother blindly shed his brother's blood, the father rashly slaughtered his own son, the son was forced to butcher his father. All this divided York and Lancaster, split apart in their terrible division. Oh, now let Richmond and Elizabeth, the true heirs of each royal house, be joined together by God's fair decree! And let their heirs, God, if it is your will, enrich the future with smooth-faced peace, smiling plenty and fair, prosperous days! Blunt the swords of traitors, gracious Lord, who would bring these bloody days back and make poor England weep streams of blood! Let them not live to enjoy this country's harvest who would wound this fair land's peace with treason! Now the wounds of civil war are healed and peace lives again. That she may live here long, God say amen!
